fields.title: Portraits of Courage – C. T. Studd
fields.subtitle: A Cricketer for England, a Fortune Given Away, and the Road to the Heart of Africa
fields.description: A Christian biography of C. T. Studd (1860–1931), the Eton and Cambridge cricketer who played in the 1882 Oval Test that gave the world “the Ashes,” sailed for China with the Cambridge Seven, gave away his inheritance, and at fifty-two went to the north-eastern Belgian Congo, where he founded the mission that became WEC International and died at Ibambi. Built on the public record and checked against modern reference works, it tells the whole story honestly, from the courage and the joy to the quarrels, the morphine, the long separation from his wife and the split of 1931, and keeps the Chinese and Congolese Christians who built the churches in view. All Scripture from the public-domain ASV (1901).

qa.question: What is this biography of C. T. Studd about?
qa.answer: It is a Christian biography of Charles Thomas Studd (1860–1931). It follows him from a wealthy family home and the cricket fields of Eton, Cambridge and the Oval, through his conversion and restoration, the Cambridge Seven of 1885, the gift of his inheritance, nine years in Shanxi with his wife Priscilla, America and India, to the Heart of Africa Mission he founded in 1913 and his death at Ibambi, in the Belgian Congo, in July 1931.

qa.question: Who was C. T. Studd?
qa.answer: He was an England Test cricketer who became a missionary with the China Inland Mission as one of the Cambridge Seven, gave away a fortune reported at £25,000 to £29,000, served as a pastor at Ootacamund in India, and at the age of fifty-two went to the north-eastern Congo. The mission he founded there became the Worldwide Evangelisation Crusade, now WEC International, and the Congolese church that grew from it, CECCA 16, counts its members and adherents in the hundreds of thousands.

qa.question: What part did he play in the birth of the Ashes?
qa.answer: He played for England in the only Test of the 1882 Australian tour, at the Oval on 28–29 August. He was bowled by Spofforth for 0 in the first innings and was left not out, without facing a ball, when the last wicket fell and Australia won by seven runs. The mock obituary of English cricket that followed gave the series its name, and that winter he toured Australia with Ivo Bligh’s team, which went to win the Ashes back.

qa.question: Did Studd write “Only one life, ’twill soon be past”?
qa.answer: Probably not. He loved the couplet and is recorded as quoting it to his grandchildren in a farewell letter in 1931, but the longer poem printed under his name says its author first heard the couplet from someone else, and no evidence has been found that he wrote them. The book also notes that the saying traditionally attributed to him, “If Jesus Christ be God and died for me, then no sacrifice can be too great,” and the “rescue shop” rhyme credited to him have not been traced to anything he published.

qa.question: How does the book handle the hard parts of his later life?
qa.answer: Plainly and fairly. It tells of his conflicts with colleagues, his dismissal of his son-in-law Alfred Buxton, the offence caused by his 1928 D.C.D. booklet, his regular use of morphine for pain in his last years, the twelve years of separation from his wife Priscilla, and the crisis of 1931 in which the home committee tried to remove him and the mission split. It neither hides these things nor lets them erase the courage and fruit of his life.

qa.question: How does the book treat the Chinese and Congolese people in the story?
qa.answer: As agents, not as scenery. It describes the Chinese Christians who led the churches of Shanxi, the colonial setting of the Congo after the Free State, the burdens of tax and forced labour, and the Congolese evangelists who carried the gospel through the Uele and Ituri forests in their own languages and at their own cost. Where the names of Congolese believers have not survived in the sources, the book says so rather than inventing them.

qa.question: How is Scripture used in the book?
qa.answer: Each chapter opens with a passage from the American Standard Version (1901) that carries its theme, from “I count all things to be loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” to “Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone.” Further passages are woven through the story, including Paul’s warning that giving everything without love profits nothing. Every quotation was checked against the ASV text.

qa.question: Where should a reader begin?
qa.answer: At the beginning. The preface and introduction explain the sources and which famous stories and sayings can be trusted; the chapters then follow his life in order, from Tedworth and the Oval to China, India and the Congo. Appendix A gathers lessons from his life, Appendix B is a study guide for groups, Appendix C a chronology, and Appendix D a note on sources and method.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
“Yea verily, and I count all things to be loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but refuse, that I may gain Christ”

— Philippians 3:8, ASV

The earlier volumes of this series told of a Chinese church leader who died in a Communist labour camp, an American who prayed his way through the villages of the Punjab, a Dutch watchmaker who hid Jews behind a false wall, a Scottish mill girl who went alone up the rivers of Calabar, an African bishop who had once been sold as a slave, an Indian widow who built a home for thousands of outcast women, an Oxford don who was found by God against his will, a young widow who carried her daughter into the Ecuadorian forest to live among the men who had killed her husband, an Irish missionary who made a home at Dohnavur, in South India, for children rescued from temple service, and a Scottish mill boy who crossed Africa and spent his last years exposing the East African slave trade. This eleventh volume tells the story of a man who began with almost every advantage his country could give, and spent the rest of his life giving the advantages away.

Charles Thomas Studd was born in 1860 into a family made rich by indigo grown in India. He was educated at Eton and Cambridge. Before he was twenty-two he was playing cricket for England, in the match at the Oval in August 1882 that gave the world “the Ashes.” Three years later he sailed for China as one of seven young men from Cambridge whose departure made headlines across Britain. Within two more years he had given away almost the whole of his inheritance. He worked in China for about nine years, served as a pastor in the hills of southern India for six, and then, past fifty, ill, and against the advice of doctors, went to the north-east of what was then the Belgian Congo. He spent most of his last eighteen years there, and he died there in July 1931. The mission he founded for that one corner of Africa grew into WEC International, which still sends workers around the world, and the churches that grew from it in Congo are still there.

Why Courage?

Studd’s courage is not hard to find. It took courage to stand on platforms in 1885 and tell rooms full of undergraduates that he was leaving the cricket field for inland China. It took a different kind of courage to write cheques for thousands of pounds before he even knew how much he was going to inherit. It took courage, of a kind that many of his friends thought simply foolish, to set out for the centre of Africa at fifty-two with asthma, a history of broken health, and a wife who at first did not want him to go.

But this book will suggest that his life also asks a harder question about courage. Studd believed with his whole heart that if Christ had died for him, nothing he could give back would be too much. He lived by that conviction more completely than almost anyone of his generation. He also expected others to live by it at his pace and in his manner, and when they did not, he could be harsh, suspicious and unjust. The same fierceness that carried the gospel into the Ituri forest drove away colleagues, wounded his own family, and brought the mission he had founded close to breaking in the year he died. Courage of his kind is not always the same thing as love, and the New Testament says so plainly. “If I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but have not love, it profiteth me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3, ASV). Studd gave his goods and gave his body. The question his life puts to its readers is what it means to do that with love, and what it costs when love grows thin.

How This Book Is Written

Like the earlier volumes, this book tries to be honest about its sources, and the reader deserves to know what they are.

The standard life of Studd is C. T. Studd: Cricketer and Pioneer by his son-in-law Norman Grubb, first published in 1933. It is a vivid book, and it is the source of many of the stories that are told about him. It is also still in copyright, and so this book has not quoted it, or followed its wording, at any point. Where a fact comes chiefly from Grubb and from nowhere else, this book says so.

Some older material is in the public domain and has been used. It includes the record of the Cambridge Seven that Benjamin Broomhall of the China Inland Mission published in 1886 and enlarged as The Evangelisation of the World in 1887; the published scores and records of Studd’s cricket; and Studd’s own tracts and rhymes published in his lifetime, such as The Chocolate Soldier, Quaint Rhymes for the Battlefield (1914) and Christ’s Etceteras (1915). Studd is quoted sparingly, partly because his voice was so emphatic that a little of it goes a long way, and partly because some of the sayings most often attributed to him cannot be traced to anything he published. The introduction explains which ones.

The book has also drawn on modern reference works and studies, including the entries on Studd and his colleagues in the Dictionary of African Christian Biography, the diary of an American who worked beside him in Congo in 1914, and the histories published by WEC International and by the Congolese church that grew from his mission. Those works are used for facts and judgements, not quoted at length.

Three things need particular care. The first is that Studd’s story is told almost entirely by people who loved him or worked with him, and the African side of it has been recorded far less. This book tries to keep Congolese men and women in view as people who chose, argued, preached, carried, built and suffered, and not as scenery for a European hero. Where their names have not survived in the sources available, it does not invent them. The second is that Studd went to Congo only five years after the end of the Congo Free State, whose regime of forced labour had killed and maimed on a terrible scale, and he worked under Belgian colonial rule. The story cannot be told as if that did not matter. The third is that Studd’s last years included illness, morphine, broken friendships, a strained marriage, and a damaging quarrel with the people who ran his mission at home. Those things are told here as plainly and as fairly as the evidence allows, without either hiding them or making them the whole story.

Scripture in This Book

As in the earlier volumes, all Scripture quotations are from the American Standard Version of 1901, which is in the public domain. Each chapter opens with a passage that carries its theme, and further passages are woven through the story. Where Studd himself quoted the Bible, he used the King James Version, and his words are given as he wrote them.

The verse at the head of this preface is the one that best explains him. Paul had been, by the standards of his world, a man with every advantage, and he wrote that he counted all of it “but refuse, that I may gain Christ.” Studd read those words as a plain instruction and carried them out more literally than most Christians ever try to. He would not have wanted his life told as a success story, and it was not one, in any simple sense. It was a life spent, sometimes wisely and sometimes not, by a man who had decided early that Christ was worth everything. This book is an attempt to tell that life truthfully, so that readers can see both what it was worth and what it cost.

fields.title: Introduction: The Cricketer, the Crusader, and the Record
fields.body_html:
“He that pleadeth his cause first seemeth just; But his neighbor cometh and searcheth him out.”

— Proverbs 18:17, ASV

A Life Told Many Times

Few missionary lives have been retold as often as C. T. Studd’s, and few have been retold with so many exclamation marks. He is the Eton and Cambridge cricketer who gave up the game for China, the young man who gave away a fortune, the old man who went to the heart of Africa when the doctors said he would die, the man traditionally credited with the rhyme about running “a rescue shop within a yard of hell,” and the man whose last word, it is said, was “Hallelujah.” Popular books for adults and children have told the story in nearly every decade since his death. A good deal of it is true.

A legend is a kind of compliment, but it also flattens a life. Retellings of Studd’s story tend to fall into two kinds. In the first he is a hero of total surrender, and the conflicts of his last years are either left out or explained away as the price of greatness. In the second, which is less common but has grown in recent decades, he is a warning: a rich man’s son who made an idol of sacrifice, drove his colleagues and family hard, and ended addicted to morphine and at war with his own committee. Neither picture is simply false. Both are too tidy. The verse at the head of this chapter is a proverb about lawsuits. The first person to tell a story always sounds right, until the neighbour comes and asks questions. This introduction explains which stories this book trusts, and why.

Grubb’s Biography

Nearly everything vivid that is known about Studd’s inner life comes from one book, C. T. Studd: Cricketer and Pioneer, written by Norman Grubb and published in 1933, two years after Studd’s death. Grubb had married Studd’s youngest daughter, Pauline, in 1919. He had worked beside Studd in Congo through most of the 1920s, and after Studd died he led the mission for more than thirty years. He had access to the family’s letters and to Studd’s own papers, and he wrote with love, energy and a good deal of candour.

Grubb was not a neutral witness. He was a son-in-law, a disciple and a successor, and in the crisis of Studd’s last year he had taken Studd’s side against the mission’s committee in London. His book is a defence as well as a biography. Yet it is also more honest than many later retellings. Grubb did not hide that Studd quarrelled with colleagues, that he wrote and spoke in language that shocked people, or that he used morphine in his last years. Later writers who depend on Grubb sometimes forget how much of the evidence against Studd comes from his own admirer.

Grubb’s book is still in copyright. This volume uses it only for facts, never for wording, and where an important fact rests on Grubb alone it says so.

What Can Be Checked

Some parts of Studd’s life can be checked against records made at the time, and where they can, this book checks them.

His cricket is the best documented part of his life. Scores, averages and the reports of the season were printed in his own day and are now gathered in the standard cricket databases. They show a player of real distinction: one of the leading amateur all-rounders in England in 1882 and 1883, a member of the England side at the Oval in August 1882, and a member of the team that went to Australia that winter to win the Ashes back. They also correct some of the popular stories. Studd did not score heavily in his five Test matches, and in the famous Oval match he made no runs in either innings, though in the second he was left stranded, not out, when the last wicket fell.

The story of the Cambridge Seven was published within a year of their sailing by Benjamin Broomhall, secretary of the China Inland Mission, in A Missionary Band (1886), enlarged the next year as The Evangelisation of the World. That book prints reports of their meetings and testimonies from the seven themselves. It was written to stir up missionary zeal, and it reads like it, but it is a record made at the time, and it is in the public domain.

Studd’s own publications survive too. The best known is The Chocolate Soldier, a short and furious tract on the lack of heroism in Christian life, which is in the public domain and freely available. There are also his Quaint Rhymes for the Battlefield, published in London in 1914 under the pen-name of a Quondam Cricketer, the pamphlet Christ’s Etceteras (1915), from which the constitution of his mission later developed, and a booklet of 1928 with a deliberately shocking title, discussed later in this book.

Some independent witnesses have also survived. The most valuable for the Congo years is the diary of Hayes Perkins, an American who worked at Studd’s first station at Niangara in 1914 and recorded his impressions, which were not all flattering. Later historians, notably the contributors to the Dictionary of African Christian Biography, have assessed Studd and his colleagues more coolly than his first biographer did. The Dictionary judges, in substance, that in Congo he proved an obstinate and unreasonable leader and colleague, whose conflicts reached his family, his fellow missionaries and Africans alike. That judgement has to be weighed alongside the fruit of his work, but it cannot be ignored.

Sayings and Their Sources

Studd is one of the most quoted missionaries in the English language, and several of the sayings most often given as his need care.

The best known, “If Jesus Christ be God and died for me, then no sacrifice can be too great for me to make for Him,” is everywhere attributed to him, and it sums up his life so well that it is hard to imagine anyone else saying it. But this book has not been able to trace it to anything Studd published in his lifetime, and the wording varies from one printing to another. It is quoted here as the saying traditionally associated with him, not as a sentence whose source is known.

The lines about the “rescue shop” are similar. They are always attributed to Studd, usually in rhyming form, and they sound like his rhymes. Their original printing has not been traced for this book.

The couplet most often linked with his name, “Only one life, ’twill soon be past, Only what’s done for Christ will last,” is the hardest of all. A longer poem built around it is often printed under his name, but the poem itself says that its author first heard the couplet from someone else. Studd certainly loved the couplet and is recorded as quoting it to his grandchildren in a farewell letter in the last year of his life. Whether he wrote any of the longer poem is not known. This book treats the couplet as words he loved and lived by, not as his composition.

Finally, the story that his last word on earth was “Hallelujah” comes from those who were with him or heard from them. It may well be true. It belongs to the testimony of his family and colleagues rather than to any record that can be checked.

His World and Ours

Studd lived at the high noon of the British Empire. He was born into wealth made in British India. He went to China under the protection of treaties forced on the Chinese government by war, and to Congo under Belgian rule only five years after the end of King Leopold’s Congo Free State, whose methods of extracting rubber had become an international scandal. He did not create any of those arrangements, and in his own way he despised the love of money that drove them. But he depended on them, and he sometimes spoke of the people among whom he worked in the language of his class and time. This book quotes such language only where it is needed to understand him, and it does not adopt it.

He was also, in some ways, ahead of his world. He wore Chinese clothes and ate Chinese food when many Europeans thought that degrading. In Congo he lived in African-built houses, on very little, and insisted that the Congolese church should support its own evangelists. Congolese Christians, not European missionaries, did most of the preaching that spread the church through the forest, and the church that came out of his mission is now led by Congolese men and women and counts its members in the hundreds of thousands.

What This Book Is For

The purpose of telling Studd’s story truthfully is not to cut him down to size. It is to let a real man be seen, so that what was good in him can be learned from without copying what was not. Jesus said, “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (John 8:32, ASV). A legend of total surrender can shame its readers for a while, but it cannot teach them much. A real life, with its fire and its failures, can show how God works through people whose zeal outruns their wisdom, and how much he is able to bring out of a life given away, even when the giver gets many things wrong. Studd would not have minded. He had no patience with polite Christianity, and he would have preferred the truth told plainly to a monument.

The best known, “If Jesus Christ be God and died for me, then no sacrifice can be too great for me to make for Him,” is everywhere attributed to him, and it sums up his life so well that it is hard to imagine anyone else saying it. But this book has not been able to trace it to anything Studd published in his lifetime, and the wording varies from one printing to another. It is quoted here as the saying traditionally associated with him, not as a sentence whose source is known. The lines about the “rescue shop” are similar. They are always attributed to Studd, usually in rhyming form, and they sound like his rhymes. Their original printing has not been traced for this book. The couplet most often linked with his name, “Only one life, ’twill soon be past, Only what’s done for Christ will last,” is the hardest of all. A longer poem built around it is often printed under his name, but the poem itself says that its author first heard the couplet from someone else. Studd certainly loved the couplet and is recorded as quoting it to his grandchildren in a farewell letter in the last year of his life. Whether he wrote any of the longer poem is not known. This book treats the couplet as words he loved and lived by, not as his composition. Finally, the story that his last word on earth was “Hallelujah” comes from those who were with him or heard from them. It may well be true. It belongs to the testimony of his family and colleagues rather than to any record that can be checked. His World and Ours Studd lived at the high noon of the British Empire. He was born into wealth made in British India. He went to China under the protection of treaties forced on the Chinese government by war, and to Congo under Belgian rule only five years after the end of King Leopold’s Congo Free State, whose methods of extracting rubber had become an international scandal. He did not create any of those arrangements, and in his own way he despised the love of money that drove them. But he depended on them, and he sometimes spoke of the people among whom he worked in the language of his class and time. This book quotes such language only where it is needed to understand him, and it does not adopt it. He was also, in some ways, ahead of his world. He wore Chinese clothes and ate Chinese food when many Europeans thought that degrading. In Congo he lived in African-built houses, on very little, and insisted that the Congolese church should support its own evangelists. Congolese Christians, not European missionaries, did most of the preaching that spread the church through the forest, and the church that came out of his mission is now led by Congolese men and women and counts its members in the hundreds of thousands. What This Book Is For The purpose of telling Studd’s story truthfully is not to cut him down to size. It is to let a real man be seen, so that what was good in him can be learned from without copying what was not. Jesus said, “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (John 8:32, ASV). A legend of total surrender can shame its readers for a while, but it cannot teach them much. A real life, with its fire and its failures, can show how God works through people whose zeal outruns their wisdom, and how much he is able to bring out of a life given away, even when the giver gets many things wrong. Studd would not have minded. He had no patience with polite Christianity, and he would have preferred the truth told plainly to a monument.

fields.title: A Goodly Heritage
fields.body_html:
“The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; Yea, I have a goodly heritage.”

— Psalm 16:6, ASV

Indigo

The money that made the Studds came from a plant. Indigo, the blue dye that coloured the uniforms and workclothes of half the world, was grown and processed in the nineteenth century on great estates in the plains of Bihar, in north-eastern India, under the management of European planters. The work in the fields and vats was done by Indian peasants, often on terms that left them in debt and with little choice about what they planted. In 1859 and 1860, the year of Charles Studd’s birth, the indigo districts of Bengal were shaken by a revolt of the cultivators against the planters, and the system was investigated by a government commission. The fortune that later paid for Eton, Cambridge, racehorses and, in the end, a good part of the missionary work of three continents, rested on that labour. Studd’s biographers seldom mention it. It belongs at the start of his story all the same, because he grew up on money that other people had sweated for, and he spent his adult life giving it away.

His father, Edward Studd, was born in Bombay on Christmas Day 1819. He made his fortune as an indigo planter in Tirhut, in Bihar, and returned to England a rich man while still in middle life. His first marriage produced a son, also called Edward, who was born in Tirhut in 1849. In 1856, at Bedford, he married again. His second wife was Dorothy Sophia Thomas, known as Dora, the daughter of John Thomas, a Calcutta merchant with property at Bletsoe in Bedfordshire. They had six sons and a daughter. The eldest of the second family, John Edward Kynaston Studd, always called Kynaston, was born at Netheravon in Wiltshire in 1858. George Brown Studd followed in 1859.

Charles Thomas Studd, the third son of that marriage, was born on 2 December 1860. The family was then living at Spratton, a village a few miles north-west of Northampton, at a house the census of the following year calls Spratton Hill House. Three more sons, Arthur, Herbert and Reginald, and a daughter, Dora, born in 1867, completed the family. In the family and among his friends Charles was usually called Charlie. The world came to know him by his initials, C. T.

The Sporting Squire

Edward Studd lived the life that a rich man of his tastes could live in mid-Victorian England. He hunted, he kept horses, and he raced them. His great ambition was to win the Grand National, the steeplechase at Aintree that was already the most famous horse race in the country. In 1866 he did. His horse Salamander, a long-priced outsider, won the race, and Edward Studd was said to have backed it heavily. Racing men remembered it for years.

In 1871 he took the lease of Tedworth House, a large country house at Tidworth on the edge of Salisbury Plain, together with its home farm. He did not buy it; it belonged to a family that let it to wealthy tenants. There he made a racecourse and, for his sons, a cricket ground. The boys grew up with horses, servants, open country and every kind of game. Accounts of the household in these years describe a father who was generous, energetic and fond of his children, but not, in any sense that his sons later used the word, religious. The family went to church as people of their class did. Nobody expected it to change their lives.

It is worth pausing on what that life gave the young Charlie Studd, because it shaped the man as much as anything that came later. It gave him physical confidence and a body trained by games from childhood. It gave him the habit of command, and the assumption, rarely examined, that people of his kind led and other people followed. It gave him a horror, which never left him, of being thought soft. It also gave him a kind of carelessness about money. He never had to earn his living, and he never feared poverty, because he had never known it. Much later he would choose poverty deliberately, and live in it for decades, but he always chose it as a man who could have done otherwise. That was both his freedom and, at times, his blindness. It is easier to demand that others give up comfort when one has never had to fight one’s way into it.

Eton

All the Studd boys went to Eton. Charlie arrived there in the early 1870s and, like Kynaston and George before him, he went into the cricket eleven. Eton cricket was serious. The annual match against Harrow at Lord’s was one of the great social events of the London summer, and a boy who played well in it was talked about in the newspapers and in the clubs. The three brothers became a kind of dynasty. All three played for Eton, all three would play for Cambridge, and all three would captain the University eleven in consecutive years. According to his biographers, Charlie was captain of the Eton eleven in his last year at the school, 1879. He was remembered as a tall, upright, attractive batsman and a useful fast-medium bowler, and the scores bear out that he was already one of the best schoolboy cricketers in England.

His other interests were few. He was not a scholar and never claimed to be. He was popular, cheerful and well liked, and he seems to have taken it for granted that life would go on much as it was: school, university, cricket in the summers, and some suitable occupation afterwards for which no one was in any hurry.

Muscular Christianity

The world of Eton and its cricket had its own religion, and it is worth understanding, because Studd absorbed it long before he was converted and never entirely shook it off. In the middle of the nineteenth century writers such as Charles Kingsley and Thomas Hughes, the author of Tom Brown’s School Days, had popularised an ideal that its critics nicknamed “muscular Christianity.” It held that manliness, physical courage, team spirit and fair play were Christian virtues, and that the games field was a school of character. Headmasters built chapels and cricket pavilions with equal enthusiasm. Boys were taught that a gentleman played hard, did not complain of pain, did not let his side down, and served his country.

There was much that was good in this. It taught courage and loyalty, and it made thousands of young men willing to serve in hard places. It was also, in many ways, a religion of the English upper class, more concerned with character than with grace, and more at home with duty than with mercy. It despised weakness. It made it hard to admit fear. It confused the kingdom of God, at times, with the British Empire, and the Christian soldier with the officer on the frontier.

Charlie Studd grew up inside that ideal. When he became a wholehearted Christian, he did not reject it so much as turn it towards Christ. His later writing is full of its language: pluck, heroism, soldiers, the team, the refusal to give in. Paul too could speak of the athlete and the soldier, and wrote that “bodily exercise is profitable for a little; but godliness is profitable for all things” (1 Timothy 4:8, ASV). But Paul could also boast of his weaknesses, and say that God’s power was made perfect in them. That was a lesson Studd would have to learn, slowly and painfully, and some of it he never learned at all.

A Family of Cricketers

The Studd brothers were a sporting family to an extraordinary degree. Edward, the half-brother born in India, played first-class cricket. Kynaston, George and Charlie all played for Cambridge and for Middlesex, and George and Charlie for England. Two of the younger brothers also played first-class cricket. Kynaston would later become one of the great figures of the cricket establishment as well as of evangelical work in London, and he served as Lord Mayor of London. In the 1870s and 1880s the name of Studd on a scorecard was enough to draw a crowd.

It is worth remembering that background when reading the rest of this story. Studd did not give up cricket because he was bad at it, or because he had grown tired of it, or because it had nothing more to give him. He gave it up at the height of his powers, in a family where it was the very centre of life and honour. That was what made the decision so striking to his contemporaries, and why it still impresses people who know the game.

What a Heritage Is For

The psalmist who wrote, “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; Yea, I have a goodly heritage,” was not talking about money. In the next breath he says, “I have set Jehovah always before me” (Psalm 16:8, ASV). The lines, the boundary-lines of a man’s portion of land, are pleasant because of the God who drew them, and the heritage is good because the Lord himself is its best part. “Jehovah is the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup,” the psalm begins (Psalm 16:5, ASV).

Charlie Studd had a goodly heritage in every sense his world recognised. He had health, wealth, a famous school, a father who loved him, brothers he admired, and a gift for the most admired game in England. He did not yet have the thing the psalmist meant. When he found it, it would turn the rest of his inheritance upside down. Few people have taken the words of Jesus to the rich young man more literally: “go, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me” (Mark 10:21, ASV). The young man in the Gospel went away sorrowful, “for he was one that had great possessions” (Mark 10:22, ASV). Studd, as this book will tell, did not go away. But the habits and assumptions of a rich man’s son did not vanish when he gave his money away. Some of his greatest strengths, and some of his worst faults, were learned at Tedworth.

The change, when it came, did not begin with Charlie. It began with his father, and it began at a meeting the father had to be persuaded to attend.

fields.title: The Squire Who Sold His Horses
fields.body_html:
“And they said, Believe on the Lord Jesus, and thou shalt be saved, thou and thy house.”

— Acts 16:31, ASV

Moody in London

In 1873 an American shoe salesman turned evangelist, Dwight L. Moody, arrived in Britain with his singing partner, Ira D. Sankey. Neither had any theological training. Moody spoke plainly, in an American accent, about the love of God and the need of every man and woman to decide for Christ. Sankey sang simple gospel songs to the accompaniment of a small organ. In two years they held meetings in Scotland, Ireland and the north of England, and in the spring and summer of 1875 they came to London, where crowds of many thousands came night after night to halls, theatres and an exhibition building in Islington. Society people came out of curiosity, and some of them stayed to pray.

Edward Studd was one of them. According to the family account, a friend persuaded him to go to one of Moody’s London meetings, and he went expecting little. He came away changed. The sources disagree about the date. Some give 1874, some 1875, others 1876 or 1877, but the account fits best with Moody’s great London campaign of 1875, when meetings were held in the West End as well as in the poorer districts. What all the accounts agree on is what happened next.

Edward Studd gave up the Turf. He kept a horse for each of his elder sons to ride as a hunter and sold the rest. He cleared the great hall at Tedworth and filled it with chairs and benches, so that preachers could hold evangelistic meetings for the neighbourhood, and he invited them to stay. Servants, tenants and neighbours were urged to come and hear the gospel. To the racing world it was a scandal and a joke. To his family it was, at first, an embarrassment.

What Moody Preached

It is worth asking what Edward Studd heard. Moody was not a learned preacher, and he had little interest in theological controversy. His sermons were built around a few great themes: the love of God for sinners, the sufficiency of the death of Christ, the need to be born again, and the urgency of deciding now. He told stories, many of them from his own experience in Chicago, and he spoke to his hearers as if each of them were the only person in the room. He did not shout or rant. Those who heard him often said that what struck them was not his eloquence but his directness and his evident love for them.

He also expected results, and he arranged for them. After the sermon, those who wished to know more were invited into an “inquiry room,” where Moody and his helpers spoke to them one by one, opened the Bible, and urged them to trust Christ there and then. The method has been criticised, then and since, for encouraging hasty decisions. But it suited a man like Edward Studd, who was used to making up his mind quickly and acting on it. It would also suit his son, whose conversion three years later followed almost exactly the same pattern: a personal conversation, a promise from Scripture, and a decision on the spot.

Moody’s preaching had a special appeal to the English upper classes, who had seldom heard the gospel put so simply. Some of them were shocked by his American manners and his grammar. Others found in him something they had never met in the polite religion of their parish churches. Edward Studd was one of the second kind, and the change in him was immediate and lasting.

The Embarrassed Sons

Kynaston, George and Charlie were at Eton when their father was converted, and they were not pleased. A father who talked about horses and cricket was one thing. A father who asked them, at home in the holidays, whether they were saved, was quite another. Their biographers record that the three young men did what they could to avoid being alone with him, and that the preachers who came to stay at Tedworth were not popular with them either. They were polite, because they had been brought up to be polite, and they went on as before.

Edward Studd did not live to see what came of his efforts. He died in July 1877, at the age of fifty-seven. Most sources give the date as 27 July 1877, though one local history puts his death in 1876. He had been a Christian, by any reckoning, for only two or three years. In that short time he had turned his house into a mission hall and given away his chief pleasure, and he had prayed for his sons. Accounts of his last years, all of them coming from the family, describe a man of transparent happiness, generous to preachers and to the poor, and almost reckless in speaking of Christ to anyone he met. The word “reckless” could be applied to his son later, and with more reason.

A Summer Visitor, 1878

The prayers were answered the following summer. In the school holidays of 1878 one of the Christian men who had been a friend of Edward Studd’s was staying at Tedworth. The accounts do not agree about his name, and this book does not guess it. During his visit he spoke privately to each of the three brothers about Christ.

The story of Charlie’s conversion comes chiefly from Charlie himself, as he told it in later testimony, and it is a very plain story. The visitor caught him alone. Asked whether he was a Christian, Charlie said he believed in Jesus Christ as much as anyone did. The visitor pressed him further: did he believe that Christ had died for him, and did he believe the promise that whoever believes in him has eternal life? If so, he had it, and he ought to thank God for it. The accounts do not say which verse the visitor used, but the best known of all such promises is in the third chapter of John’s Gospel: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth on him should not perish, but have eternal life” (John 3:16, ASV). Charlie saw, as he put it afterwards, that if the promise was true he could not doubt it without making God a liar. He knelt and thanked God for eternal life. He said later that joy and peace came into his soul, and that from that moment he knew what it was to be born again.

It is an evangelical conversion of a very nineteenth-century kind, built on a simple promise and a decision made in a few minutes, and it would be easy to make light of it. But it is worth noticing how much it rested on the plain word of Scripture. “He that heareth my word, and believeth him that sent me, hath eternal life,” Jesus said, “and cometh not into judgment, but hath passed out of death into life” (John 5:24, ASV). Charlie Studd did not have a dramatic experience. He was told what God had promised, and he believed it. Many years later, when he had become a man of extreme and sometimes alarming feelings, this simple foundation remained. Whatever else changed, he never doubted that he had passed from death into life on that day in 1878.

Three on One Day

According to the family tradition, the same visitor spoke to each of the other two brothers on the same day, and each of them, without telling the others, made the same decision. It was only some time later that they discovered it. Not every account agrees. One says that the three were impressed by the visitor’s arguments but did not decide until later; another says that Kynaston had already made a quiet decision in his own room at Eton. What is not in doubt is that by the end of 1878 all three of the eldest brothers counted themselves Christians, and that they connected it with their father’s prayers.

The verse at the head of this chapter is what Paul and Silas said to the jailer at Philippi: “Believe on the Lord Jesus, and thou shalt be saved, thou and thy house.” It is not a promise that faith is passed down automatically from parents to children. The jailer’s household heard the word for themselves and believed for themselves (Acts 16:32-34). But it does show that God delights to work through families, and that the faith of one person can open a door for a whole household. Edward Studd did not see the door open. His sons walked through it a year after his funeral.

A Faith That Cost Nothing

For one of the three, the change showed at once. Kynaston, the eldest, became an earnest Christian at Cambridge and an organiser of evangelistic work among the students. In time he would become Sir Kynaston Studd, serve as Lord Mayor of London, and be remembered for decades of Christian work among young men. His brothers, for the time being, went on much as before.

Charlie later said so himself, without excuses. He had been converted, he said, but instead of going out to tell others of the love of Christ, he had grown cold, and the love of the world had come back. Jesus told of seed that fell among thorns: “the cares of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in, choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful” (Mark 4:19, ASV). In Charlie’s case the thorns were not wicked. They were the pleasant things of a privileged young man’s life, and above all, cricket. For about six years, by his own account, he was what he afterwards called a backslider. He did not doubt his salvation. He simply did not let it cost him anything.

It is one of the most honest parts of his story, and it would have been easy for him to leave it out. He did not. In the years when he called thousands of others to total surrender, he told them that he had once been a Christian who wanted to keep his religion in a private corner, and that he knew from experience how comfortable that corner could be.

Some give 1874, some 1875, others 1876 or 1877, but the account fits best with Moody’s great London campaign of 1875, when meetings were held in the West End as well as in the poorer districts. What all the accounts agree on is what happened next. Edward Studd gave up the Turf. He kept a horse for each of his elder sons to ride as a hunter and sold the rest. He cleared the great hall at Tedworth and filled it with chairs and benches, so that preachers could hold evangelistic meetings for the neighbourhood, and he invited them to stay. Servants, tenants and neighbours were urged to come and hear the gospel. To the racing world it was a scandal and a joke. To his family it was, at first, an embarrassment. What Moody Preached It is worth asking what Edward Studd heard. Moody was not a learned preacher, and he had little interest in theological controversy. His sermons were built around a few great themes: the love of God for sinners, the sufficiency of the death of Christ, the need to be born again, and the urgency of deciding now. He told stories, many of them from his own experience in Chicago, and he spoke to his hearers as if each of them were the only person in the room. He did not shout or rant. Those who heard him often said that what struck them was not his eloquence but his directness and his evident love for them. He also expected results, and he arranged for them. After the sermon, those who wished to know more were invited into an “inquiry room,” where Moody and his helpers spoke to them one by one, opened the Bible, and urged them to trust Christ there and then. The method has been criticised, then and since, for encouraging hasty decisions. But it suited a man like Edward Studd, who was used to making up his mind quickly and acting on it. It would also suit his son, whose conversion three years later followed almost exactly the same pattern: a personal conversation, a promise from Scripture, and a decision on the spot. Moody’s preaching had a special appeal to the English upper classes, who had seldom heard the gospel put so simply. Some of them were shocked by his American manners and his grammar. Others found in him something they had never met in the polite religion of their parish churches. Edward Studd was one of the second kind, and the change in him was immediate and lasting. The Embarrassed Sons Kynaston, George and Charlie were at Eton when their father was converted, and they were not pleased. A father who talked about horses and cricket was one thing. A father who asked them, at home in the holidays, whether they were saved, was quite another. Their biographers record that the three young men did what they could to avoid being alone with him, and that the preachers who came to stay at Tedworth were not popular with them either. They were polite, because they had been brought up to be polite, and they went on as before. Edward Studd did not live to see what came of his efforts. He died in July 1877, at the age of fifty-seven. Most sources give the date as 27 July 1877, though one local history puts his death in 1876. He had been a Christian, by any reckoning, for only two or three years. In that short time he had turned his house into a mission hall and given away his chief pleasure, and he had prayed for his sons. Accounts of his last years, all of them coming from the family, describe a man of transparent happiness, generous to preachers and to the poor, and almost reckless in speaking of Christ to anyone he met. The word “reckless” could be applied to his son later, and with more reason. A Summer Visitor, 1878 The prayers were answered the following summer. In the school holidays of 1878 one of the Christian men who had been a friend of Edward Studd’s was staying at Tedworth. The accounts do not agree about his name, and this book does not guess it. During his visit he spoke privately to each of the three brothers about Christ. The story of Charlie’s conversion comes chiefly from Charlie himself, as he told it in later testimony, and it is a very plain story. The visitor caught him alone. Asked whether he was a Christian, Charlie said he believed in Jesus Christ as much as anyone did. The visitor pressed him further: did he believe that Christ had died for him, and did he believe the promise that whoever believes in him has eternal life? If so, he had it, and he ought to thank God for it. The accounts do not say which verse the visitor used, but the best known of all such promises is in the third chapter of John’s Gospel: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth on him should not perish, but have eternal life” (John 3:16, ASV). Charlie saw, as he put it afterwards, that if the promise was true he could not doubt it without making God a liar. He knelt and thanked God for eternal life. He said later that joy and peace came into his soul, and that from that moment he knew what it was to be born again. It is an evangelical conversion of a very nineteenth-century kind, built on a simple promise and a decision made in a few minutes, and it would be easy to make light of it. But it is worth noticing how much it rested on the plain word of Scripture. “He that heareth my word, and believeth him that sent me, hath eternal life,” Jesus said, “and cometh not into judgment, but hath passed out of death into life” (John 5:24, ASV). Charlie Studd did not have a dramatic experience. He was told what God had promised, and he believed it. Many years later, when he had become a man of extreme and sometimes alarming feelings, this simple foundation remained. Whatever else changed, he never doubted that he had passed from death into life on that day in 1878. Three on One Day According to the family tradition, the same visitor spoke to each of the other two brothers on the same day, and each of them, without telling the others, made the same decision. It was only some time later that they discovered it. Not every account agrees. One says that the three were impressed by the visitor’s arguments but did not decide until later; another says that Kynaston had already made a quiet decision in his own room at Eton. What is not in doubt is that by the end of 1878 all three of the eldest brothers counted themselves Christians, and that they connected it with their father’s prayers. The verse at the head of this chapter is what Paul and Silas said to the jailer at Philippi: “Believe on the Lord Jesus, and thou shalt be saved, thou and thy house.” It is not a promise that faith is passed down automatically from parents to children. The jailer’s household heard the word for themselves and believed for themselves (Acts 16:32-34). But it does show that God delights to work through families, and that the faith of one person can open a door for a whole household. Edward Studd did not see the door open. His sons walked through it a year after his funeral. A Faith That Cost Nothing For one of the three, the change showed at once. Kynaston, the eldest, became an earnest Christian at Cambridge and an organiser of evangelistic work among the students. In time he would become Sir Kynaston Studd, serve as Lord Mayor of London, and be remembered for decades of Christian work among young men. His brothers, for the time being, went on much as before. Charlie later said so himself, without excuses. He had been converted, he said, but instead of going out to tell others of the love of Christ, he had grown cold, and the love of the world had come back. Jesus told of seed that fell among thorns: “the cares of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things entering in, choke the word, and it becometh unfruitful” (Mark 4:19, ASV). In Charlie’s case the thorns were not wicked. They were the pleasant things of a privileged young man’s life, and above all, cricket. For about six years, by his own account, he was what he afterwards called a backslider. He did not doubt his salvation. He simply did not let it cost him anything. It is one of the most honest parts of his story, and it would have been easy for him to leave it out. He did not. In the years when he called thousands of others to total surrender, he told them that he had once been a Christian who wanted to keep his religion in a private corner, and that he knew from experience how comfortable that corner could be.

fields.title: Fenner’s and the Oval
fields.body_html:
“Know ye not that they that run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? Even so run; that ye may attain. And every man that striveth in the games exerciseth self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.”

— 1 Corinthians 9:24-25, ASV

Trinity College

Charlie Studd went up to Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1879, following Kynaston and George. He took his degree in 1883. He read for an ordinary pass degree, and nobody, least of all himself, thought of him as a student first. At Cambridge in the early 1880s cricket was not a pastime but a world, with its own heroes, rituals and newspapers, and the Studd brothers were among its princes. He played for Cambridge University from 1880 to 1883, and for Middlesex from 1879 to 1884. The three brothers set a record that was much talked about: each captained the University eleven in successive seasons, Charlie leading the side in 1883.

The figures of his career, as they stand in the cricket records, are those of a very good all-round cricketer. In first-class matches he scored 4,391 runs, with eight centuries and a highest score of 175 not out, and took 444 wickets. Most of that was done in five summers. Writers on the game in his day spoke of him as one of the best amateurs in England, a correct and stylish batsman and a bowler who could win matches. If he had gone on playing, many thought, he would have been among the greatest of his generation.

The Year of the Australians

The summer of 1882 was his finest. That year a touring team from Australia came to England, led by Billy Murdoch and with the fast bowler Fred Spofforth, the most feared bowler in the world, whom the newspapers called “the Demon.” They swept through the English counties. One of the few sides to beat them was Cambridge University. At Fenner’s, the University ground, at the end of May 1882, Cambridge won by six wickets. The match was remembered as a triumph of the Studds. Charlie made 118 in the first innings and 17 not out in the second, and took eight wickets in the match. Later in the season he made another century against the Australians, playing for the Marylebone Cricket Club.

On 14 August 1882 he completed what cricketers call the “double,” a thousand runs and a hundred wickets in a single season. Only W. G. Grace, the most famous cricketer who ever lived, had done it before him. According to the season’s records, Charlie reached his hundredth wicket by dismissing Grace himself.

He was twenty-one. He was chosen, as a matter of course, to play for England against the Australians at the Oval at the end of the month.

Seven Runs

The Oval Test of 28 and 29 August 1882 is one of the most famous matches ever played. It was the only Test match of the tour. The pitch was wet, the scores were low, and the tension in the last hour was so great that one spectator is said to have died of heart failure and another to have chewed through the handle of his umbrella. England needed only 85 to win in the fourth innings and, with Grace at the crease, seemed sure of them. Then Spofforth, bowling at his fastest and cleverest, took seven wickets. Wickets fell with the score hardly moving.

Charlie Studd had been bowled by Spofforth without scoring in the first innings. In the second, for reasons that have been argued about ever since, the England captain held him back until number ten in the order. Some said it was because he was the best batsman left and was being saved for a crisis; others that he was unwell, or that his nerves had gone in his first Test. He went in when the eighth wicket fell, and before he had faced a ball the ninth had gone too, with England still ten runs short. The last man, the Yorkshire bowler Ted Peate, came in to join him. Peate swung his first ball from Harry Boyle away for two, and a few balls later Boyle bowled him. Australia had won by seven runs. Charlie Studd walked off not out, without having faced a ball. When Peate was asked afterwards why he had not tried simply to give the strike to his partner, his answer passed into cricket legend: in substance, that he could not trust his partner. The exact words vary from one telling to another, but in every version he speaks of him as Mr Studd.

A few days later, on 2 September, the London paper The Sporting Times printed a mock obituary in affectionate remembrance of English cricket, which, it said, had died at the Oval on 29 August, adding that the body would be cremated and the ashes taken to Australia. That joke gave the contest between England and Australia its name. The young man who had stood helpless at the other end while English cricket “died” was, without any choice of his own, part of the birth of the Ashes.

To Australia

That autumn an English team under the Honourable Ivo Bligh sailed for Australia, with the declared purpose of bringing back the Ashes. Charlie and George Studd were both in it. The tour lasted the winter of 1882–83. England won the series of three matches against Murdoch’s team, and Bligh came home with a small urn, presented to him in Australia, which became the trophy itself. Charlie played in all four of the matches now counted as Tests on that tour, which with the Oval made five in his career. His Test record is modest: 160 runs at an average of 20, with a highest score of 48, and three wickets. He was a much greater cricketer than his Test figures suggest, but he never played for England again after February 1883.

Gentlemen and Players

There is a small detail in the story of the Oval that says a great deal about the world in which Studd played. When Ted Peate explained why he had not given his partner the strike, every version of his answer has him speak of Mr Studd. He did not call him Studd, or Charlie. He called him Mr Studd, because Studd was a gentleman and Peate was a professional.

English cricket in the 1880s was divided by class. The amateurs, called “gentlemen,” played for the love of the game and were paid nothing, or at least nothing officially. They came from the public schools and universities and were addressed as “Mr.” The professionals, called “players,” were paid to play. Most were working men from the mining and mill towns of the north and Midlands, and they were addressed by their surnames alone. The two groups often changed in separate dressing rooms and came onto the field by separate gates. Captains of England were almost always amateurs. The annual match between the Gentlemen and the Players was one of the great fixtures of the season.

Ted Peate was one of the best slow left-arm bowlers in England, and a far more experienced Test cricketer than the twenty-one-year-old Studd. But on the field at the Oval, in the most important moment of the match, he deferred to the young gentleman, and afterwards he was reprimanded by W. G. Grace for not trusting him enough. Whatever the rights and wrongs of the cricket, the scene is a picture of the world Studd came from. He grew up being called Mr Studd by men older, poorer and more experienced than himself, and taking it as natural.

The Bible has hard words for that kind of world. “My brethren, hold not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons” (James 2:1, ASV). “Hearken, my beloved brethren; did not God choose them that are poor as to the world to be rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he promised to them that love him?” (James 2:5, ASV). When Studd gave up his fortune, he stepped out of that world in one sense. In another he never fully left it. The habit of command, and of expecting deference, went with him to China and to Africa.

The Corruptible Crown

It is important not to make Studd’s cricket a mere prelude to his “real” life. He loved the game and played it superbly, and even in his most severe years he did not teach that games were sinful in themselves; he told young Christians to play and enjoy them with thanksgiving. His complaint against himself was not that he had played cricket, but that cricket had taken the place of Christ.

Paul knew the games of his own day, and he wrote about them with respect. Every athlete, he said, “exerciseth self-control in all things.” The runners at the Isthmian games near Corinth trained for months for a wreath of pine leaves that withered within days. Paul did not sneer at them. He used them as a rebuke to Christians who would not take the same trouble for something that would last. “Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.”

Studd came to see his cricket in exactly those terms. He had given it all the discipline, energy and ambition that he had. He had trained, practised, studied the bowling of his opponents and rejoiced in his success. When he looked back on those years he could not condemn the game, but he could not forgive himself for having given a game what he had not given to God. Later, he would ask other Christians, sometimes harshly, why they would not work as hard for Christ as he had once worked for a bat and ball. The question was fair, and it came from experience. It was also a question he would sometimes press without mercy on people who had never had his advantages, his strength or his freedom.

In the late summer of 1883, with his degree taken and his fame at its height, nothing in his outward life suggested that anything was about to change. Then his brother George fell ill.

fields.title: “This Sickness Is Not unto Death”
fields.body_html:
“But when Jesus heard it, he said, This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified thereby.”

— John 11:4, ASV

George

George Studd was the brother closest to Charlie in age and, in many ways, in temperament. He was a fine batsman, a Cambridge captain, and Charlie’s companion on the voyage to Australia in the winter of 1882–83. In November 1883, back in England, he fell desperately ill. The illness is variously described in the family accounts, and its exact nature is not recorded in any source that can now be checked, but for some days the doctors did not expect him to live.

Charlie sat by his brother’s bed. In later life he described what passed through his mind there, and it is the turning point of his story. He found himself asking what all George’s fame was worth now. The runs, the wickets, the praise of the newspapers, the admiration of thousands of people who had watched him play, none of it could do anything for him as he lay between life and death. The only thing that seemed to matter was whether he was ready to meet God. And Charlie, who had been a Christian for five years, found that he was ashamed of the way he had lived. He had been converted, and he had kept his faith to himself. He had given cricket his strength and Christ almost nothing.

George recovered. The family regarded his recovery as an answer to prayer, and so did Charlie. But he never forgot the questions he had asked at the bedside, and he was never again able to go back to the comfortable faith of the previous six years. Jesus said of his friend Lazarus, “This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God.” Studd came to believe that George’s illness had been sent, in part, for his sake.

Moody Again

In the same season Moody and Sankey were back in Britain, in the second of their great campaigns, and in the winter of 1883–84 they were holding meetings in London. Charlie went to hear Moody. It was the preaching that had converted his father, and it now did for the son what it had done for him. He came back, as he later told it, to the joy of his first conversion, and this time he did not keep it to himself.

He began at once to speak to his friends about Christ. Some of them were cricketers, and he invited them to the meetings. He gave away Christian books and spoke of the gospel to people he met, with an enthusiasm that some found attractive and others found alarming. The quiet young man who had kept his religion in a private corner had become, almost overnight, an evangelist. His family noticed the change, and not all of them liked it.

What Should He Do?

The question that followed was the one that faces every young Christian whose faith becomes serious: what was he to do with his life? Studd had a degree, a famous name and a large fortune coming to him. He could have taken holy orders and become a clergyman, like many of his Cambridge contemporaries. He could have done Christian work at home, as Kynaston was doing among young men. He could have gone on playing cricket and spoken of Christ to the people he met. He tried, by his own account, to find out what God wanted, and for some months he did not know.

He seems to have found two things during this time. The first was a deeper understanding of what it meant to give his life completely to God. Like many young evangelicals of the 1880s, he was influenced by the teaching about the surrendered life that was spreading through the holiness meetings of the period, and especially through the Keswick Convention, which began in 1875. That teaching stressed that a Christian could not have both a divided heart and peace with God, and that the way to joy was to hand everything over to Christ. Studd took it literally, as he took everything.

The second thing he found was the mission field. The China Inland Mission, founded by J. Hudson Taylor in 1865, was by then the most talked-about missionary society in Britain. It asked its workers to go inland, far from the treaty ports, to wear Chinese dress and live in Chinese houses, and to trust God for their support without being promised a salary. To some people it looked like folly. To young men like Studd, it looked like the New Testament. He had heard that another Cambridge man, the rowing stroke Stanley Smith, had already offered himself to the Mission. During 1884 he met Hudson Taylor and made his own offer. He would go to China.

The Family Objects

His family was dismayed. According to the family accounts, his mother, a widow for seven years, pleaded with him not to go. Kynaston, himself a committed Christian, argued that Charlie was being carried away by emotion, and that he could serve God just as well at home. Friends told him that it was a waste of his gifts and his position. It is easy to read these objections as worldliness, and Studd’s admirers usually do. But they were the natural fears of a loving family who had already lost a husband and father, and who could see that the climate of inland China killed missionaries with depressing regularity. They were not entirely wrong to fear for him.

Studd later said that he had struggled hard with their opposition, and that he found it one of the most painful parts of the whole decision. He said, too, that he had been settled by turning to the Bible and finding there what he took as God’s own direction. The details of that experience are given by his biographer, and this book does not repeat them. What matters is the result. He decided that he must obey God rather than his family, and he told them so.

Jesus warned that following him could divide families: “He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37, ASV). That word has been used, sometimes cruelly, to justify neglect and harshness in the name of a higher calling. Studd would later be accused of exactly that, and not without reason. But there is no sign that he was harsh with his family in 1884. He was sorry to grieve them, and he went anyway. In time, most of them came round. Kynaston would help the seven with their preparations for departure and became one of the most effective advocates of foreign missions among students on both sides of the Atlantic.

First Love

The letters to the seven churches in the book of Revelation include a warning to the church at Ephesus, a church that had worked hard, endured much and refused to tolerate false teachers. “But I have this against thee, that thou didst leave thy first love. Remember therefore whence thou art fallen, and repent and do the first works” (Revelation 2:4-5, ASV).

Charlie Studd’s six cold years were not years of open sin. By the standards of his world he was an admirable young man: sober, honest, hard-working at his sport, loyal to his friends. He had not denied Christ. He had simply let him drift to the edge of his life. The Ephesian church had done the same in a different way, by being so busy with right doctrine and hard work that it forgot what it was all for.

What brought Studd back was a crisis, and that is often how it happens. But it is worth noticing that the crisis did not create anything new in him. It reminded him of what he had already received in 1878, and made him ashamed of what he had done with it. The call of the risen Christ to the Ephesians was not “find something new” but “remember … and do the first works.” In 1883 and 1884 Studd remembered. He went back to the simple faith of his conversion, and from it, this time, he went out.

It is also worth noticing what he did not do. He did not despise his earlier conversion, or say that he had never really been a Christian before. In later years, when he told his story to students, he was careful to say that he had been truly converted at eighteen, and that his trouble had been, not unbelief, but a faith that had never been allowed to cost anything. That is a more common condition than unbelief, and in some ways a more dangerous one, because it feels so safe.

Glory, Not Fame

When John wrote about the sickness of Lazarus, he chose his words with care. The sickness was “for the glory of God, that the Son of God may be glorified thereby.” Glory and fame are not the same thing. Fame is what people give, and it can be taken away. Glory, in the Bible, is the weight and splendour of God himself, made visible. Charlie Studd had had a great deal of fame, and at George’s bedside he had seen what it was worth. From then on he wanted something else: that whatever he did would make Christ visible.

He did not always see clearly how to do that. He would make many mistakes. But from 1884 until his death, the direction of his life did not change. The famous cricketer had decided to stop playing for the corruptible crown, and the newspapers were about to discover it.
