fields.title: The Seven
fields.body_html:
“And I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then I said, Here am I; send me.”

— Isaiah 6:8, ASV

An Unlikely Band

By the end of 1884 seven young men had offered themselves to the China Inland Mission, and the newspapers had noticed that they had something in common. Most of them were Cambridge men, and all of them came from the class that ran Britain.

Stanley Smith, born in 1861, had stroked the Cambridge boat. Montagu Beauchamp was the son of a baronet and a Cambridge oarsman. William Cassels, a Cambridge graduate who had been ordained, was a curate in south London. Arthur and Cecil Polhill-Turner were the sons of a wealthy family in Bedfordshire; Arthur had been at Cambridge and had meant to take orders, and Cecil was an officer in the Dragoon Guards. Dixon Hoste, the one who had not been at Cambridge, was a lieutenant in the Royal Artillery, trained at the Royal Military Academy at Woolwich, and the son of a general. And there was Charlie Studd, the England cricketer.

They were not a natural team. Some were Anglicans of the evangelical school, and others were drawn to the newer independent churches. Some were quiet and some exuberant. Hoste, the soldier, was so reserved that he was later described as the odd man out of the group. But they had one thing in common, which their contemporaries found almost incomprehensible. They were giving up careers, comfort and position in order to go to the interior of China, where they would wear Chinese clothes, live as Chinese people lived, and rely on God, not a salary, for their support. Somebody, in the excitement of the following weeks, called them “the Cambridge Seven,” and the name stuck.

Hudson Taylor’s Gamble

For the China Inland Mission, the Seven were a gift and a risk. The Mission was nineteen years old. It had grown fast, but it had been criticised for sending out workers of little education, and some in the established churches thought it extreme. Here were seven gentlemen of the most respectable kind, two of them famous sportsmen, choosing it above every other society. Hudson Taylor saw at once what their example might do among students, and he and the Mission’s secretary, Benjamin Broomhall, encouraged them to tell their story before they sailed.

Taylor was also cautious. He did not want the Seven to become heroes, and he did not want young men to offer for China out of excitement rather than conviction. The Mission did not change its rules for them. They would sail as ordinary probationary missionaries, learn Chinese like everyone else, and be posted where the Mission sent them.

The Tour

In January and the first days of February 1885, the Seven, singly and in groups, spoke at meetings in universities and cities in England and Scotland. The meetings were crowded. Studd and Stanley Smith, the two famous athletes, were the main attraction, and they went to the universities in particular. The meetings with the students of Edinburgh are remembered as among the most remarkable of all. Students who had never before thought of the mission field went away asking whether God was calling them too.

Contemporary reports give some sense of what they heard. The Seven did not talk much about China, of which they knew almost nothing yet. They talked about Christ, and about what it meant to give him everything. Stanley Smith was the orator. Studd was not a natural speaker, and the reports describe his testimony as quiet but intense, the words of a man who had found something better than everything he was leaving. He told them that he had loved cricket as much as anyone could, and that he had found in Christ something far better. He told them that cricket would not last, and honour would not last, and nothing in this world would last, but that it was worth living for the world to come. He told them, too, about his six years of backsliding, and warned them that it was possible to be a Christian and still keep Christ out of the centre of one’s life.

Exeter Hall

The farewell meeting was held on the evening of 4 February 1885 at Exeter Hall in the Strand, the great London meeting place of evangelical societies. The hall was packed, with a crowd reported at about three thousand, and The Times reported it. Each of the Seven spoke. The next morning, Thursday 5 February, they left London for China.

Broomhall’s account of their meetings and testimonies, A Missionary Band, appeared in 1886 and was enlarged in 1887 as The Evangelisation of the World. Copies went to every corner of the English-speaking evangelical world. It is not a subtle book. Its purpose was to stir up young people to offer themselves, and it succeeded. Its title would echo for decades in the student missionary movement.

Across the Atlantic

The influence of the Seven was felt far beyond Britain. In 1885 and 1886 Kynaston Studd toured colleges in the United States, telling the story of his brother and his friends. At Cornell University, in January 1886, a young student named John R. Mott heard him, and later described that meeting as a decisive hour of his life. Mott became the leading figure in the Student Volunteer Movement for Foreign Missions, which was formed in 1886 and in the following half-century sent many thousands of young Americans and Canadians overseas as missionaries. The Movement’s watchword, “the evangelization of the world in this generation,” was shaped in part by the story of the Seven.

No single event created the great missionary expansion of the late nineteenth century, and the Seven did not do it alone. But few people have ever done more simply by going.

The Ones Who Were Not Famous

The fame of the Seven had a shadow, and it is right to notice it. In the same years, and in the years that followed, the China Inland Mission sent out hundreds of other missionaries whose names no one remembers: shop assistants, clerks, nurses, farmers’ sons, teachers and domestic servants, many of them with very little education. Many of them were women. They went to the same provinces, wore the same Chinese clothes, learned the same difficult language, and in many cases died young of the same diseases. Nobody published books about them in 1886. Nobody packed Exeter Hall to hear them.

Hudson Taylor knew this, and it was part of the reason for his caution. He was glad of the Seven, and he used their fame for the sake of the Mission. But he did not want the Mission to believe that its work depended on the sons of baronets and England cricketers. It depended on God, and on ordinary men and women who would go where they were sent.

Some of the Seven seem to have understood this very well. Dixon Hoste, in particular, spent the rest of his long life deliberately avoiding the limelight, and became known for his humility and his deference to Chinese Christian leaders. Studd understood it in his own way. He never thought of himself as a hero, and he spent much of his life telling ordinary Christians that they could do as much as he had done, and more. But the publicity of 1885 also set a pattern in his life that was not entirely healthy. From the age of twenty-four, he was a public figure in the missionary world, whose decisions were reported, discussed and admired. It is not easy for anyone to live under that kind of attention without coming to believe that his own judgement is especially to be trusted.

Paul reminded the Corinthians of something that the publicity around the Seven tended to obscure: “For behold your calling, brethren, that not many wise after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: but God chose the foolish things of the world, that he might put to shame them that are wise” (1 Corinthians 1:26-27, ASV). The Seven were exceptions, and they were celebrated because they were exceptions. Most of the work of the gospel in China, as everywhere, would be done by people who were not.

Here Am I

Isaiah’s call came in a vision of the Lord “high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1, ASV). It began with a sense of the holiness of God, and of his own uncleanness, and only after his lips had been touched with a coal from the altar did he hear the question, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” The answer, “Here am I; send me,” was not the boast of a confident volunteer. It was the reply of a man who had been forgiven and had nothing left to protect.

The Seven are sometimes remembered as a band of heroes, and the publicity that surrounded them made it hard to see them any other way. Their lives in China would be very different from one another. Hoste would succeed Hudson Taylor as head of the Mission, and lead it from 1902 to 1935. Cassels would become the first Anglican bishop of Western China. Stanley Smith would serve in China until his death in 1931, the same year as Studd. Beauchamp would serve there for many years and become an army chaplain in the First World War. Cecil Polhill would leave China in poor health and become one of the founders of the Pentecostal movement in Britain. Studd would stay less than ten years. None of them knew any of that as they left London in February 1885. They knew only that they had been asked who would go, and that they had answered.

fields.title: In Chinese Dress
fields.body_html:
“For though I was free from all men, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more.”

— 1 Corinthians 9:19, ASV

Shanghai, March 1885

The Seven reached Shanghai on 18 March 1885. Hudson Taylor had gone ahead to arrange their journeys inland. Shanghai was the greatest of the treaty ports, the coastal cities that China had been forced to open to foreign trade and residence after its defeats in the Opium Wars of 1839–42 and 1856–60. It had a foreign settlement with banks, clubs, churches and racecourses, governed in effect by the foreigners who lived there. A young English gentleman could have lived very comfortably in Shanghai. The China Inland Mission existed precisely so that its workers would not.

Within days of landing, the Seven had put on Chinese clothes. That meant a long gown, cloth shoes, and, for the men, the queue: the front of the head shaved and the hair at the back grown or lengthened with false hair into a long plait, as Chinese men were then required to wear it. The practice had been begun by Hudson Taylor himself nearly thirty years earlier, and it was still mocked by many Europeans in China, who thought it lowered the dignity of the white man. For Taylor that was exactly the point. The Mission’s workers were to go among the Chinese as guests and learners, not as members of a ruling race. Studd took to it with enthusiasm. He was always more at ease with a practice that cost him something.

The Shadow of the Opium Trade

There was another reason why a missionary in China needed humility. Britain was, in the 1880s, the chief supplier of opium to China. The drug was grown under government monopoly in British India, shipped to China by British and other merchants, and sold there under treaty terms that the Chinese government had been compelled to accept. Millions of Chinese people smoked it, and it ruined many families. Missionaries were constantly told by the Chinese they met that the same nation that sent them the Bible sent them opium. Hudson Taylor had campaigned against the trade for years. Studd’s own family fortune had come from a different crop in a different part of India, but he was a son of the same empire, and he could not have been unaware of the contradiction. It is part of the background of everything the Seven did in China.

Up the Han River

The Seven were divided. Studd and the two Polhill-Turner brothers were sent west, up the Yangtze to Hankou and then by boat up the Han River towards Hanzhong, in Shaanxi province, where the Mission had a station. It was a journey of many weeks. The river boats were slow, cramped and uncomfortable, and the three young men used the time to study Chinese. They had been told to learn the language before they did anything else, and they were in earnest about it.

The language was hard. Studd had never been a scholar, and nothing in the record suggests that study came easily to him. He learned to speak Chinese well enough to live and work in it, but he never became one of the Mission’s linguists. He was a man of action, and his gift was not for patient study but for wholehearted commitment.

Later, he was moved north to Shanxi, the province where several of the Seven eventually worked. Shanxi had been devastated by the great famine of 1876–79, in which millions died, and the Mission had gone there partly in response. It was also the province of one of the most remarkable Chinese Christians of the century.

Pastor Xi

Xi Shengmo, known to English readers as Pastor Hsi, was a Confucian scholar from southern Shanxi who had been an opium addict. He had been converted in about 1879, through reading the New Testament, while helping a missionary with an essay competition, and he had broken his addiction through prayer. He took the name Shengmo, “conqueror of demons,” and set up refuges where opium addicts could come to be cured, with medicine, care and prayer. By the late 1880s there were refuges in many towns, run by Chinese Christians. In 1886 Hudson Taylor recognised him as a pastor of the churches in his district.

Several of the Seven worked closely with Xi. Stanley Smith and Dixon Hoste were with him for years in the district of Hongtong, and Hoste in particular learned from him a respect for Chinese leadership that shaped the whole of his later direction of the Mission. Studd’s connection with Xi was less close, though some accounts say that it was Xi who conducted his wedding. The point to grasp is that the church in Shanxi was already being built by Chinese men and women. The young foreigners who arrived in Chinese gowns were joining a work that Chinese Christians were leading, often at great cost to themselves. Many of the converts in Shanxi were former opium smokers who had been rescued in Chinese-run refuges. The missionaries brought money, medicine and Bible teaching. They did not bring the church. Its life was Chinese from the beginning.

Hudson Taylor’s Principles

The China Inland Mission that Studd joined was built on a few clear principles, and they shaped him for life. Its workers were to go inland, to the provinces where no Protestant missionary was at work, rather than staying in the coastal cities. They were to adopt Chinese dress and, as far as possible, Chinese ways of living. They were to be led by directors in China, who knew the field, rather than by a committee in London. They were to receive no fixed salary, and the Mission would not make public appeals for money or go into debt; it would share among its workers whatever God sent, and trust him for the rest. And it was interdenominational: Anglicans, Baptists, Methodists, Presbyterians and Brethren worked side by side.

Every one of those principles appears again, in a sharper form, in the mission Studd would found in Africa a quarter of a century later. He took from Hudson Taylor the idea of going to the unreached, of living close to the people, of trusting God for money without appeals, and of leadership from the field rather than from home. What he did not take, or did not take enough of, was Taylor’s patience, his willingness to consult, and his deep respect for the judgement of others, including his Chinese colleagues. Taylor was a strong leader and could be immovable. But he built a mission that could survive him. Studd would build one that very nearly did not.

There is a further lesson in these first months that is easy to miss. For the first time in his life, Studd was a beginner at something. At Eton and Cambridge he had been a star; in the cricket world he had been admired; at the meetings of 1885 crowds had hung on his words. In China he could not ask for a cup of tea without help. Every child in the street knew more than he did. The China Inland Mission deliberately put its new workers in that position, because it believed that a missionary who had not first been a learner would never be a servant. It is a position that every cross-cultural worker knows, and that most find humbling. Some of Studd’s later difficulties may be traced to the fact that, in Africa, he came as a leader from the start, and never had to spend long years as a learner among the people he served.

Thirty years after Hudson Taylor, then a young and unknown missionary, first put on Chinese dress in 1855, the practice was still controversial. Some missionaries of other societies regarded the China Inland Mission’s workers as eccentric, and some officials thought they were deliberately provoking trouble by going where foreigners were not expected. To Taylor and those who followed him, the question was simple. Chinese people would listen more readily to someone who honoured their customs than to someone who despised them. The Seven accepted that from the start, and Studd never forgot it.

Free and a Servant

Paul wrote, “For though I was free from all men, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more.” A few verses later he said, “I am become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22, ASV). Paul was a free man, a Roman citizen, a scholar with every reason for pride. He chose to live as a servant, adapting himself to the customs of the people he wanted to reach, so that nothing about him would stand between them and the gospel.

Wearing Chinese dress was a small thing, and it did not make Studd Chinese. He remained a wealthy Englishman, with a family fortune behind him and the protection of the British consul if he needed it. But it was a sign that he understood something important. A messenger who refuses to change anything about himself is saying, without meaning to, that his own ways are the gospel. The Seven, for all their naivety, had grasped that the gospel must cross into the culture of those who hear it. Christ himself “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men” (Philippians 2:7, ASV).

It was a lesson Studd would carry to Africa. It was also, in a way, the beginning of the next great step of his life. If he was to be a servant, what was he doing with a fortune?

fields.title: Treasure in a Field
fields.body_html:
“The kingdom of heaven is like unto a treasure hidden in the field; which a man found, and hid; and in his joy he goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.”

— Matthew 13:44, ASV

Coming of Age

Under the terms of his father’s will, Charlie Studd was to receive his share of the family fortune when he reached the age of twenty-five. He turned twenty-five on 2 December 1885, in China. The money took time to reach him, as legacies do, and it was not until the turn of 1886 and 1887 that he was in a position to dispose of it.

He had already decided what to do. He had been reading the Gospels, and he could not get past the plain words of Jesus to the rich young ruler: “go, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me” (Mark 10:21, ASV). He knew that most Christians did not take that command as addressed to them. He thought that it was addressed to him. He was in a mission that told its workers to trust God for their daily bread. He did not see how he could do that honestly while holding a fortune in reserve.

The Cheques

The day most often given for the decisive step is 13 January 1887. On that day, according to the accounts, he wrote a series of cheques before he even knew the exact size of his inheritance. Later, when he learned the full amount, he gave away most of what was left.

The total is variously given. Some accounts say twenty-five thousand pounds; others, including the modern reference works, say about twenty-nine thousand. Either sum was an immense fortune in the 1880s, equal by most reckonings to several million pounds today. It was not the whole of his family’s wealth, which was shared among many children, but it was the whole of his own.

The best-known gifts are these. Five thousand pounds went to D. L. Moody, the evangelist who had converted his father and restored his own faith. It is said that Studd hoped Moody would use it to start gospel work in Tirhut, the district of India where his father had made his money, and that when Moody could not do that, he used it towards the training school for Christian workers that he was founding in Chicago, which became the Moody Bible Institute. Five thousand pounds went to George Müller of Bristol, famous for running orphanages for thousands of children without ever asking anyone but God for money; the accounts say that Studd asked for four thousand of it to be used for missionary work and one thousand for the orphans. Five thousand went to George Holland, who ran a mission among the poor of Whitechapel in London’s East End. Five thousand went to Frederick Booth-Tucker, the Salvation Army officer who was leading the Army’s work in India, and who had himself given up a career in the Indian civil service to live among the poor in Indian dress. Further sums, recorded less precisely, went to other Christian causes.

There is a pattern in these gifts that is worth noticing. They went to men who themselves lived by faith and among the poor: an evangelist who had once sold shoes, an orphan-father who asked no one for money, a mission in a slum, and an Englishman who had taken off his uniform to wear the clothes of India. They also went, in two cases, to India, the land from which the fortune had come. Whether Studd thought of it as restitution is not recorded. It looks like it.

The Men He Gave To

The men who received Studd’s money were not chosen at random, and a word about each of them helps to explain his choice.

George Müller, a German-born pastor in Bristol, had begun caring for orphans in 1836. By the 1880s his orphan houses on Ashley Down cared for some two thousand children at a time, and over his lifetime more than ten thousand passed through them. Müller made it a rule never to ask anyone but God for money, and published the record of the gifts that came in answer to prayer. He was, for evangelicals of Studd’s generation, the living proof that a work could be carried on by faith alone. He also supported many missionaries abroad, which is why Studd asked that most of his gift should go to missionary work.

George Holland ran a mission in George Yard, Whitechapel, in one of the poorest and most dangerous districts of London, with schools, meetings and practical help for families who had nothing. The gift to Holland was a sign that he did not think the poor of London any less in need than the people of China.

Frederick Tucker had been a member of the Indian Civil Service before he joined the Salvation Army, married the daughter of its founder, William Booth, and took the name Booth-Tucker. In 1882 he had led the Army’s first party to India, where its officers, to the scandal of many Europeans, wore Indian clothes, went barefoot, begged their food and lived among the poor. Studd, who had just put on a Chinese gown, cannot have missed the parallel.

Moody, finally, was the man to whom the Studds owed most, and the gift to him was in part a gift of gratitude. If, as is usually said, it went to the training school in Chicago, it went to the new kind of work Moody was beginning in his later years: the training of ordinary men and women, without university degrees, to be evangelists and Christian workers. Studd would spend much of his later life recruiting exactly such people.

What He Kept

He did not give away quite everything. When the gifts were made, he kept back a sum, usually given as about three thousand four hundred pounds. The accounts say that he meant it for a future wife, and by the time he married, a year later, he had found one. The story of what happened to it belongs to the next chapter.

It is also worth being clear about what he did not give up. He remained a member of a wealthy and well-connected family, who would help him and his children when he was ill and at home, and whose connections opened doors for him all his life. He had given up his own fortune, which was a great thing. He had not given up the security of being an English gentleman, and he could not have done so if he had tried. That does not lessen his gift. It does help to explain why, later in life, he sometimes failed to understand that people without his background could not live as he did.

Was It Wise?

People argued about it at the time, and they still do. Some thought it a magnificent act of faith. Others thought it rash and even irresponsible. A fortune wisely invested could have supported missionary work for generations; given away at once, it was spent within a few years. Studd had no answer for those who argued in that way, except that he believed he had been told to do it.

The New Testament does not command every Christian to give away everything. Paul told Timothy to “charge them that are rich in this present world, that they be not highminded, nor have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches, but on God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy; that they do good, that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to distribute, willing to communicate” (1 Timothy 6:17-18, ASV). That is a command to generosity, not to poverty. But the Gospels also record that Jesus sometimes asked particular people for everything, and that some of them obeyed. Studd believed that he was one of those people. It is not easy to prove him wrong.

Paul, saying goodbye to the elders of Ephesus, reminded them of “the words of the Lord Jesus, that he himself said, It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35, ASV). The saying is not recorded in any of the Gospels; Paul knew it from those who had heard Jesus. Studd believed it, and in 1887 he found it to be true. Many people who have given generously can say the same. The gift does something to the giver. It loosens the grip of money on the heart, and it makes room for trust. Studd would need that trust for the rest of his life, and he never seems to have lost it, even when everything else was hard.

Joy

The parable at the head of this chapter is one of the shortest Jesus told. A man finds treasure buried in a field. He covers it up again, goes away, sells everything he owns, and buys the field. The key words are three: “in his joy.” He is not making a sacrifice. He is making the best bargain of his life.

All the accounts agree that this is how Studd felt. He did not regard his gift as a loss. He regarded it as a release. He never afterwards spoke of it with regret, and he never seems to have been tempted to wish he had the money back, even in the years of real poverty that lay ahead. The joy of the man in the parable is the key to understanding him at his best. It is also, later, the thing that would be most obviously missing at his worst. Giving away a fortune with joy is one thing. Asking others to give away what they have, with anger at their slowness, is another.

In 1887 the joy was all there. He had found the treasure, and he had bought the field. Now he was about to find a woman who would see the matter exactly as he did.

fields.title: Scilla
fields.body_html:
“Salute Prisca and Aquila my fellow-workers in Christ Jesus, who for my life laid down their own necks; unto whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles”

— Romans 16:3-4, ASV

An Irish Girl

Priscilla Livingstone Stewart was born on 28 August 1864, in or near Belfast. Most accounts give her birthplace as Lisburn, a linen town a few miles to the south-west of the city; some give Belfast itself. Those who knew her as a young woman described her as warm, quick and full of fun, with an Ulster directness that never left her. Her family and friends called her Scilla. Her middle name, Livingstone, was a reminder of the most famous missionary of the age, though there is no evidence of any family connection with him.

She became a committed Christian as a young woman, and offered herself to the China Inland Mission. The Mission had appealed for a hundred new workers to be sent out during 1887, and “the Hundred,” as they were called, were a mixed company, many of them young women, many of them without any of the advantages of the Cambridge Seven. Priscilla Stewart was one of them. She reached Shanghai in 1887 and, after a time there, was sent inland with three other young women to work at a town called Ta-ku-tang, on the great Poyang Lake in Jiangxi.

The Hundred

The appeal that brought Priscilla Stewart to China was one of the boldest in the history of missions. In 1886 Hudson Taylor and his colleagues in China, meeting to pray about the needs of the provinces, asked God for a hundred new workers to be sent out in the course of 1887. The Mission then had fewer than two hundred missionaries in the whole of China. Taylor published the appeal and, true to his principles, did not ask for money to send them. By the end of 1887 a hundred and two new missionaries had sailed.

A great many of the Hundred were women, and many of them, like Priscilla, were sent to live and work in inland cities. That itself was controversial. Most missionary societies of the time thought it improper and dangerous for unmarried women to live in the interior of China without the protection of a missionary husband or father. Hudson Taylor disagreed. He believed that Chinese women could be reached only by women, and he trusted the women he sent. Some of the most effective missionaries in the Mission’s history were single women living in Chinese towns, far from any European.

Priscilla Stewart came out of that tradition. She was not a missionary’s wife who happened to have a calling of her own. She was a missionary who happened, after a year in China, to become a wife. That order of things is important to understanding her, and her later role in the mission she and her husband built.

Courtship

How and where she and Charlie Studd first met is not recorded in any source available to this book, and the story of their courtship has been decorated by later retellings. What seems clear is that he fell deeply in love with her, and that he pursued her in his usual way, with complete conviction. Each of them later insisted, with some humour, that the other had done the proposing. He always said that she had proposed to him. She did not agree.

By early 1888 they were engaged. Then she became seriously ill, with pneumonia according to the modern accounts, and he went to her, though he was himself recovering from an illness of the lungs. Before the wedding, Studd gave his bride the money he had kept back from his inheritance, about three thousand four hundred pounds. It was meant to give her some security. She did not keep it. The story is usually told with dialogue invented by later writers, and this book does not repeat it. The facts are simple and remarkable enough. Two young people in their twenties, with every reason to want some security for a family they hoped to have, chose to have none. Their marriage would test that choice many times over, in illness, in the births of children far from any hospital, in the deaths of two sons, and in years of separation. Neither of them ever seems to have said that they regretted it.

The choice of the Salvation Army as the recipient of that last gift is worth a moment’s thought. In 1888 the Army was barely ten years old under that name. It was noisy, unconventional and widely despised by respectable church people, and it was one of the very few Christian bodies of the time in which women preached, led congregations and held command on equal terms with men. Catherine Booth, the wife of its founder, was one of the best-known preachers in England. Whether that weighed with Priscilla Stewart is not recorded. But a young woman who had come to China to preach the gospel herself, and who would later lead a mission in all but name, chose to give her marriage portion to a movement that let women do exactly that.

The gift also showed something about the two of them as a couple. Studd had kept the money for her, as a husband of his class was expected to do. She refused to let him. From the very beginning of their marriage she was not content to be protected. She wanted to share his risks, and she did, for forty years.

The Preacher of Ecclesiastes wrote, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him that is alone when he falleth, and hath not another to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10, ASV). In their years together in China and India, Charles and Priscilla Studd lifted each other up more than once. They were both ill, often at the same time, and both lost children. Each depended on the other’s faith when their own ran low. It is worth keeping those years in mind when reading the later story, in which they were so often apart. The partnership that sustained the mission in Africa had been forged in a Chinese city, in illness and grief, long before anyone outside the family knew or cared what became of them.

Fellow-Workers

The verse at the head of this chapter is Paul’s greeting to another Priscilla, called Prisca for short, and her husband Aquila. They were tentmakers, Jewish Christians who had been driven out of Rome, and Paul lived and worked with them in Corinth. They travelled with him to Ephesus. In Rome they opened their house to the church. Paul calls them his “fellow-workers,” and in the New Testament Priscilla’s name is usually put first, which suggests that she was the better known of the two, or the more gifted teacher (Acts 18:26). They had risked their necks for him.

The marriage of Charles and Priscilla Studd was in many ways a partnership of that kind. She was not simply his wife; she was a missionary in her own right, with her own call, her own gifts and her own strong opinions. In China she worked among women whom he could not reach. fields.title: Lungan
fields.body_html:
“They that sow in tears shall reap in joy. He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing seed for sowing, Shall doubtless come again with joy, bringing his sheaves with him.”

— Psalm 126:5-6, ASV

A City That Did Not Want Them

After their wedding, the Studds went to live in Lungan, a prefectural city in the south-east of Shanxi province. In the romanised spelling of the day it was usually written Lungan-fu or Lu-an-fu; the city is now known as Changzhi. The China Inland Mission had marked it as a place where a station ought to be opened, and the Studds were the ones who went.

The record of their years there is thin. Studd’s biographer drew on family letters that have not been published in full, and the Mission’s own reports of the period mention the station only briefly. What follows is therefore an outline, not a detailed narrative, and the reader should know that much of what popular books say about these years cannot now be checked.

The outline is clear enough. Foreigners were not welcome in Lungan. In the late 1880s and early 1890s feeling against missionaries ran high in many parts of China. Placards accused them of terrible crimes, including the kidnapping and mutilation of children, and in 1891 a wave of riots against missions swept the cities of the Yangtze valley. Some of that suspicion was the product of ignorance and rumour. Some was the natural resentment of a proud people who had been defeated in war by foreign powers and forced to accept their merchants, their opium and their missionaries. A young couple who arrived in a Chinese city and rented a house to preach a foreign religion could expect to be watched, insulted and sometimes threatened. The Studds were.

They stayed. Accounts agree that they lived as simply as their neighbours, that for a long time they had almost no visible results, and that the hostility only slowly gave way to tolerance and then, in some quarters, to friendship. Like many China Inland Mission stations in Shanxi, theirs became connected with the work of opium refuges, where men and women who wanted to break their addiction could come for treatment, care and teaching. Such refuges in Shanxi were very often run by Chinese Christians, many of them former addicts themselves. Priscilla worked among the women of the city, whom her husband, as a man and a foreigner, could hardly reach at all.

Some people in Lungan became Christians. How many is not recorded in any source available to this book, and the round numbers given in some popular accounts have not been traced. The names of the Chinese Christians who worked with the Studds have not survived in those sources either. They should not be forgotten simply because they were not written down. Every station of the Mission depended on Chinese evangelists, teachers, Bible-women, cooks, carriers and landlords, people who took real risks in associating with foreigners and who carried the gospel into homes and villages where no missionary could go.

Four Daughters and Two Sons

Four daughters were born to the Studds in China. The eldest, born in 1889, was given the names Salvation Grace Faith, a choice which says a good deal about her parents. She was always called Grace. Dorothy Catherine followed on 9 July 1891, born at Lungan, and Edith Mary Crossley in 1892. The youngest, Pauline Evangeline Priscilla, was born at Lungan on 10 February 1894. All four survived, and all four would grow up to share in some way in their parents’ work. Grace married Martin Sutton and, after his death, David Munro, an army officer. Dorothy married Gilbert Barclay, a clergyman who would help to run the mission at home. Edith married Alfred Buxton, her father’s companion in Africa. Pauline married Norman Grubb, his successor.

The Studds also had two sons, and both died in infancy. The details are uncertain. One record compiled by a modern historian of the family says that a son named Paul was born in China and lived only a day; another son, born later, is recorded as having lived for two days. Parents in their position, far from doctors and hospitals, in a climate and conditions that killed many foreign children, knew that such losses were possible. That did not make them easier to bear.

Studd rarely wrote about these deaths, at least in anything that has been published. It would be wrong to fill the silence with invented feelings. But it is right to notice it. Every missionary biography of the period contains small graves. They were part of the price that missionary families paid, and that their children paid, and it is a price that the heroic retellings tend to pass over quickly. The words of Job, “Jehovah gave, and Jehovah hath taken away; blessed be the name of Jehovah” (Job 1:21, ASV), are words of faith, but they are also words spoken by a man sitting in the ashes, and the Bible does not hurry past his grief.

Broken Health

Studd had never been as strong as his cricket suggested, and China wore him down. He suffered from asthma, which troubled him for the rest of his life, and from recurring illnesses of the chest. Priscilla’s health was also poor. By 1894 both of them were in a state that the accounts call broken. The Mission’s doctors, and their own families, urged them to go home.

They left China in 1894. They had been there, Charlie for about nine years and Priscilla for about seven. Before they left, they handed over to the Mission the property they had paid for at Lungan, so that the work could continue. Accounts say that they afterwards severed their formal connection with the China Inland Mission. Studd never returned to China.

1900

Six years after the Studds left China, the province where they had worked became the scene of one of the worst massacres of missionaries and Chinese Christians in modern times. In 1900 the movement known in the West as the Boxer Rising, which blamed foreigners and Christians for the drought, poverty and humiliations that China was suffering, spread through the north of the country with the encouragement of parts of the imperial government. In Shanxi the governor, Yuxian, was one of the most hostile officials in China. In July 1900 dozens of missionaries and their children were executed at Taiyuan, the provincial capital, and others were hunted down across the province.

The China Inland Mission lost fifty-eight missionaries and twenty-one children in that year, more than any other society. Many of them died in Shanxi. Far more Chinese Christians died than foreigners: across the north of China, thousands of Protestant and Catholic believers were killed, many of them refusing to deny their faith to save their lives. Some of them were members of churches that the young men of the Cambridge Seven and their colleagues had helped to plant.

The Studds were in England, about to leave for India. It is not recorded in any source available to this book how they received the news, or whether they knew personally any of those who died. It would be strange if they did not. The Mission’s workers at Lu-an, the city where the Studds had lived, were among those whose lives were in danger that summer. One of them, Archibald Glover, escaped with his family and others on a long and terrible journey to the Yangtze, which he described in his book A Thousand Miles of Miracle in China. Had the Studds stayed in China, their daughters would have been children in Shanxi in 1900.

The story belongs here because it is a reminder of what was at stake for the Chinese Christians whom missionaries like the Studds left behind. Missionaries could go home when their health broke. Chinese believers could not. They bore the cost of their faith in their own communities, and in 1900 many paid with their lives. Their courage is part of the story of the Studds’ years in Shanxi, even though it came after the Studds had gone.

The psalmist knew that kind of grief, and wrote, “Jehovah is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart, And saveth such as are of a contrite spirit” (Psalm 34:18, ASV). The Studds left Lungan with broken health and, it may be supposed, with broken hearts. The promise was not that they would be spared, but that they would not be alone.

Sowing in Tears

By any outward measure, the Studds’ years in China were not a great success. They opened one station in a hostile city. They saw some converts, but not many. They buried two sons. They lost their health and came home. There were no great revivals, no crowds, and no famous stories, and later biographers have found little to say about these years compared with the drama of the Seven before them and of Africa after.

The psalm at the head of this chapter was written for people who had sown seed in difficult ground. “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing seed for sowing, Shall doubtless come again with joy.” It is a promise about the harvest, but it does not promise that the sower will see it. The church in Shanxi would suffer terribly in 1900, when the Boxer uprising killed many missionaries and a far larger number of Chinese Christians in that province. It would suffer again in the twentieth century. And it would survive. The Studds were a small part of its early history. Their part was to sow, to weep, and to go home. Whatever came of it belongs to the Chinese Christians who stayed.

fields.title: Students and Soldiers
fields.body_html:
“preach the word; be urgent in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all longsuffering and teaching.”

— 2 Timothy 4:2, ASV

Home, 1894

The Studds came home to England in 1894 with four small daughters, the youngest a baby, and no money of their own. Their health was poor and their future uncertain. Charlie was thirty-three. He had been a famous cricketer at twenty-one and a famous missionary at twenty-four, and now he was a semi-invalid with asthma, a family to support, and no obvious work to do.

The years that followed are among the least known of his life, and they deserve more attention than they usually receive, because they show what he was like when there was no great adventure to carry him. He did not sink into self-pity, so far as the record shows, and he did not try to recover the fortune he had given away. The family lived simply, and, it seems, with help from relatives and friends. Studd spoke at meetings when his health allowed, and he went on believing, as he always would, that God would provide for those who trusted him. By the standards of most people of his class, the family was poor. By the standards of the poor, they were still very fortunate, and they knew it.

America, 1896–97

In 1896 Studd crossed the Atlantic. The Student Volunteer Movement for Foreign Missions, which had grown in part from the stir his brother Kynaston had caused in American colleges ten years earlier, invited him to speak in the universities of the United States. He spent about eighteen months, through 1896 and 1897, travelling from campus to campus.

It was a remarkable opportunity for a man with his story. American students in the 1890s were fascinated by British sport and British gentlemen, and here was both, in the person of a former England cricketer who had given away a fortune for Christ. Studd did not talk about cricket for long. He was ill, poor and without a clear task. He had been famous, and his fame was fading. Many men in his position have grown bitter, or tried to recapture the excitement of their youth in unwise ways. There is no sign that Studd did either. He accepted the work that came to him, in American colleges and in a hill-station church, and did it faithfully. Those twelve years are a quiet witness that his faith did not depend on drama.

Paul’s charge to Timothy at the head of this chapter is often quoted to young preachers, and Studd would have taken it as a description of his whole life. “Preach the word; be urgent in season, out of season.” There were seasons in Studd’s life when the preaching was easy and the crowds were large, as in 1885. The same verse ends with a warning that is easy to overlook: “reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all longsuffering and teaching.” Studd was always good at reproving and exhorting. fields.title: A Notice in Liverpool
fields.body_html:
“How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? and how shall they preach, except they be sent?”

— Romans 10:14-15, ASV

Liverpool, 1908

In 1908, walking in Liverpool, Studd saw a notice outside a hall. It read, in effect, that cannibals wanted missionaries. The wording, as it has come down in the accounts, was meant to catch the eye, and it did. Inside, a German explorer and missionary named Karl Kumm was speaking about Africa.

The words on the notice reflect the attitudes of the time, and they need comment. Stories of cannibalism in central Africa were common in European travel writing, and they were often exaggerated or invented. They served, among other things, to make Africans seem utterly other, and to justify European rule over them. Missionary societies used the same language to raise interest and money, and it worked. This book mentions the phrase only to report the notice that Studd saw. It is not a description of any people.

Kumm himself was a serious man. Born in Germany in 1874, he had worked in North Africa and had married Lucy Guinness, daughter of the famous missionary teacher Henry Grattan Guinness. In 1902 they had founded the mission that took the name Sudan United Mission in 1904, with the aim of planting a chain of mission stations across the broad belt of Africa south of the Sahara that Europeans then called the Sudan, from the Niger to the Nile. In 1909 and 1910 Kumm crossed that whole region, from Nigeria to the Nile, and he published an account of the journey, From Hausaland to Egypt, in 1910. When Studd heard him, Kumm was speaking about the peoples of the interior who had never heard the gospel, and about the traders, hunters, officials and slavers who were reaching them first.

The Question That Would Not Go Away

Studd came out of the meeting with a question he could not shake off. Why had no Christians gone to these people? The answer, as he heard it, was that no one had been sent. Kumm’s account seemed to him to fit exactly the words of Paul at the head of this chapter: “how shall they hear without a preacher? and how shall they preach, except they be sent?” And the question that followed, according to his own later account, was a personal one. Why should he not go himself?

He had every reason not to. He was forty-seven. He had asthma and a history of serious illness in China and India. He had no money of his own, and no mission behind him. His wife was in poor health and did not want him to go. His friends thought the idea absurd. A middle-aged invalid setting off for the interior of tropical Africa, where young and healthy missionaries died of fever every year, looked to them less like faith than like a death wish.

Studd did not think so. He thought it was a matter of obedience. In his view, if God was calling him, the doctors, the climate and his age were simply beside the point. This was the strength and the danger of his faith in one sentence. He was right that God sometimes calls people to do what common sense forbids. He was not always willing to consider that common sense might, sometimes, be God’s way of speaking too.

The Sudan, 1910–11

Towards the end of 1910, Studd sailed for Africa to see the need for himself. His route took him to the southern Sudan, where the Church Missionary Society had begun work among the peoples of the upper Nile, and the accounts say that two of its senior missionaries showed him something of the country. Some later accounts say that he travelled alone; at least one says that the young Alfred Buxton was with him. The record is not clear, and this book leaves the question open.

What he found on that journey, and what he heard from traders and officials, convinced him that between the upper Nile and the great lakes, in the north-eastern corner of the Belgian Congo, lay a large and populous region in which no Protestant missionary was at work. The Catholic missions were present in parts of it. But to Studd, who shared the deep suspicion of Catholicism common among British evangelicals of his day, that did not count as the gospel having been preached. A modern reader may judge that differently. What is not in doubt is that the peoples of that region had very few Christians among them in 1910, of any kind.

On the voyage out, according to his later account, he became convinced that the journey was not for one corner of Africa only but for the whole unevangelised world. That conviction would shape everything he did for the rest of his life. It would also make him impatient with any mission, or any committee, that seemed to him to be thinking too small.

Home Again

He came back to England in 1911, a year after he had left, more certain than ever. He began to plan a new mission to the heart of Africa. His first approaches, to existing societies, did not go smoothly. The accounts of his biographers say that a committee he approached was unwilling to support his plan, at least on his terms, and that he told them he would go anyway. Records of the Africa Inland Mission, examined in modern times, show that he applied to that mission in November 1912 and was accepted; but that soon after he left for Africa, he asked for changes in its constitution, the council refused, and within a few weeks both sides agreed that his membership should end. The episode is little known, and it is told here because it is the first clear example of a pattern that would recur. Studd found it very hard to work inside any structure he did not control.

It would be unfair to treat that only as a fault. Studd was trying to do something new, and new things often need new structures. The missions he approached had their own commitments and limits, and they were right to protect them. He was right to look for another way. But the speed with which his relationships with committees broke down, then and later, says something about him. He had decided that he was obeying God, and he found it hard to believe that people who disagreed with him might be doing the same.

A Continent Divided

The Africa that Kumm described in 1908 had been carved up by European powers within living memory. At the Berlin Conference of 1884 and 1885, the year the Cambridge Seven sailed for China, the governments of Europe had agreed among themselves the rules by which they would claim African territory. No African ruler was present. Over the next twenty years almost the whole continent was divided into colonies and protectorates, often by straight lines drawn on maps in European capitals, and conquered, sometimes with great violence. By 1908 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.

Missionaries were caught up in that process in complicated ways. Some had been in Africa long before the colonial powers, and some opposed the worst abuses of colonial rule; it was missionaries, among others, who had exposed the atrocities of the Congo Free State. But missions also benefited from colonial peace and colonial roads, depended on colonial permission to work, and often shared the assumption that European rule was good for Africa. When Studd began to dream of the heart of Africa, he dreamed of it as a mission field, not as a colony. But he would reach it by the routes the colonial powers had opened, and live in it under their authority.

None of that changes the sincerity of his call. It does help to explain why, a century later, the story of missionaries in Africa is told with more caution than it once was, and why the African side of the story matters so much. The Africans of the Uele and the Ituri had not been consulted by the Berlin Conference, and they were not consulted by the Heart of Africa Mission either. What they did with the gospel when it came was their own decision, and it would turn out to be the most important part of the story.

It is worth adding that Studd’s complaint against the missions of his day was not entirely unfair. In 1910 there were, by the estimates of the missionary conference that met in Edinburgh that very year, vast regions of Africa and Asia where no missionary of any kind was at work, and most missionary resources were concentrated where churches already existed. The World Missionary Conference of 1910 itself called attention to the “unoccupied fields.” Studd was not alone in seeing the gap. He was unusual in deciding, at fifty, to go and stand in it himself.

Sent

Paul’s chain of questions in Romans begins with calling on the name of the Lord and ends with sending: “how shall they preach, except they be sent?” The Church has often read the passage as a call to go, and Studd read it that way. It is also a reminder that going is not a solitary act. In Paul’s own experience, those who went were sent by a church, which prayed for them, laid hands on them, and received them back to hear their report (Acts 13:1-3; 14:26-27). The sending and the going belonged together.

Studd’s whole Africa venture would be marked by a struggle over that relationship. He had a fierce sense of being sent by God, and a much weaker sense of being sent by anyone else. In the years ahead he would found his own mission, with his own family and friends to support it at home, and that would give him great freedom. It would also leave him, at the end, almost without anyone who could tell him he was wrong.

In Paul’s own experience, those who went were sent by a church, which prayed for them, laid hands on them, and received them back to hear their report (Acts 13:1-3; 14:26-27). The sending and the going belonged together. Studd’s whole Africa venture would be marked by a struggle over that relationship. He had a fierce sense of being sent by God, and a much weaker sense of being sent by anyone else. In the years ahead he would found his own mission, with his own family and friends to support it at home, and that would give him great freedom. It would also leave him, at the end, almost without anyone who could tell him he was wrong.

fields.title: The Heart of Africa
fields.body_html:
“By faith Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out unto a place which he was to receive for an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.”

— Hebrews 11:8, ASV

A Mission of His Own

At the end of 1912, with no society willing to take him on his own terms, Studd and a small circle of friends formed a new venture. They called it the Heart of Africa Mission. The order of events is not entirely clear from the sources, since Studd was also, briefly, a member of the Africa Inland Mission; but within weeks of his sailing in 1913 that membership had ended, and the Heart of Africa Mission stood on its own. Its aim, at first, was simple: to carry the gospel to the peoples of the north-eastern Belgian Congo, beyond the reach of any Protestant mission then at work. Its methods were those Studd had learned in the China Inland Mission, made stricter. Its workers would receive no salaries and would make no appeals for money. They would live simply, close to the people, and trust God to supply what they needed.

The new mission needed a base at home. The Studds took a house at 17 Highland Road, Upper Norwood, in south London, and it became both the family home and the mission’s headquarters. It would remain so for many years.

Priscilla

Priscilla Studd did not want her husband to go. The sources agree on that, and it is to their credit that they do not hide it. She had been seriously ill; she had a heart condition that would at times leave her an invalid; and she could see, as anyone could, that her husband was not fit for tropical Africa. She was also being asked to accept that he would leave her and their daughters, perhaps for years, and quite possibly for good.

Studd’s admirers have generally told this part of the story as a test of his faith, which he passed by going anyway. It was that. It was also a test of their marriage, and it is not obvious that it was handled well. A husband who believes himself called by God to a task his wife opposes faces one of the hardest questions in Christian life, and there is no easy rule for answering it. Studd answered it in the way he answered everything, completely and at once. He went.

What happened afterwards is a story about Priscilla as much as about him. Within a short time she not only accepted his going but threw herself into the work at home with an energy that astonished those who knew how ill she had been. She took charge of the mission’s correspondence, its finances and its recruitment. She spoke at meetings around the country. She became, in effect, the home director of the Heart of Africa Mission, and for most of the next sixteen years the mission in Africa depended on her work in England as much as on her husband’s in the field. Whatever the cost of his decision to her, she did not let it defeat her. That, too, was a kind of courage, and it has been less celebrated than his.

Alfred Buxton

Studd did not go alone. His companion was a young man of about twenty-one named Alfred Barclay Buxton. Buxton came from one of the great evangelical families of England. His father, Barclay Fowell Buxton, had been a missionary in Japan, and the family was descended from Thomas Fowell Buxton, who had led the campaign in Parliament against slavery in the British Empire. According to the accounts, Alfred had been a student at Cambridge preparing for a medical career. He gave it up to go with Studd. He would later marry Studd’s daughter Edith, in the Congo in 1917.

By the accounts of those who knew them both, Buxton was in many ways the opposite of Studd: patient where Studd was impatient, a quick learner of languages where Studd was slow, gentle where Studd was fierce. He became the first real linguist of the mission, and an American who worked with the two men in 1914 noted that it was Buxton, not Studd, who preached in the local trade language. For more than ten years he would be Studd’s closest partner. Their eventual parting, told later in this book, was one of the saddest events of Studd’s life.

Living by Faith

The Heart of Africa Mission adopted, from the start, the financial principles that Studd had learned from Hudson Taylor and George Müller. It would not ask anyone for money. It would not go into debt. It would pay no salaries. Whatever came in would be shared among the workers, and if nothing came in, they would go without. Missions run on these lines came to be called “faith missions,” and in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries they sent thousands of workers into parts of Africa, Asia and Latin America where the older denominational societies had not gone.

The principle had great strengths. It freed the missions from dependence on wealthy patrons and denominational committees, and allowed them to go where they believed God was leading without waiting for a budget. It attracted people who were willing to live simply and trust God for their needs. It meant that missionaries were close in their standard of living to the people they served.

It also had real dangers, and Studd’s mission would discover many of them. In faith missions generally, missionaries with no guaranteed income sometimes went short of food and medicine. The refusal to ask for money did not always prevent the mission from making its needs known in ways that came very close to asking. And the principle could be turned into a test of spiritual quality, so that those who worried about money were treated as lacking in faith. In the hands of a leader as demanding as Studd, that test could be applied without mercy.

But in 1913 none of that was yet apparent. A small group of friends in Norwood, an ailing man of fifty-two and a young medical student had committed themselves to a mission with no money, no committee of any standing, and no promise of support. If God did not provide, it would fail. They believed he would.

The Journey

Studd and Buxton sailed from England in the early weeks of 1913. Most accounts give 30 January as the date of sailing. Studd was fifty-two. Their route took them by sea to the coast of East Africa, then inland through what are now Kenya and Uganda by railway, steamer and on foot, to Lake Albert, and across into the Belgian Congo. The whole journey took about nine months. It was hard travelling, much of it on foot, through country that the doctors had told Studd would kill him. He did not turn back.

They reached Niangara, a government post on the Uele River in the north-east of the Congo, on 16 October 1913. The date is still remembered by the church that grew from their work, which celebrated its centenary in 2013. At Niangara they obtained permission from the Belgian authorities to settle and the use of land for a first station.

The Congo in 1913

The land Studd entered had only lately emerged from one of the worst episodes in the history of colonial rule. From 1885 to 1908 the Congo had been the personal possession of King Leopold II of Belgium, under the name of the Congo Free State. Leopold’s regime had extracted wild rubber and ivory by forced labour enforced with terror. Villages that failed to meet their quotas were burned, hostages taken, and men and women beaten, mutilated and killed. Millions of people died through violence, famine, disease and the collapse of village life. An international campaign of protest, led by Protestant missionaries, journalists and humanitarians, forced the Belgian state to take over the colony in 1908.

The north-east, where Studd came, had seen its own share of violence. The Azande and Mangbetu kingdoms of the Uele had resisted conquest for years, and the Belgian authorities still kept a large force of African soldiers at Niangara, partly from fear of a Zande uprising. The peoples of the region had suffered raids by slavers from the north long before the Belgians came, and then the demands of the Free State. They had every reason to be wary of white men who arrived uninvited, whatever they said they had come for.

Studd and Buxton came as missionaries, not as agents of the state, and the Belgian authorities of the time were generally more favourable to Catholic missions, most of them Belgian, than to Protestant missions run by foreigners. But to the people of the Uele, the distinction between one white man and another was not always clear, and the missionaries depended on the colonial authorities for permission to live and work. That was the world in which the Heart of Africa Mission began.

Not Knowing Whither

Abraham, the letter to the Hebrews says, “went out, not knowing whither he went.” It was an act of faith, and the Bible honours it. It was also an act with consequences for other people. Sarah went with him, and so did Lot, and the people of the lands through which they passed were not consulted.

Studd’s going to Africa was, in its own way, an act of the same kind of faith. He went because he believed God had called him, and he went at great cost to himself. It is right to honour that. It is also right to remember that his going depended on his wife’s willingness to carry the burden at home, on a young man who gave up his own plans to go with him, and on the permission of a colonial government that had only just stopped killing the people he had come to serve. The heart of Africa did not ask for Studd. He came anyway, and the people of the Uele would decide for themselves what to make of him.

fields.title: Niangara
fields.body_html:
“For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.”

— 2 Corinthians 4:5, ASV

A Witness Who Was Not an Admirer

For most of Studd’s life in Africa we depend on the accounts of people who loved him and worked under him. For one short period we have something different. In 1914 an American named Hayes Perkins was working at the mission’s station at Niangara, and he kept a diary. Perkins did not share all of Studd’s convictions. His diary, which has since been published online, is frank, sometimes sharp, and occasionally unfair. It is also the only record of the first year of the Heart of Africa Mission written by someone who was there and was not writing for its supporters. This chapter uses it with care, as one man’s view, but it uses it.

Bwana

Niangara stood on the Uele River, in a region where many peoples met: Mangbetu, Azande, Medje, Babua and others, each with their own language, customs and history. Belgian officials, traders, African soldiers in the colonial army, and porters and workers recruited from many districts lived side by side with the people of the surrounding villages. The common language of trade and government was Bangala, a form of the Lingala spoken along the Congo River; in other parts of the north-east people used Kingwana, a Congolese form of Swahili.

Perkins records a small detail that says a good deal. Studd, he notes, had announced that his African name was to be “Bwana,” a Swahili word for “master.” Perkins pointed out, with some irritation, that the word was not even used in Bangala. White men across East and Central Africa were commonly addressed as bwana, and to many of them it meant no more than “sir.” But it is not a title Jesus would have chosen for himself. “Whosoever would become great among you shall be your minister; and whosoever would be first among you shall be your servant” (Matthew 20:26-27, ASV). The man who had worn a Chinese gown in Shanxi had, in Africa, slipped back into the role of the white master. The detail is a reminder that the habits of the English country house and the colonial order did not vanish because a man had given away his fortune.

Perkins also records that in 1914 it was Buxton, not Studd, who preached to the people in Bangala. Studd had not yet learned it. He was fifty-three, unwell, and impatient to be moving on to new districts, and he relied on his young colleague and on African interpreters to speak for him. He would gain some command of the languages of the region in the years that followed, and he would share in the translation of Scripture into Kingwana late in life, but he was never as fluent as Buxton or the younger missionaries who came after.

Services and the Freedom to Come

One of the most revealing entries in the diary concerns worship. The mission employed local men as workers, building houses, clearing ground and carrying loads. Perkins records that when he was left in charge of the station, during one of Studd and Buxton’s journeys, the first thing he did was to line up the men and tell them that they were no longer required to attend the morning and evening services.

It is not clear from the diary how the requirement had been enforced, or whether Studd or Buxton had ordered it in so many words. Perkins disliked Studd’s methods and may have overstated the matter. But if workers who depended on the mission for wages had been made to attend prayers, the effect is easy to imagine. They were not choosing the gospel; they were doing what the white man required. Perkins’s instinct, that faith must be freely chosen, was a sound one, and it is the instinct that Studd himself, at his best, had learned from Hudson Taylor in China.

The people of the Uele were not passive in all this. They decided whether to work for the mission and on what terms, whether to come to its services, and whether to believe what they heard. It is reasonable to suppose that, as at every new station, many came to listen out of curiosity and went away unconvinced, and that some came back. In time, Congolese men and women accepted the gospel through the mission, were baptised, and became evangelists themselves. Their names do not survive in the sources available to this book, but it was their choices, and not the missionaries’ plans, that decided whether there would be a church at all.

Four Stations

Studd and Buxton did not stay long in one place. In their first year and a half they travelled widely through the region, looking for places to settle and asking permission of officials and chiefs. By the time Studd left for England, the accounts say, they had opened four stations among peoples of eight different languages. Among the places named in the records of these years are Niangara itself and Nala, which would later be Studd’s main base for a time.

Perkins describes their comings and goings. On 1 August 1914 they returned to Niangara, he writes, full of renewed zeal. On 19 August an official telegram arrived from Rejaf, on the upper Nile, with the news that war had broken out in Europe. The Belgian authorities immediately sent most of their African troops from Niangara to the front, a reminder of how thinly the colonial state was spread and how much it depended on Congolese soldiers. In October Studd and Buxton set off again, in a large canoe paddled by Bakango boatmen, for Bambili, some hundred and sixty miles down the river.

Perkins was not a friend of Studd’s methods, but his diary records that Studd thought highly of him, and once described him as too good a man to lose. The two men seem to have respected each other more than they agreed.

A word should be said about how to read a witness like Perkins. He was not an admirer, and some of what he wrote was coloured by his own disagreements with Studd and Buxton. But a critical witness who was present is often more valuable than an admiring one who was not. The book of Proverbs says, “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; But the kisses of an enemy are profuse” (Proverbs 27:6, ASV). Perkins was neither a friend nor an enemy, but his candour serves the same purpose. He shows us the mission as it looked to an outsider in its first year, and that view is worth having, even when it is uncomfortable.

War Comes to the Uele

The telegram that reached Niangara in August 1914 brought a war that would cost the Congo dearly. Belgium itself was invaded and almost entirely occupied by Germany within weeks. Its colony fought on. The Force Publique, the colonial army of African soldiers under Belgian officers, fought in Cameroon and then in German East Africa, where in 1916 it captured the town of Tabora. The campaigns in East Africa were fought across vast distances, and the armies depended on huge numbers of African porters to carry their supplies. Tens of thousands of Congolese men were conscripted as soldiers and carriers, and very many died, of disease, exhaustion and hunger, far from home.

The north-east of the Congo, where the Heart of Africa Mission had just begun, was close to the frontier with British territory and on the routes to the eastern front. Soldiers were withdrawn from posts like Niangara and sent east. Villages were required to provide men, food and labour. The people whom Studd and Buxton had come to serve were drawn into a European war of which they had known nothing a few months before, and they paid a heavy price for it.

The missionaries’ own accounts of these years say little about this, and that silence is itself part of the record. It is a reminder that the history of the mission was being lived inside a much larger and harsher history, which shaped the lives of the Congolese far more than anything the missionaries did.

Called Home

Towards the end of 1914 news came from England that Priscilla was seriously ill. Studd left the work in Congo in Buxton’s hands and went home, reaching England in the early part of 1915. He had been in Africa for less than two years. He had seen enough to be certain that this was where he would spend the rest of his life.

Servants for Jesus’ Sake

Paul’s words to the Corinthians at the head of this chapter describe exactly the relationship that every missionary is meant to have with the people he serves: “we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.” The missionary is a servant, and Christ is Lord.

The first year of the Heart of Africa Mission shows how hard that was to live out in colonial Africa, even for a man who had given away everything. Studd lived simply, far more simply than most Europeans in the colony. He was entirely sincere in his love for the people. But he also took the name of master, relied on others to speak for him, and seems to have expected his workers to come to prayers. None of that was unusual for a European in Congo in 1914. Much of it was milder than what most Europeans did. It is told here not to condemn him, but because the gospel he came to preach called him to something better, and in later years, with Congolese Christians beside him, he would sometimes reach it.

The book of Proverbs says, “Faithful are the wounds of a friend; But the kisses of an enemy are profuse” (Proverbs 27:6, ASV). Perkins was neither a friend nor an enemy, but his candour serves the same purpose.
