The first year of the Heart of Africa Mission shows how hard that was to live out in colonial Africa, even for a man who had given away everything. Studd lived simply, far more simply than most Europeans in the colony. He was entirely sincere in his love for the people. But he also took the name of master, relied on others to speak for him, and seems to have expected his workers to come to prayers. None of that was unusual for a European in Congo in 1914. Much of it was milder than what most Europeans did. It is told here not to condemn him, but because the gospel he came to preach called him to something better, and in later years, with Congolese Christians beside him, he would sometimes reach it.

fields.title: The Chocolate Soldier
fields.body_html:
“Suffer hardship with me, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier on service entangleth himself in the affairs of this life; that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier.”

— 2 Timothy 2:3-4, ASV

England at War

Studd came home in the early months of 1915 to a country at war. The great armies had dug themselves into trenches across Belgium and France, and the casualty lists in the newspapers grew longer every week. Hundreds of thousands of young men had volunteered for the army in the first months of the war. They were cheered through the streets, and those who did not go were often treated with contempt.

Priscilla was ill, and for a time her life seemed in danger, but she recovered. Studd, for his part, threw himself into meetings. From the spring of 1915 he was speaking wherever he could, calling on Christians to give themselves to the evangelisation of the world as completely as the soldiers were giving themselves to the war. It was the one thing he wanted to talk about, and the war gave him a comparison that everyone understood.

Heroism, the Lost Chord

The fullest statement of what he was saying in these years is the tract that has become his best-known work, The Chocolate Soldier, or Heroism—The Lost Chord of Christianity. It is usually dated to 1912, and it may have been begun then, but the text as it was published speaks of the Great War, so in its familiar form it cannot be earlier than the war years. It is short, angry and memorable.

The title needs explaining. A chocolate soldier was a toy, a soldier made of chocolate, who would melt as soon as he was exposed to heat. The phrase had been made popular by George Bernard Shaw’s play Arms and the Man (1894), whose hero carries chocolate instead of cartridges. Studd used it for the Christian who looked like a soldier of Christ but melted at the first touch of hardship or danger. The tract opens by declaring that heroism is the lost chord of present-day Christianity. It compares the Church, unfavourably, with the courage of the aviators and polar explorers of the day, the suffragettes, and the men who had volunteered for the war. If Christians had the pluck of the airmen, the polar explorers or the volunteers of the Great War, he argued, every soul on earth could know the name and salvation of Jesus Christ within ten years. It ends by putting to each reader Christ’s own question, as Studd framed it: would he be a malingerer or a militant?

There is real power in it. Studd had a gift for the short, sharp phrase, and he was saying something that needed to be said: that Christians who would admire a soldier’s courage often expected to follow Christ without any courage at all. Paul had used the same comparison. “Suffer hardship with me, as a good soldier of Christ Jesus.” There is no Christian life without some cost, and Studd was right to say so.

There is also something troubling in it, and a reader a century later is likely to feel it more than his first readers did. In the years of the war millions of young men went to their deaths, and some of them had volunteered because they had been shamed into it. Studd’s tract praises their courage without any hint of the horror of the war, and it uses the language of military recruitment, with its contempt for shirkers and its glorification of sacrifice, to recruit for Christ. The comparison is understandable, and Paul made a version of it. But a gospel that recruits by shame is in danger of forgetting that the Captain of salvation does not force anyone into his army, and that his soldiers are first of all his children. Studd’s rhetoric would grow more extreme over the years, and some of the conflicts of his later life can already be heard in this tract.

It should be added that Studd never seems to have doubted his own courage, and that he was right not to. He had faced the hostility of a Chinese city, the climate of the Congo and the opposition of his own family, and he had not flinched. But courage of that kind can make a man impatient with the fears of others. The Christians he rebuked in The Chocolate Soldier were often people with families to feed, debts to pay and no fortune behind them, even a fortune given away. The tract has no word of understanding for them. That silence is part of what it teaches, too.

Rhymes and Etceteras

In 1914 a London publisher brought out a small book of his verse, Quaint Rhymes for the Battlefield, credited only to a Quondam Cricketer. A quondam cricketer is a former one. The verses carry the same call to Christian heroism, and the title and the pen-name show another side of Studd: a man who liked a rhyme and a joke, and who could make fun of his own past.

The following year he published a pamphlet called Christ’s Etceteras. It is only a few pages long, but it is important, because it is the first statement of the principles on which his mission would be built, and in later years WEC International described it as the manifesto from which its own constitution developed. In it Studd cast the existing missions and their workers as the people of real standing in God’s work, and described his own little band as Christ’s etceteras: the humble helpers who would go to the places no one else was reaching, not to compete with anyone, but to fill the gaps. It is one of the gentlest things he wrote, and it shows how he wanted his mission to be seen. In time, the gaps he wanted to fill would grow to include not only the heart of Africa but every part of the world where the gospel had not been preached.

It is striking to set Christ’s Etceteras beside The Chocolate Soldier. The one is all trumpets and reproach; the other is almost shy, describing Studd’s band as the humblest of helpers, filling in behind the real missionaries. Both were written by the same man in the same years. The contrast shows that Studd was not only a man of one register. When he thought about his own mission, he could be modest, even self-deprecating. When he thought about the Church at large, he could only shout. The trouble, in later years, was that the shout increasingly drowned out the modesty, and that the people on the receiving end of it were his own colleagues.

Recruits

The meetings of 1915 and 1916 were meant to find people, and they did. Studd was looking for men and women who would go to the Congo on his terms: without salary, without promise of furlough, ready to live as simply as he did and to work as hard. He did not much care whether they had been to university or theological college. He cared whether they were wholehearted.

Those who answered him were a varied company. Some were young people from evangelical homes who had grown up on missionary stories. Some were working men and women who would never have been accepted by the older societies. Some had been deeply stirred by the war and wanted to give their lives to something as costly and as great. They were brave, and many of them were very able. Some of them would serve for decades and become pillars of the mission. Others would find, once they reached the Congo, that the life Studd demanded was more than they could bear.

The pattern of recruitment, then, carried the seeds of later trouble. Studd called people to heroism and offered them hardship. Those who came were by nature the kind of people who would not easily accept being told what to do, and Studd was the kind of leader who expected to be obeyed. It was an explosive combination, and in the 1920s it would explode.

Back to Africa

In 1916 Studd sailed again for the Congo, taking with him a party of new missionaries recruited through the meetings of the previous year. His daughter Edith went with him; she would marry Alfred Buxton in the Congo in 1917. Priscilla remained at Highland Road to run the mission at home.

Studd was fifty-five. So far as the record shows, he never saw England again. For the remaining fifteen years of his life he lived in the Congo, and he and Priscilla met only once more, for a few days, near the end. The daughters who stayed in England saw him, if at all, only rarely. That was the price of the decision he made in 1916, and the family paid it with him.

A Good Soldier

Paul’s picture of the soldier at the head of this chapter has two parts. The good soldier suffers hardship, and the good soldier does not entangle himself in civilian affairs, “that he may please him who enrolled him as a soldier.” Studd took both parts literally. He would suffer any hardship, and he would let nothing, not health, home, family or comfort, entangle him.

The soldier’s aim, though, is to please the one who enlisted him, and the one who enlisted Christians is not a general but a Saviour who “came not to be ministered unto, but to minister” (Matthew 20:28, ASV). Studd knew that perfectly well. In his best moments, he lived it. But there was in him, from these years onward, a tendency to forget that a soldier of Christ is also a member of a family, and that the family of God includes those who are slow, weak and afraid. The chocolate soldiers of his tract were real enough. So were the ordinary Christians who were not heroes, and whom Christ also loved.

fields.title: Nala and Ibambi
fields.body_html:
“Except Jehovah build the house, They labor in vain that build it: Except Jehovah keep the city, The watchman waketh but in vain.”

— Psalm 127:1, ASV

Return to the Uele

Studd returned to the Congo in 1916 with his daughter Edith and a party of new recruits. The journey was long, and wartime made it longer. When he arrived, he found that the little work he had left in Buxton’s hands had held together. The handful of stations opened in 1913 and 1914 were still there. A few Congolese had become Christians and been baptised; the accounts suggest that the first baptisms took place around 1917. The new missionaries were sent out to learn languages and to open further stations. The Heart of Africa Mission was becoming a real mission, not just the venture of one man and a young companion.

In 1917 Edith Studd and Alfred Buxton were married in the Congo. For a father so often accused of putting his family second, it must have been a deep joy to see one of his daughters married to the young man he trusted more than anyone in Africa. For a time, the Buxtons lived and worked at Ibambi, in the forest country to the south, while Studd had his own centre at Nala, two days’ journey away.

The Forest Country

The region in which the mission now worked lay where the savanna of the Uele gave way, to the south, to the great Ituri forest: a vast, dense rainforest crossed by rivers and footpaths, with clearings for villages and gardens. Several peoples lived there. The most numerous around Ibambi were the Budu, known to Europeans then as the Mabudu, a farming people whose villages were scattered through the forest. To the north and east lived the Mangbetu and the Azande, with their own kingdoms and courts. In the forest itself lived the Mbuti, the forest hunters whom Europeans called Pygmies, who traded meat and forest products with the farming villages and had their own long traditions.

It is important to say what the mission found when it came, and not only what it brought. The people of the forest country had their own beliefs about God, the spirits, the dead and the moral order of the world. They had elders, chiefs, healers and diviners, their own ways of settling disputes, and a deep knowledge of the forest. They had also been through a generation of upheaval: raids by slavers from the north in the nineteenth century, conquest by the Congo Free State, forced labour for rubber and ivory, and now the Belgian colonial administration with its taxes, its demands for porters and road-workers, and its African soldiers. The world into which the missionaries came was not timeless and unchanged. It was a world that had already been turned upside down, and in which people were looking for ways to make sense of what had happened to them.

The missionaries were also not the first Christians in the region. Catholic missionaries had reached some of these peoples, including the Budu, before Studd did. Studd, who shared the anti-Catholic convictions of most British evangelicals of his time, regarded their work as no work at all, and relations between the two missions in the Congo were often bitter. A modern reader is likely to see the matter differently, and to regret that the two missions spent so much energy competing with one another. But it is a fact of the story, and it shaped the way Studd thought about his own task.

Ibambi

About 1921 or 1922 Studd moved his own centre from Nala to Ibambi, which became the headquarters of the mission in Africa. The sources differ on the exact year. Ibambi lay in the territory of Wamba, in Budu country, and the area around it was thickly populated. Studd lived there for the rest of his life.

His way of life at Ibambi became legendary, and some of the legends are probably true. He lived in a simple house built in the local manner, ate local food, and worked very long hours, often far into the night, writing letters, preparing addresses, and later translating. He rarely took a day off. He refused most of the small comforts that other missionaries thought necessary in the tropics. He held meetings for the Christians and enquirers, sometimes very large ones, and he loved to preach to them. Those who came, by the accounts, often walked long distances through the forest to do so.

Those who worked with him found it exhausting, and some found it frightening. Studd expected his colleagues to keep his hours, live as he lived, and share his urgency. He had little patience with illness, rest or caution in others, though he suffered constantly from illness himself. In later years this would be the root of many conflicts. In the early years at Ibambi, when the mission was small and those who joined it had chosen it knowing what it was, it was also part of what made the mission grow.

One more detail from these years deserves mention. As at most stations in the region, the mission’s early buildings were raised by Congolese builders in the local manner, with poles, mud and thatch. That was a matter of necessity as much as principle, but it was also a sign of how much the mission depended, from its first day, on the skills and goodwill of the people it had come to serve.

The Weight of the Colony

The 1920s were hard years for the people of the north-east Congo, and it is important to see the mission’s growth against that background. The Belgian administration was extending its control into every district. It imposed a head tax, payable in money, which forced men to find paid work or to sell crops. It required villages to provide labour for roads and for the posts of officials. In the 1910s and 1920s it began to impose the compulsory cultivation of cash crops, especially cotton, in many districts. And in the Ituri, not far from the mission’s stations, the state-run gold mines of Kilo and Moto drew in large numbers of workers, many of them recruited under heavy pressure from chiefs who were themselves under pressure from the administration.

None of this was the mission’s doing, and the missionaries had little power to change it. But it shaped the lives of the people who came to their meetings. Men who had walked for days to hear the gospel might have to leave the next week to work on a road or in a mine. Families who wanted to support an evangelist might have no money left after the tax. Christians who refused to take part in certain customs might find their chief less willing to protect them from the demands of the state.

It also helps to explain why the gospel was heard as it was. The message that God loved them, that every person was precious to him, that the poor and the despised were welcome in his kingdom, and that a day was coming when every wrong would be judged, came to people who had good reason to long for it. They did not hear it as a European message, whatever the messengers thought. Many of them heard it as good news for themselves.

Norman and Pauline

In 1919 Studd’s youngest daughter, Pauline, married Norman Grubb, a young man who had served as an officer in the war and been wounded, and who had gone up to Cambridge afterwards. The following year, 1920, they sailed for the Congo. Grubb was a gifted linguist and a thoughtful, energetic man, and he quickly became one of the leading missionaries of the field. He worked on the translation of the New Testament into Bangala, the trade language of the region.

The Grubbs knew grief in the Congo, as so many missionary families did. Their son Noel died on his first birthday and was buried at Nala. Studd’s grandson lies there still.

So by the early 1920s two of Studd’s daughters and two sons-in-law were working beside him in Africa. To his admirers it looked like a family entirely given to the cause. It was. It also meant that the mission was, to an unusual degree, a family business, and that when disagreements came, they would be family quarrels, with all the pain and bitterness that family quarrels carry.

Except Jehovah Build the House

The psalm at the head of this chapter was a song for pilgrims going up to Jerusalem, and it is a song about building. “Except Jehovah build the house, They labor in vain that build it.” The builders still have to build, and the watchmen still have to watch. But neither the building nor the watching will last unless God is in it.

Studd believed that with all his heart. He also, at times, acted as if the building depended on his own unceasing effort, and on the effort of everyone around him. Those two convictions sat side by side in him, and he does not seem to have noticed the tension between them. The psalm goes on, “It is vain for you to rise up early, To take rest late, To eat the bread of toil; For so he giveth unto his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2, ASV). Studd rose early and took rest late, every day, for years. It is a strange and moving verse to read beside his life. God gave the increase in the Ituri forest, as the next chapter tells. Much of that increase came through people who were not driven, as Studd was, but who had heard good news and could not keep it to themselves.

He lived in a simple house built in the local manner, ate local food, and worked very long hours, often far into the night, writing letters, preparing addresses, and later translating. He rarely took a day off. He refused most of the small comforts that other missionaries thought necessary in the tropics. He held meetings for the Christians and enquirers, sometimes very large ones, and he loved to preach to them. Those who came, by the accounts, often walked long distances through the forest to do so. Those who worked with him found it exhausting, and some found it frightening. Studd expected his colleagues to keep his hours, live as he lived, and share his urgency. He had little patience with illness, rest or caution in others, though he suffered constantly from illness himself. In later years this would be the root of many conflicts. In the early years at Ibambi, when the mission was small and those who joined it had chosen it knowing what it was, it was also part of what made the mission grow. One more detail from these years deserves mention. As at most stations in the region, the mission’s early buildings were raised by Congolese builders in the local manner, with poles, mud and thatch. That was a matter of necessity as much as principle, but it was also a sign of how much the mission depended, from its first day, on the skills and goodwill of the people it had come to serve. The Weight of the Colony The 1920s were hard years for the people of the north-east Congo, and it is important to see the mission’s growth against that background. The Belgian administration was extending its control into every district. It imposed a head tax, payable in money, which forced men to find paid work or to sell crops. It required villages to provide labour for roads and for the posts of officials. In the 1910s and 1920s it began to impose the compulsory cultivation of cash crops, especially cotton, in many districts. And in the Ituri, not far from the mission’s stations, the state-run gold mines of Kilo and Moto drew in large numbers of workers, many of them recruited under heavy pressure from chiefs who were themselves under pressure from the administration. None of this was the mission’s doing, and the missionaries had little power to change it. But it shaped the lives of the people who came to their meetings. Men who had walked for days to hear the gospel might have to leave the next week to work on a road or in a mine. Families who wanted to support an evangelist might have no money left after the tax. Christians who refused to take part in certain customs might find their chief less willing to protect them from the demands of the state. It also helps to explain why the gospel was heard as it was. The message that God loved them, that every person was precious to him, that the poor and the despised were welcome in his kingdom, and that a day was coming when every wrong would be judged, came to people who had good reason to long for it. They did not hear it as a European message, whatever the messengers thought. Many of them heard it as good news for themselves. Norman and Pauline In 1919 Studd’s youngest daughter, Pauline, married Norman Grubb, a young man who had served as an officer in the war and been wounded, and who had gone up to Cambridge afterwards. The following year, 1920, they sailed for the Congo. Grubb was a gifted linguist and a thoughtful, energetic man, and he quickly became one of the leading missionaries of the field. He worked on the translation of the New Testament into Bangala, the trade language of the region. The Grubbs knew grief in the Congo, as so many missionary families did. Their son Noel died on his first birthday and was buried at Nala. Studd’s grandson lies there still. So by the early 1920s two of Studd’s daughters and two sons-in-law were working beside him in Africa. To his admirers it looked like a family entirely given to the cause. It was. It also meant that the mission was, to an unusual degree, a family business, and that when disagreements came, they would be family quarrels, with all the pain and bitterness that family quarrels carry. Except Jehovah Build the House The psalm at the head of this chapter was a song for pilgrims going up to Jerusalem, and it is a song about building. “Except Jehovah build the house, They labor in vain that build it.” The builders still have to build, and the watchmen still have to watch. But neither the building nor the watching will last unless God is in it. Studd believed that with all his heart. He also, at times, acted as if the building depended on his own unceasing effort, and on the effort of everyone around him. Those two convictions sat side by side in him, and he does not seem to have noticed the tension between them. The psalm goes on, “It is vain for you to rise up early, To take rest late, To eat the bread of toil; For so he giveth unto his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2, ASV). Studd rose early and took rest late, every day, for years. It is a strange and moving verse to read beside his life. God gave the increase in the Ituri forest, as the next chapter tells. Much of that increase came through people who were not driven, as Studd was, but who had heard good news and could not keep it to themselves.

fields.title: The Church in the Forest
fields.body_html:
“For from you hath sounded forth the word of the Lord, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place your faith to God-ward is gone forth; so that we need not to speak anything.”

— 1 Thessalonians 1:8, ASV

Whose Story?

Most of what has been written about the Heart of Africa Mission was written by Europeans for Europeans. It tells of missionaries arriving, opening stations, preaching, translating and dying. The Congolese appear in it mostly as crowds, converts, carriers and problems. That is not because the Congolese were unimportant. It is because they did not write the books.

This chapter tries to tell the story the other way round, as far as the sources allow. They do not allow very much. The names of most of the Congolese men and women who first carried the gospel through the forests of the Uele and the Ituri have not been preserved in any source available to this book, and it would be wrong to invent them. But the outline of what they did is clear, and it changes the shape of Studd’s story.

How the Church Grew

In the Congo, as in almost every part of Africa, the great majority of those who became Christians in the early twentieth century did not hear the gospel first from a missionary. They heard it from another African: a relative, a neighbour, a fellow worker, a trader, or an evangelist from their own people. The missionaries were few. In the whole of the Heart of Africa Mission, at the time of Studd’s death, there were only about thirty or thirty-five European workers, spread over a vast area. The Congolese Christians were many, and they lived in the villages.

From early on, the mission sent Congolese evangelists out to villages where there was no church. They lived among the people, taught them to read, explained the Scriptures as far as they had them, led worship, and gathered little congregations. Some were former students at the mission stations; some were simply converts who had heard and believed and could not stay silent. Many walked long distances, through a forest where paths were narrow and travel was hard. They depended on the hospitality of villages that had no reason to welcome them, and sometimes they met hostility from chiefs, elders, colonial officials, or rival missions. The accounts say that in time some churches were supporting their own evangelists, sending them, at the church’s own expense, to distant peoples. One later account speaks of a single congregation in Budu country that was sending out no fewer than fifty evangelists, all supported by the gifts of the Christians themselves. The date of that report is uncertain, and it may describe the years after Studd’s death; but the pattern began in his lifetime.

According to the mission’s own accounts, Studd insisted on that pattern. He did not believe that the mission should pay Congolese evangelists from European money, as many missions did. He believed that the Congolese church should support its own workers from the start, as the churches of the New Testament had done. That principle could be applied harshly, and in a poor country under colonial taxation it placed real burdens on poor Christians. But it also meant that the evangelists belonged to the Congolese church, and not to the mission. They were not employees of white men. They were the church’s own messengers.

Words in Their Own Tongue

The gospel spread in the languages people spoke. In the north of the mission’s field, around the Uele, the trade language was Bangala, and Norman Grubb helped to translate the New Testament into it in the 1920s, working, as every such translator did, with Congolese speakers whose names are not recorded. Further south, in the forest, the common language was Kingwana, the Congolese form of Swahili. A translation of the Scriptures into Kingwana was begun by Studd with two colleagues, Stapleton and Lowder, and Luke and Acts were published in 1930. It was one of the last pieces of work Studd did, and he gave it many hours in his final years.

No translation of the Bible is ever done by foreigners alone. Every missionary translator depends on speakers of the language who explain words, correct mistakes, and tell the translator when a sentence makes no sense. Their contribution is rarely acknowledged in print. It should be acknowledged here. The Congolese men and women who sat with Grubb and Studd over the Gospels, explaining their own languages, were translators too.

The Cost of Believing

To become a Christian in the Uele and Ituri in the 1920s was not a simple step. It often meant giving up practices that were woven into the life of a village: rites for the dead and the spirits, consultation of diviners, certain dances and festivals, the brewing and drinking of beer, and marriage customs, including the taking of more than one wife. The missions, Studd’s among them, demanded a sharp break with many of these things, and they did not always distinguish carefully between what was contrary to the gospel and what was simply unfamiliar to Europeans. Some of their rules were wise, and some were not. Converts who kept the rules often found themselves at odds with their families and their elders. Those who broke them faced the discipline of the church.

One more point belongs here. The mission’s own accounts, like those of most missions of the period, describe the Congolese chiefly as converts or as those who had not yet believed. They say much less about the Congolese who chose not to become Christians, or who came for a while and then went back to the ways of their fathers, or who joined the Catholic mission instead. Those choices, too, were real choices made by real people, for reasons that seemed good to them. A church that grows by persuasion rather than force must accept that some will say no. That is part of the dignity of those who heard, and it should be respected in the telling.

There was also the colonial state. The Belgian administration demanded taxes, labour for roads and plantations, and porters for officials. Christians were not exempt. Catholic missions, most of them Belgian, received state subsidies for schools and hospitals that Protestant missions did not, and in some districts Protestant converts found that officials and chiefs favoured their Catholic neighbours. To join a small British Protestant mission was, in a sense, to join a minority within a minority.

And there was Studd himself. The Dictionary of African Christian Biography says plainly that his conflicts in the Congo were not only with his family and fellow missionaries but also with Africans. The details are not recorded in the sources available to this book, and it would be wrong to guess at them. But it is not hard to imagine how a European of his temperament, with his absolute convictions and his impatience, might have dealt with Congolese Christians who did not agree with him about discipline, money or the pace of the work. The Congolese church that came out of his mission learned the gospel from him, and it also learned to survive his severity.

A Church That Lasted

The proof of the Congolese contribution is what happened after the missionaries left. In 1960 the Congo became independent, and in the years that followed it was torn by rebellion and war. In 1964 the Simba rebellion swept through the north-east, including the area around Ibambi, and missionaries and Congolese Christians alike suffered terribly. Many foreign missionaries left and some never came back. The churches did not disappear. They were led by Congolese pastors and evangelists, and they continued to grow.

Today the church that grew from Studd’s mission is known as the Communauté Évangélique du Christ au Cœur d’Afrique, or CECCA 16, one of the member communities of the Church of Christ in Congo. Its main centre is at Isiro, in the north-east. Estimates of its size vary, from about 120,000 members to some 250,000 people involved in its wider community. It celebrated the centenary of the mission’s arrival in 2013. It is a Congolese church, led by Congolese Christians, and it is the most lasting fruit of Studd’s life in Africa.

There is a picture in the book of Revelation that every missionary movement has loved. John sees “a great multitude, which no man could number, out of every nation and of all tribes and peoples and tongues, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, arrayed in white robes, and palms in their hands” (Revelation 7:9, ASV). It is worth noticing what John does not say. He does not say that the multitude was brought there by missionaries, or that they spoke the missionaries’ language. They come from every tongue, and they keep their tongues before the throne. The Budu, Azande, Mangbetu and Mbuti Christians of the north-eastern Congo will be in that multitude in their own right, not as anyone’s converts, but as the Lamb’s own people.

Sounded Forth

Paul wrote to the Christians of Thessalonica, a young church in a Greek city, that “from you hath sounded forth the word of the Lord, not only in Macedonia and Achaia, but in every place.” He did not say that the word had sounded forth from Paul. He had preached in Thessalonica for a few weeks. The church there had done the rest, so well that Paul had nothing left to say.

That is the true shape of the story of the Heart of Africa Mission. Studd and his colleagues brought the message to the Uele and the Ituri. They gave their health and their years to do it. But the word sounded forth from the Congolese Christians, in their own villages and languages, through their own evangelists, and at their own cost. Studd would have been the first to say that God gave the increase. He might not always have remembered that God gave it, very largely, through them.

fields.title: The Crusade
fields.body_html:
“We are fools for Christ’s sake, but ye are wise in Christ; we are weak, but ye are strong; ye have glory, but we have dishonor.”

— 1 Corinthians 4:10, ASV

A New Name

In 1919 the Heart of Africa Mission took a new name. It became the Worldwide Evangelisation Crusade, usually shortened to WEC. The change was made at home in England, where Priscilla Studd ran the mission from Highland Road, with the help of Gilbert Barclay, a clergyman who had married the Studds’ daughter Dorothy and who became the mission’s Home Overseer that year. The Congo work kept its old name as the first field of the new body, and later fields took titles of their own in the same pattern.

The name said what Studd had believed since his voyage to the Sudan in 1910: that his task was not one corner of Africa but the whole unevangelised world. The word “Crusade,” which would later be dropped because of what it meant to Muslims and to many others, was chosen in the spirit of The Chocolate Soldier. Studd thought of the mission as an army at war, and he wanted its members to think of themselves as soldiers under orders. In later decades, recognising how the word was heard by others, the mission changed its name again, to Worldwide Evangelisation for Christ, and it is now known as WEC International.

New Fields

In the early 1920s the mission began to send workers beyond the Congo. The first new field was in the Amazon basin of Brazil, entered in the early 1920s under the name of the Heart of Amazonia Mission; by the time of Studd’s death it had about sixteen missionaries, working among three different peoples. Over the next few years, according to the mission’s own history, workers were also sent to Arabia and India. These ventures were small and often struggled, but they were the beginning of what would become one of the larger interdenominational missions of the twentieth century.

Studd took a fierce interest in all of it from Ibambi. He wrote long letters, appeals and articles, which Priscilla and the home staff printed and circulated. He prayed for each new field and pressed for more recruits. He believed that if Christians would only obey Christ’s command, the world could be evangelised within a generation, and he had little patience with anyone who thought that unrealistic.

The Language of War

Studd’s writing in these years grew steadily more vehement. He had always liked to put things in the most startling way he could. Now he used the language of the battlefield, of the sports field and sometimes of the barrack room to shake complacent Christians. He wrote of heroism, of sacrifice, of soldiers who would die at their posts rather than retreat. He mocked comfortable churchgoers and cautious committees. He was capable of real humour and tenderness, but in print he was usually at full volume.

For many young people his words were a trumpet call. They read his tracts and letters and offered themselves to the mission, often for the hardest and loneliest posts. Some of them did great things. For others, the call to heroism became a weight they could not carry. The history of the mission in these years is full of departures, and it is not hard to see why some who went out expecting to live as Studd lived found that they could not.

What the Crusade Got Right

Before turning to the darker side of these years, it is fair to say what Studd’s vision achieved, because it was a great deal.

He insisted, at a time when most missionary societies were consolidating the work they already had, that the first priority was the people who had never heard. That conviction, which he took from Paul, was not original to him, but he lived it so vividly that it shaped a generation. Many later missionary movements that speak of “unreached peoples” stand, whether they know it or not, in his tradition.

He refused to let money, education or social class decide who could serve. His mission accepted people whom other societies turned away, and many of them served with great distinction. It gave a large place to women, as the China Inland Mission had done, and some of the most effective workers in its history were women.

He insisted that the churches founded by the mission should support and send out their own evangelists, rather than depending on foreign money. That principle, harsh as it sometimes was in practice, helped the Congolese church to stand on its own feet long before independence.

And he kept before Christians, in an age of growing comfort, the uncomfortable truth that following Christ costs something. “Seek ye first his kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you” (Matthew 6:33, ASV). Studd believed that promise and acted on it. Whatever his faults, he made it impossible for those who knew him to pretend that Jesus had said something easier.

D.C.D.

The most notorious of Studd’s writings appeared in 1928. It was a booklet with a title made of three initials, D.C.D., which, as later reprints spell out on their covers, stood for “Don’t Care a Damn.” Studd said that he had taken the phrase from a retired military man who used it to describe the spirit of complete devotion to king and country, careless of every personal risk and comfort. Studd wanted Christians to have the same spirit: not to care a damn for anything except the glory of Jesus, obedience to God and the evangelisation of the world. He tied it to Paul’s words in the letter to the Philippians, about counting everything loss for Christ and pressing on to the prize (Philippians 3:7-14).

The idea was not new. It was the same conviction that had driven him all his life. But the phrase caused a scandal. Many Christians in Britain in the 1920s regarded the word “damn” as profanity, not to be used by any Christian, still less printed on the cover of a missionary tract. Some of the mission’s supporters were deeply offended. Members of the committee in London, who had to answer for the mission’s reputation, were alarmed. One modern writer says that the mission tried to bury the booklet as quickly as it could; that cannot be confirmed, but it is clear that it did the mission no good with its more cautious friends. In Norman Grubb’s recorded reminiscences, made many years later, the D.C.D. is linked with the decision of the committee at home to try to remove Studd from the leadership of his own mission.

Studd seems to have been genuinely surprised by the reaction, and then defiant. To him, the shock was the point. If Christians were more offended by a strong word than by the millions who had never heard of Christ, that only proved how badly they needed to be shocked. There is some force in that argument. Jesus, too, used strong and startling language, and the prophets used stronger. But the argument also allowed Studd to dismiss every criticism of his manner as a sign of the critic’s worldliness. It made him almost impossible to correct.

Studd himself would probably have said that the end justified the language, and that if a strong word made one more person think seriously about the millions without Christ, it was worth the offence. That is an argument that every generation of preachers has to weigh. The answer of the New Testament seems to be that the gospel itself is offensive enough, and that its messengers should take care not to add offences of their own. “Let your speech be always with grace,” Paul wrote, and he was not a timid man.

It is also worth noticing who had to live with the consequences of the language. Studd wrote his tracts and letters at Ibambi, far from the people who read them. It was Priscilla, the home staff and the committee in London who faced the offended supporters, answered the letters of complaint, and tried to keep the mission’s friends. Words written in the forest landed in drawing rooms and church halls in England, and others had to deal with what they caused. A leader who speaks without counting that cost asks others to pay it for him.

Fools for Christ’s Sake

Paul wrote to the Corinthians, “We are fools for Christ’s sake, but ye are wise in Christ.” He was being ironic. The Corinthians thought themselves wise, strong and honoured; Paul and his fellow apostles looked like fools, weak and despised. Paul accepted that. He did not mind looking foolish to the world, if that was the price of faithfulness.

Studd could have recognised himself in that verse, and he lived it. He did not mind looking foolish. He had given away a fortune, gone to Africa as an invalid, and lived in poverty for decades, and he did not care what anyone thought of him. That freedom from the opinion of others was one of the finest things about him.

But being a fool for Christ’s sake is not the same as being careless of how one’s words affect others. Paul, who called himself a fool for Christ, also wrote, “Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer each one” (Colossians 4:6, ASV), and “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but such as is good for edifying as the need may be, that it may give grace to them that hear” (Ephesians 4:29, ASV). The same apostle who could be fierce with the Galatians could be as gentle as a nursing mother with the Thessalonians. He knew which was needed when.

Studd did not always know. In his last years he often seemed to have only one register, and it was a shout. Many who loved him found it hard to bear. Some who heard only the shout never heard the love behind it, and that was a loss to them and to him. The next chapters tell what it cost.

It became the Worldwide Evangelisation Crusade, usually shortened to WEC. The change was made at home in England, where Priscilla Studd ran the mission from Highland Road, with the help of Gilbert Barclay, a clergyman who had married the Studds’ daughter Dorothy and who became the mission’s Home Overseer that year. The Congo work kept its old name as the first field of the new body, and later fields took titles of their own in the same pattern. The name said what Studd had believed since his voyage to the Sudan in 1910: that his task was not one corner of Africa but the whole unevangelised world. The word “Crusade,” which would later be dropped because of what it meant to Muslims and to many others, was chosen in the spirit of The Chocolate Soldier. Studd thought of the mission as an army at war, and he wanted its members to think of themselves as soldiers under orders. In later decades, recognising how the word was heard by others, the mission changed its name again, to Worldwide Evangelisation for Christ, and it is now known as WEC International. New Fields In the early 1920s the mission began to send workers beyond the Congo. The first new field was in the Amazon basin of Brazil, entered in the early 1920s under the name of the Heart of Amazonia Mission; by the time of Studd’s death it had about sixteen missionaries, working among three different peoples. Over the next few years, according to the mission’s own history, workers were also sent to Arabia and India. These ventures were small and often struggled, but they were the beginning of what would become one of the larger interdenominational missions of the twentieth century. Studd took a fierce interest in all of it from Ibambi. He wrote long letters, appeals and articles, which Priscilla and the home staff printed and circulated. He prayed for each new field and pressed for more recruits. He believed that if Christians would only obey Christ’s command, the world could be evangelised within a generation, and he had little patience with anyone who thought that unrealistic. The Language of War Studd’s writing in these years grew steadily more vehement. He had always liked to put things in the most startling way he could. Now he used the language of the battlefield, of the sports field and sometimes of the barrack room to shake complacent Christians. He wrote of heroism, of sacrifice, of soldiers who would die at their posts rather than retreat. He mocked comfortable churchgoers and cautious committees. He was capable of real humour and tenderness, but in print he was usually at full volume. For many young people his words were a trumpet call. They read his tracts and letters and offered themselves to the mission, often for the hardest and loneliest posts. Some of them did great things. For others, the call to heroism became a weight they could not carry. The history of the mission in these years is full of departures, and it is not hard to see why some who went out expecting to live as Studd lived found that they could not. What the Crusade Got Right Before turning to the darker side of these years, it is fair to say what Studd’s vision achieved, because it was a great deal. He insisted, at a time when most missionary societies were consolidating the work they already had, that the first priority was the people who had never heard. That conviction, which he took from Paul, was not original to him, but he lived it so vividly that it shaped a generation. Many later missionary movements that speak of “unreached peoples” stand, whether they know it or not, in his tradition. He refused to let money, education or social class decide who could serve. His mission accepted people whom other societies turned away, and many of them served with great distinction. It gave a large place to women, as the China Inland Mission had done, and some of the most effective workers in its history were women. He insisted that the churches founded by the mission should support and send out their own evangelists, rather than depending on foreign money. That principle, harsh as it sometimes was in practice, helped the Congolese church to stand on its own feet long before independence. And he kept before Christians, in an age of growing comfort, the uncomfortable truth that following Christ costs something. “Seek ye first his kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you” (Matthew 6:33, ASV). Studd believed that promise and acted on it. Whatever his faults, he made it impossible for those who knew him to pretend that Jesus had said something easier. D.C.D. The most notorious of Studd’s writings appeared in 1928. It was a booklet with a title made of three initials, D.C.D., which, as later reprints spell out on their covers, stood for “Don’t Care a Damn.” Studd said that he had taken the phrase from a retired military man who used it to describe the spirit of complete devotion to king and country, careless of every personal risk and comfort. Studd wanted Christians to have the same spirit: not to care a damn for anything except the glory of Jesus, obedience to God and the evangelisation of the world. He tied it to Paul’s words in the letter to the Philippians, about counting everything loss for Christ and pressing on to the prize (Philippians 3:7-14). The idea was not new. It was the same conviction that had driven him all his life. But the phrase caused a scandal. Many Christians in Britain in the 1920s regarded the word “damn” as profanity, not to be used by any Christian, still less printed on the cover of a missionary tract. Some of the mission’s supporters were deeply offended. Members of the committee in London, who had to answer for the mission’s reputation, were alarmed. One modern writer says that the mission tried to bury the booklet as quickly as it could; that cannot be confirmed, but it is clear that it did the mission no good with its more cautious friends. In Norman Grubb’s recorded reminiscences, made many years later, the D.C.D. is linked with the decision of the committee at home to try to remove Studd from the leadership of his own mission. Studd seems to have been genuinely surprised by the reaction, and then defiant. To him, the shock was the point. If Christians were more offended by a strong word than by the millions who had never heard of Christ, that only proved how badly they needed to be shocked. There is some force in that argument. Jesus, too, used strong and startling language, and the prophets used stronger. But the argument also allowed Studd to dismiss every criticism of his manner as a sign of the critic’s worldliness. It made him almost impossible to correct. Studd himself would probably have said that the end justified the language, and that if a strong word made one more person think seriously about the millions without Christ, it was worth the offence. That is an argument that every generation of preachers has to weigh. The answer of the New Testament seems to be that the gospel itself is offensive enough, and that its messengers should take care not to add offences of their own. “Let your speech be always with grace,” Paul wrote, and he was not a timid man. It is also worth noticing who had to live with the consequences of the language. Studd wrote his tracts and letters at Ibambi, far from the people who read them. It was Priscilla, the home staff and the committee in London who faced the offended supporters, answered the letters of complaint, and tried to keep the mission’s friends. Words written in the forest landed in drawing rooms and church halls in England, and others had to deal with what they caused. A leader who speaks without counting that cost asks others to pay it for him. Fools for Christ’s Sake Paul wrote to the Corinthians, “We are fools for Christ’s sake, but ye are wise in Christ.” He was being ironic. The Corinthians thought themselves wise, strong and honoured; Paul and his fellow apostles looked like fools, weak and despised. Paul accepted that. He did not mind looking foolish to the world, if that was the price of faithfulness. Studd could have recognised himself in that verse, and he lived it. He did not mind looking foolish. He had given away a fortune, gone to Africa as an invalid, and lived in poverty for decades, and he did not care what anyone thought of him. That freedom from the opinion of others was one of the finest things about him. But being a fool for Christ’s sake is not the same as being careless of how one’s words affect others. Paul, who called himself a fool for Christ, also wrote, “Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer each one” (Colossians 4:6, ASV), and “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but such as is good for edifying as the need may be, that it may give grace to them that hear” (Ephesians 4:29, ASV). The same apostle who could be fierce with the Galatians could be as gentle as a nursing mother with the Thessalonians. He knew which was needed when. Studd did not always know. In his last years he often seemed to have only one register, and it was a shout. Many who loved him found it hard to bear. Some who heard only the shout never heard the love behind it, and that was a loss to them and to him. The next chapters tell what it cost.

fields.title: A Sharp Contention
fields.body_html:
“And there arose a sharp contention, so that they parted asunder one from the other, and Barnabas took Mark with him, and sailed away unto Cyprus”

— Acts 15:39, ASV

The Hardest Chapter

Every honest account of Studd’s life has to reach this point, and most of his admirers have reached it reluctantly. In the 1920s the Heart of Africa Mission was torn by conflict, and much of the conflict centred on Studd. Missionaries left. Supporters withdrew. His closest colleague, who was also his son-in-law, was dismissed. Long after his death, a historian writing for the Dictionary of African Christian Biography summed up his years in the Congo in a single sentence, to the effect that he proved an obstinate and unreasonable leader and colleague, provoking bitter conflict with family, fellow missionaries and Africans until his death.

That is a hard judgement, and it is not the whole truth. But it is not a judgement made by enemies. The evidence for it comes very largely from people who loved him, including the son-in-law who wrote his biography. It has to be faced.

What the Quarrels Were About

The full story of the conflicts has never been told in print, and the sources available to this book do not allow it to be told here. What they do show is the general shape.

Studd demanded total commitment from everyone in the mission. He expected his missionaries to live on very little, work very long hours, take few rests, and put the work before health, family and comfort, as he did. He regarded caution as unbelief and disagreement as disloyalty. He was the founder and leader of the mission, and he did not share his authority easily with anyone, whether colleagues in the field or the committee at home. He could be warm, generous and funny, and many people loved him. He could also be suspicious, harsh and unjust, and he could write letters that wounded deeply.

Some of the missionaries who came to the Congo in the 1920s found that they could not live and work under him. Some resigned. Others were dismissed. One missionary’s letter, written from Niangara in 1925 and since published online, admired Studd’s sacrifices and at the same time described him as domineering. That combination of admiration and dismay runs through almost every account of him in these years.

Alfred

The saddest of the partings was with Alfred Buxton. Buxton had gone with Studd to Africa in 1913, at the age of twenty-one. He had held the work together when Studd was in England. He had learned the languages, preached, travelled, and married Studd’s daughter Edith. For more than a decade he was Studd’s right hand.

When the differences between Studd and some of his colleagues grew serious in the 1920s, Buxton found that he could not simply take his father-in-law’s side. He thought that some of the criticisms were fair, and he said so. In 1927 he travelled to the United States, where the mission had friends and supporters, to try to repair relationships that had been damaged. Studd regarded his conduct as disloyal and dismissed him from the mission. One account says that the letter of dismissal included Edith as well. The exact date and the exact terms are not clear from the sources available to this book.

It is a painful story, and it does Studd no credit. Buxton had done nothing worse than disagree with him and try to make peace. To dismiss him for it, and his own daughter with him, was the act of a man who could no longer tell the difference between loyalty to Christ and loyalty to himself.

And yet there is another side, and it should be told. According to the Dictionary of African Christian Biography, the personal links between Studd and Buxton were never broken. They had loved each other for many years, and they went on loving each other through the quarrel. Buxton did not turn bitter. He went on to join Thomas Lambie of the Sudan Interior Mission in opening new work in Ethiopia and Somaliland. He was killed in October 1940, with his brother Murray, when a German bomb struck Church House in Westminster during a committee meeting. He was in his late forties.

Paul and Barnabas

The verse at the head of this chapter describes one of the saddest moments in the history of the early Church. Paul and Barnabas had been partners in the first great missionary journey. Barnabas had vouched for Paul when the other apostles were afraid of him. But when they planned a second journey, they quarrelled over John Mark, Barnabas’s cousin, who had left them in the middle of the first. Paul would not take him again. Barnabas would not go without him. “And there arose a sharp contention, so that they parted asunder one from the other.”

Luke does not tell us who was right. Perhaps both were, in part. Paul was right that the work needed people who would not turn back; Barnabas was right that a young man who had failed deserved a second chance. What we do know is how the story ended. Years later, writing from prison near the end of his life, Paul asked Timothy to bring Mark with him, “for he is useful to me for ministering” (2 Timothy 4:11, ASV). The man he had refused to take had become a man he could not do without.

The Bible does not hide the quarrels of its heroes. It records them because they happened, and because God’s work went on through them. The parting of Paul and Barnabas led to two missionary journeys instead of one. The parting of Studd and Buxton led, among other things, to the beginning of evangelical work in parts of Ethiopia. That does not make the quarrels good. It shows that God is not defeated by them.

The Founder’s Temptation

Studd was not the first founder of a Christian work to find that he could not let go of it, and he was far from the last. The New Testament itself records a church leader named Diotrephes, “who loveth to have the preeminence,” who refused to receive the messengers of the apostle John and threw out of the church those who did (3 John 9-10, ASV). It is a short and bitter note in a short letter, and it shows that the problem is as old as the Church.

Founders are often people of extraordinary vision, energy and courage. Without those qualities nothing new would ever be begun. But the same qualities can make it very hard for them to share authority, to hear criticism, or to accept that the work they began now belongs to others as well. They tend to identify the work with themselves, and to regard disagreement with their methods as disloyalty to the work, and even to God. Those around them, who owe them a great deal, often find it very hard to tell them the truth.

Studd showed almost all of these tendencies in his last years. That does not make him a Diotrephes; the comparison would be unjust, because he did not seek preeminence for its own sake and he never used the work to enrich himself. But it does mean that the troubles of the Heart of Africa Mission in the 1920s were not simply caused by worldly colleagues and timid committees, as his admirers often claimed. A good deal of the cause lay in the founder himself.

Why Was He Like This?

It is worth asking why a man of such evident love for Christ, and such evident willingness to sacrifice himself, could be so hard on others. There is no single answer, but several things can be said.

He was ill, in pain and exhausted for most of his last fifteen years, and illness and pain make most people harder to live with. He lived in great isolation, far from his wife and from any equal who could speak to him frankly. He had founded the mission and built it in his own image, and he had come to identify its success with his own obedience. He had grown up in a class and a culture that expected leaders to command, not to consult. And he had a theology of sacrifice so absolute that it left little room for weakness, his own or anyone else’s. If no sacrifice was too great for Christ, then anyone who held back must be failing Christ. It was a short step from there to treating those who disagreed with him as traitors.

None of that excuses him. All of it helps to understand him. The same convictions that made him great made him, in the end, very hard to love. Paul’s description of love is a quiet rebuke to the Studd of these years: “Love suffereth long, and is kind; love envieth not; love vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not its own, is not provoked, taketh not account of evil” (1 Corinthians 13:4-5, ASV). Studd had given away all his goods. Not all who worked with him felt that he had love.

Yet some did, to the end. Norman and Pauline Grubb stayed loyal to him. Others stayed too, and the crowds of Congolese Christians at his funeral suggest how many of them loved him. The story of the 1920s is not simply a story of a tyrant. It is the story of a great-hearted man whose virtues had hardened into vices, and of the people who loved him enough to stay, and those who loved him enough to tell him he was wrong.

fields.title: A Short Visit
fields.body_html:
“Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can floods drown it: If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned.”

— Song of Solomon 8:7, ASV

Twelve Years Apart

When Studd sailed for Africa in 1916, he and Priscilla had been married for twenty-eight years. They would not see each other again for twelve.

It is hard for a modern reader to take that in, and it ought to be. They were not estranged. They wrote to each other constantly, and every account says that they loved each other to the end. They were separated by a decision that both of them, in the end, accepted: that he would lead the work in Africa and she would lead it at home, and that neither would leave their post for the other’s sake. Priscilla’s health would not allow her to live in the Congo, and Studd would not leave it. So for twelve years their marriage was carried on by letter, across a journey of many weeks, with all the delays and misunderstandings that letters bring.

Their admirers have usually told this as a story of shared sacrifice, and it was. But it is also right to say that it was a strain, and to ask what it cost. The apostle Paul, who had no high view of marriage as a distraction from the Lord’s work, still told married couples not to deprive each other “except it be by consent for a season, that ye may give yourselves unto prayer, and may be together again” (1 Corinthians 7:5, ASV). A season is not twelve years. The Studds had reasons for what they did, and they did it with consent. But the long separation must be counted among the costs of Studd’s way of life, and not only among its glories. It cost Priscilla the companionship of her husband through years of illness and heavy responsibility. It cost Studd the one person who knew him well enough to tell him the truth and be heard. Some of the harshness of his later years may be connected with that loss. It is impossible to prove, but it is hard not to wonder.

Priscilla’s Work

Through those twelve years Priscilla carried the mission at home. She ran the headquarters at Highland Road. She dealt with the letters, the money and the candidates. She spoke at meetings around Britain, and she is remembered as an effective and moving speaker, warm and direct. She did all this while suffering from a heart condition that, at times, left her unable to work at all.

It is not too much to say that without her there would have been no Heart of Africa Mission and no WEC. Studd was the visionary and the pioneer. She was the one who found the people and the money to make the vision real. She is a figure of real courage in her own right, and her story has been told far less often than his. A woman of her gifts in the early twentieth century could not easily have led a mission in her own name. She led one in his.

She also had to stand between her husband and the mission’s friends at home when his letters and tracts caused offence. That cannot have been easy. She loved him and shared his convictions, but she lived among the people who were shocked by him, and she had to keep the mission’s supporters loyal. Some of the strains that erupted after her death had been held in check, while she lived, by her patience and her diplomacy.

The Visit

In 1928 Priscilla made the long journey to the Congo to see her husband. It was the only time she ever visited the field. She stayed only briefly. One account says thirteen days; the others say only that it was a short visit. Then she went home.

No reliable record of what passed between them during those days is available to this book, and it would be wrong to invent one. It is enough to say that they were together again, after twelve years, at Ibambi, among the people for whom they had both given so much, and that it was the last time they saw each other.

One thing about the visit can be said with confidence, because it is in the nature of the case. For a woman with a heart condition, in her sixties, to make the journey from England to the north-eastern Congo in 1928 was an undertaking of real danger and great discomfort: weeks at sea, then a long journey overland by whatever transport could be found, into a climate that had broken the health of many younger travellers. She did it for a few days with her husband. Whatever else is said about their marriage, that journey says that the love between them was not a matter of words only.

Málaga

A few months later, on 15 January 1929, Priscilla Studd died at Málaga, in southern Spain. One source dates her death to 1928, but the date of January 1929 is given by the fuller records. The circumstances of her being in Spain are not described in the sources available here. She was sixty-four.

The news had to travel to Ibambi by the slow routes of the time. What Studd felt when it reached him can only be imagined; the sources available to this book do not record his words. He had given her up, in a sense, many years before, when he went to Africa. Now she was gone in a way that could not be undone, and he had not been with her. He had lost his partner, his defender at home, and the person who, more than anyone, had made his life’s work possible.

The effect on the mission was also great. With Priscilla gone, there was no one in England with her authority, her knowledge of her husband, and her ability to hold the home side together. Within two years the relationship between Studd and the committee in London would break down entirely.

“Weeping may tarry for the night, But joy cometh in the morning” (Psalm 30:5, ASV). The psalm does not deny the weeping. It says that the night is not the end. For Charles and Priscilla Studd, the night of separation was long, and it ended, on earth, in her death far from him. They both believed that the morning would come.

The Daughters

The four Studd daughters grew up in a household where the mission came first, and the separation of their parents shaped their lives as well. When their father left for Africa in 1913, the youngest was eighteen; all four were grown women when he left for the last time in 1916. Each of them chose, in her own way, to share in the work their parents had given their lives to. Edith married Alfred Buxton and went to the Congo. Pauline married Norman Grubb and went too. Dorothy married Gilbert Barclay, who helped run the mission at home. Grace married Martin Sutton, and after his death David Munro, who would stand with Norman Grubb in the crisis of 1931.

Their loyalty to their parents was remarkable. It was also tested. At least one of the four was married to a man who found himself at odds with their father. Edith was dismissed from the mission with her husband. The family quarrels of the late 1920s ran through the daughters’ own marriages. How they felt about it is not recorded in any source available to this book, and it would be wrong to guess. It is enough to say that the cost of their father’s choices did not fall only on him and their mother.

Paul wrote, “And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but nurture them in the chastening and admonition of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4, ASV). Studd’s daughters did not, so far as the record shows, turn against him or against his faith. All four remained committed Christians, and two of them gave their lives to the work he had begun. That is no small thing to say of the children of a man so often absent and so often difficult. It may say as much about their mother as about him.

Love Stronger than Distance

The Song of Solomon is a love song, and near its end it says something about love that Christians have always applied both to human love and to the love of God. “Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can floods drown it.” And then, strangely: “If a man would give all the substance of his house for love, He would utterly be contemned.” Love cannot be bought. A man who offered all his wealth in exchange for it would be laughed at.

Charles and Priscilla Studd had given away all the substance of their house, long before, for the love of Christ. They had not bought anything with it, and they knew that. What they had, they had been given. Their love for each other survived twelve years of separation, the strains of the mission, his illness and hers, and all the misunderstandings that letters bring. It did not survive death, in the sense that death parted them. But they both believed what Paul told the Thessalonians, that those who have fallen asleep in Jesus are not lost, and that God will bring them with him (1 Thessalonians 4:13-14).

It is right to honour them for what they gave, and to admire the faith that made it possible. It is also right to grieve, as Paul did not forbid, for the years they did not have together. Those years were part of the cost. Both of them paid it, and she paid her share mostly out of sight.

They would not see each other again for twelve. It is hard for a modern reader to take that in, and it ought to be. They were not estranged. They wrote to each other constantly, and every account says that they loved each other to the end. They were separated by a decision that both of them, in the end, accepted: that he would lead the work in Africa and she would lead it at home, and that neither would leave their post for the other’s sake. Priscilla’s health would not allow her to live in the Congo, and Studd would not leave it. So for twelve years their marriage was carried on by letter, across a journey of many weeks, with all the delays and misunderstandings that letters bring. Their admirers have usually told this as a story of shared sacrifice, and it was. But it is also right to say that it was a strain, and to ask what it cost. The apostle Paul, who had no high view of marriage as a distraction from the Lord’s work, still told married couples not to deprive each other “except it be by consent for a season, that ye may give yourselves unto prayer, and may be together again” (1 Corinthians 7:5, ASV). A season is not twelve years. The Studds had reasons for what they did, and they did it with consent. It cost Priscilla the companionship of her husband through years of illness and heavy responsibility. It cost Studd the one person who knew him well enough to tell him the truth and be heard. He had lost his partner, his defender at home, and the person who, more than anyone, had made his life’s work possible. The effect on the mission was also great.
