fields.title: The Thorn and the Needle
fields.body_html:
“Wherefore we faint not; but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day.”

— 2 Corinthians 4:16, ASV

A Body Worn Out

By the late 1920s Studd’s body was failing. He had suffered from asthma since his years in China. He had lived for more than a decade in the tropical forest without proper rest, on a poor diet, in a climate that wore down young and healthy Europeans within a few years. He had suffered repeated bouts of illness of the kind that were common among missionaries in central Africa. And he had developed the gallstones that would, in the end, cause his death. Gallstones can cause attacks of intense pain, and without surgery, which was not available to him at Ibambi, there was little that could be done but to endure the attacks and relieve the pain.

Studd had always pushed his body past what was sensible. Now he could do so only at great cost. He was in his late sixties, often in pain, and often too ill to move. Yet he would not stop working, and he would not go home.

Morphine

It was in these circumstances that he began to use morphine. According to the account given by Norman Grubb, a doctor who was passing through the region recommended it, and Studd, who wanted above all to keep on working, agreed to try it. In his last years he took it regularly.

The facts of this have never been hidden by his family. His biographer recorded them, and modern reference works mention them without fuss. It is the interpretation that has been disputed, both in his lifetime and since.

To his critics, at the time and later, it was a scandal. The founder of a mission that demanded heroic self-denial was taking a narcotic drug every day. Some called him a drug addict. The controversy was not helped by the fact that his supplies of the drug, according to some accounts, had to be brought into the colony by means that critics regarded as smuggling, and that may not always have been declared to the Belgian customs. In the atmosphere of the late 1920s, when the international campaign against the opium and morphine trades was at its height, and when Studd’s own mission was demanding total holiness of its members, his use of morphine was easy to portray as hypocrisy.

To his defenders, it was medicine. Morphine was the standard treatment for severe pain in the 1920s, as it remains in many circumstances today. A man in his late sixties with gallstones and chronic asthma, living hundreds of miles from a hospital, might very reasonably be given it by a doctor, and might very reasonably take it. That he took it in order to go on working, rather than in order to escape, was in their view a sign of his devotion, not a failure of it.

What Can Fairly Be Said

A biography written nearly a century later cannot settle whether Studd was, in the medical sense, dependent on morphine. Anyone who takes the drug regularly for a long period becomes physically dependent on it; that is how it works, and it is not a moral failure. Whether his use went beyond what his pain required, and whether it affected his judgement, his moods or his relations with others, cannot be known from the sources available here. It would be unjust to assume the worst, and dishonest to pretend there is nothing to discuss.

Some things can fairly be said. The first is that there is no sign that Studd tried to hide it. He was not a man who did things in secret, the people around him knew, and his family recorded it. The second is that he lived in genuine and often severe pain, and that the Bible nowhere forbids the use of medicine to relieve it. Paul told Timothy, who seems to have suffered from stomach trouble, to “use a little wine for thy stomach’s sake and thine often infirmities” (1 Timothy 5:23, ASV). The principle is plain enough. Christians are not called to refuse the help of medicine. The third is that a drug such as morphine, taken over a long period by an old, sick and isolated man, may well have affected his temper and judgement, and that some of the harshness of his last years may have owed something to it, as well as to pain, exhaustion and grief. That is not certain, but it is possible, and it should make those who judge him a little more careful.

The fourth thing to be said is about the people who criticised him. Some of them were right to be concerned, and right to say so. A mission’s leader is accountable for his conduct, and a drug that affects the mind is not a private matter in a leader. But some of the criticism also seems to have been unkind, and to have been used as a weapon in quarrels that had other causes. Studd had made enemies by his severity. When he became weak, some of them were not gentle with him. Paul wrote to the Galatians, “Brethren, even if a man be overtaken in any trespass, ye who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1, ASV). That instruction applies whether or not Studd’s morphine was a trespass at all.

It is also worth remembering that Studd was not the only person at Ibambi who suffered. His colleagues, many of them young, lived with malaria, dysentery and exhaustion, and some of them saw their own health ruined. The Congolese Christians among whom he lived had far less access to medicine than he did, and their pain, which was at least as great as his, was seldom relieved by anything at all. A balanced account of his last years must hold all of that together.

Above all, it is worth remembering that Studd’s last years were years of genuine suffering, borne far from home, without his wife, and with very few comforts. Whatever view one takes of the morphine, the pain was real. The psalmist prayed, “Have mercy upon me, O Jehovah; for I am withered away: O Jehovah, heal me; for my bones are troubled” (Psalm 6:2, ASV). It is a prayer that Studd, in his last years, had every reason to pray, and those who judge him should remember that it is a prayer most of us will one day pray as well.

Morphine in the 1920s

To understand the controversy, it helps to know how morphine was regarded in Studd’s last years. Morphine had been isolated from opium early in the nineteenth century, and with the invention of the hypodermic syringe it had become the most powerful painkiller available to medicine. It was widely prescribed, and widely abused. By the early twentieth century governments had become alarmed at the spread of addiction, and a series of international agreements, beginning with the Hague Opium Convention of 1912 and continuing with the Geneva conventions of the 1920s, sought to control the trade in opium, morphine and cocaine. In Britain the Dangerous Drugs Act of 1920 brought morphine under strict legal control.

By the late 1920s, therefore, morphine was both an ordinary medicine and a dangerous drug, surrounded by laws, suspicion and moral alarm. Doctors prescribed it freely for severe pain, but anyone who used it regularly outside a hospital was likely to be suspected of addiction. A missionary who carried his own supply into a colony, and used it daily in the forest, was bound to attract attention.

None of this settles the question of Studd’s own use. It does show why the matter became so explosive, and why, in the climate of the time, both his critics and his defenders felt so strongly about it.

A Strange Irony

There is an irony in this part of the story that is hard to miss. The Studd family’s fortune had come from India, the same country that grew the opium the British exported to China. As a young man Studd had worked in a Chinese province where opium ruined many families, and where Chinese Christians ran refuges for addicts. Now, at the end of his life, he was himself taking morphine, a drug made from the same plant, every day.

It would be cheap to make too much of that irony, and cruel to make it a judgement. But it is a reminder that no human life is as tidy as a sermon, and that the great missionaries of the past were bound up, in ways they did not always see, with the world of empire, trade and medicine around them. Studd was a man of his time in his drugs as in much else.

The Inward Man

Paul knew what it was to be ill. He spoke of “a thorn in the flesh” that God would not take away, though he prayed three times, and of God’s reply: “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9, ASV). He spoke of the outward man decaying, and the inward man being renewed day by day.

In Studd’s last years, the outward man was decaying fast. Whether the inward man was being renewed is a question about which those who knew him disagreed. His family and closest colleagues believed that it was; that the old man in pain at Ibambi, writing, praying and translating late into the night, was more surrendered to God than ever. His critics saw a man whose virtues had turned hard and whose weaknesses had become a scandal. Perhaps both were partly right. The gospel does not promise that God’s servants will grow more attractive as they grow older and sicker. It promises that his grace will be sufficient. It was sufficient for Studd in the sense that matters most: he did not give up, and he did not stop trusting. Whether it made him gentle is a different question, and the next chapter will not make it easier.

fields.title: The Committee
fields.body_html:
“Where no wise guidance is, the people falleth; But in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.”

— Proverbs 11:14, ASV

Two Centres

From the beginning, the Heart of Africa Mission had two centres. One was at Highland Road in Upper Norwood, where Priscilla Studd and the home staff dealt with money, candidates, publicity and supporters. The other was wherever Studd happened to be in the Congo. As long as Priscilla lived, the two were held together by her loyalty to her husband and her standing with the mission’s friends. When she died in January 1929, that bond was broken.

The mission’s home affairs were overseen by a committee, as was usual for missionary societies of the period. Its members were men and women of standing in the evangelical world who had lent their names and their time to the work, and who felt responsible to its supporters for the way the mission was run. By the late 1920s many of them were deeply troubled. They had heard of the quarrels in the field, the resignations and dismissals, and the dismissal of Alfred Buxton. They had read the D.C.D. booklet and been alarmed by it. They had heard about the morphine. And they knew that the founder of the mission, now an old and sick man thousands of miles away, would accept no one’s authority but his own.

The Breaking Point

The crisis came in 1930 and 1931. The full story has never been told from the committee’s side, and the sources available to this book are mostly those of the Studd family, so what follows must be read with that in mind.

According to these accounts, the committee decided that Studd could no longer continue as leader of the mission, and planned to confront him and remove him from the leadership of the work he had founded. Norman Grubb, who had come home from the Congo and whom Studd had designated as his successor, found himself shuttling between the two sides, trying to keep the mission together while defending his father-in-law. When it became clear that the committee intended to act, Grubb and another of Studd’s sons-in-law, Colonel David Munro, the husband of Studd’s eldest daughter Grace, took the mission’s records from the headquarters, so that control of the mission would remain in the hands of those loyal to Studd. Grubb maintained that he had legal authority to do so, as Studd’s nominated successor while Studd still lived. In later life he told the story with relish and some comedy. It was, all the same, a painful and bitter episode, in which a Christian mission split along lines of personal loyalty, and in which people who had worked together for years ended on opposite sides.

The Split

The split was real and costly. A large part of the home staff, and a considerable number of missionaries, left the mission. In 1931, according to the history of the society they formed, thirty-six missionaries who had been serving in the Belgian Congo and Brazil, the mission’s two main fields, reorganised themselves as a new body, the Unevangelized Fields Mission. That society’s own brief history does not dwell on the causes, but the timing and the fields involved leave little doubt that it came out of the same crisis. That mission grew in its turn and continues today under another name; it has long cooperated with the society it came from.

The Worldwide Evangelisation Crusade was left very small. When Grubb took over its leadership, he later recalled, there were about thirty-five missionaries on its books, and for one month that year the mission had an income of about one pound a week. Its reputation in Britain was damaged, its supporters divided, and its founder near death in the Congo.

Who Was Right?

It is natural to want to take sides, and most of the books about Studd take his. In their telling the committee were cautious, worldly people who could not understand a man of faith, and Grubb and Munro saved the mission by their boldness. There is some truth in that. Studd’s mission had been founded on faith and obedience, not on committees, and those who wanted to control it from London did not always understand what they were trying to control. Without the courage of those who stayed loyal, WEC might not have survived.

But the committee also had real reasons for concern, and some of them were the same concerns expressed by the Dictionary of African Christian Biography long afterwards. They saw a mission whose founder could not work with others, who dismissed colleagues for disagreeing with him, whose public language offended many Christians, and who was ill and taking morphine. They were responsible for the mission’s good name and for the welfare of its missionaries. It is hard to see what else they could have done except try to change its leadership. It is also hard to see how Studd, being who he was, could have accepted that.

The proverb at the head of this chapter says, “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.” Studd never had much use for counsellors. He believed that God spoke to him directly, and he acted on what he heard. That conviction had carried him to China and Africa, and it had done great good. Studd had spent his life leading and never learned to be led. In 1931 the cost of that came due, and it was paid, very largely, by other people.

One further thing should be said in fairness to both sides. The crisis of 1931 was not only about Studd. It was also about what kind of body a mission should be: a fellowship of people under the direct leadership of a founder who believed he heard from God, or a society with a constitution, a committee and procedures that applied to everyone, including the founder. Both models have their dangers. The first can become a tyranny; the second can become a bureaucracy. The Church has never found a perfect way of holding vision and accountability together. In 1931 the Heart of Africa Mission did not find one either, and the result was a painful division. It is a warning that every Christian work, sooner or later, has to face.

Jesus gave his disciples a pattern for dealing with wrongs between them: “And if thy brother sin against thee, go, show him his fault between thee and him alone: if he hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother” (Matthew 18:15, ASV). The pattern continues with witnesses and then with the church. It is a pattern of patient, personal approach, aimed at winning the brother back, not at defeating him. Neither side in 1931 seems to have found a way to follow it. The distance between London and Ibambi made it almost impossible; the bitterness of the previous years made it harder still. It is a sobering thought that a mission founded to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth could not carry it, in this matter, across its own divisions.

Norman Grubb

The man who emerged from the crisis as leader of the mission deserves a word of his own. Norman Grubb was thirty-five in 1931. He had served as an officer in the First World War and been wounded, had come to the Congo with Pauline in 1920, and had spent most of the decade there, learning Bangala and working on its New Testament. He loved and admired his father-in-law, and he took his side in 1931 without hesitation. He was also, by the accounts of those who worked with him, a very different man in temperament: a thinker and writer, warm and patient, with a gift for drawing people together.

Under his leadership the mission recovered. He wrote the biography of Studd that made his father-in-law famous to a new generation, and many other books besides, and he gave WEC a spirit of faith, fellowship and mutual submission that was in some ways a corrective to Studd’s own style. It is one of the ironies of the story that the best thing to come out of the crisis of Studd’s last year was a mission that worked in a way Studd himself could never quite manage.

Whether in Pretence or in Truth

Paul, in prison, heard that other people were preaching Christ, some of them out of rivalry with him. His answer is one of the most generous passages in his letters. “What then? only that in every way, whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and therein I rejoice, yea, and will rejoice” (Philippians 1:18, ASV).

The split of 1931 left two missions where there had been one. Both went on preaching Christ. The Unevangelized Fields Mission went on to work in Congo, Brazil, Papua and elsewhere. fields.title: Hallelujah
fields.body_html:
“For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure is come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith”

— 2 Timothy 4:6-7, ASV

The Last Work

In the last two years of his life, while the quarrel with the committee in London was coming to its climax, Studd was at Ibambi, ill, often in pain, and working. One of the tasks to which he gave his remaining strength was the translation of Scripture into Kingwana, the form of Swahili spoken across much of the north-eastern Congo. With two colleagues, Stapleton and Lowder, he had begun a version of the New Testament, and in 1930 the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles were published in it.

Kingwana was not the language of a single people. It was a common tongue, used in markets, on the roads and in the posts of the administration across a wide region, and understood by people of many different mother tongues. A Scripture in Kingwana could travel far beyond the stations of one mission, carried by traders, workers and evangelists. Studd, who had always thought in terms of the whole unevangelised world, would have understood the value of that.

It is fitting that the last substantial work of his life was translation. He had never been a linguist, and he had depended on others for much of his life in Africa to speak for him. But he had come to believe that the Congolese church needed the Scriptures in its own hands more than it needed anything a missionary could give. The work was taken further by others after his death. In the Swahili of eastern Congo a New Testament and Psalms appeared in 1955 and a complete Bible in 1960, the year of Congolese independence; how much of Studd’s own draft survived into those later versions is not clear. Studd did not see it. He had helped to begin it.

A Letter to His Grandchildren

In his last year Studd wrote a farewell letter to his grandchildren. It has not been published in full in any source available to this book, and it is not quoted here, except for two lines that he is recorded as including in it:

Only one life, ’twill soon be past,

Only what’s done for Christ will last.

As the introduction explained, there is no good evidence that Studd wrote those lines. The longer poem that is often printed under his name begins by saying that its author had first heard the couplet from someone else, and the couplet itself may be older than any printing of the poem. But he loved them, and he wanted his grandchildren to have them. They sum up the conviction of his whole life better than anything he wrote himself. He had believed for more than fifty years that the only things that would last were the things done for Christ, and he had tried to live as if that were true. He had not always lived it wisely. He had lived it wholeheartedly.

The Last Illness

In the summer of 1931 his health collapsed. The cause of death recorded in the reference works is gallstones, for which he had not had surgical treatment. There seems to have been no hospital within reach of Ibambi that could have operated on him, and it is doubtful whether, at seventy and in his condition, he could have survived the journey to one. Some later writers say that he refused the care his body needed; it is fairer to say that the care his body needed was not available where he had chosen to live and die, and that he had chosen long before not to leave.

He died at Ibambi on 16 July 1931. One genealogical record gives the date as 15 July, but 16 July is the date given by most sources. He was seventy years old.

Those who were with him in his last days, or who heard from those who were, said that his last word was “Hallelujah.” Some accounts say that he repeated it several times. There is no reason to doubt it. It would have been a natural word for him to say at the end. But the reader should know that it comes from the testimony of his family and colleagues, and that nothing else records it. “Hallelujah” means “praise the Lord.” If it was his last word, it was a good one. The book of Revelation imagines the voice of a great multitude, “as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunders, saying, Hallelujah: for the Lord our God, the Almighty, reigneth” (Revelation 19:6, ASV). Studd had spent his life trying to bring more voices into that multitude.

The Funeral

He was buried at Ibambi. Accounts of the funeral agree that a great crowd of Congolese Christians came, many of them from a distance. The numbers given vary: one account says more than a thousand, another two thousand. One account says that four chiefs stood among the mourners. None of these figures comes from a record that can now be checked, but all the accounts agree that the funeral was very large, and that the people who mourned him were above all the Congolese Christians of the forest.

That is the most important fact about the end of his life, and it should not be passed over. Studd had quarrelled with his committee, with many of his missionaries and with members of his own family. He had been a difficult and sometimes harsh leader. But the people for whom he had come to Africa came in their hundreds, perhaps their thousands, to bury him. Whatever they had suffered from his severity, they had also known his love, and they honoured him. Their grief is part of the evidence, and it should weigh as much as the judgements of those who found him impossible.

Studd’s grave is at Ibambi, in what is now Wamba territory in the province of Haut-Uélé. He was never brought home to England, and he lies among the people he had come to serve. In 2013, when the Congolese church that grew out of his mission celebrated a hundred years since his arrival at Niangara, he was remembered there as one of the founders of a church that had long since become entirely Congolese.

The psalm says, “Precious in the sight of Jehovah Is the death of his saints” (Psalm 116:15, ASV). The word “saints” in the Bible does not mean people without faults. It means people set apart for God, and the Old Testament uses it of the whole people of Israel, with all their failings. Studd was a saint in that sense, set apart for God from his youth and given to him to the end. His death, at Ibambi in the forest, far from the cricket grounds and drawing rooms of his youth, was precious in God’s sight. It did not need to be anything more.

The Seven at the End

By 1931 the Cambridge Seven were old men, or dead. William Cassels, who had become the first Anglican bishop of Western China, had died there in 1925. Stanley Smith, the orator of 1885, died in China in January 1931, six months before Studd. Dixon Hoste, the quiet soldier, was still General Director of the China Inland Mission, which he had led since 1902, and would lead it until 1935. The others had gone their different ways, some still in China, some at home.

Of the seven, Studd had stayed in China the shortest time, and ended furthest from it. But in a sense he had remained more faithful than any of them to the original excitement of 1885: the conviction that the best thing a person could do with life was to give it away for the sake of people who had never heard of Christ. The others had settled, in different ways, into long and patient work in one country. Studd had never settled anywhere. He had gone to China, America, India and Africa, and he had died still looking beyond the horizon.

Neither way is simply better. The Church needs the patient builders and the restless pioneers. Studd was a pioneer to the end, with the gifts and the faults of one.

Finished the Course

Paul wrote his second letter to Timothy from prison, knowing he would soon die. “I am already being offered,” he wrote, “and the time of my departure is come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith.” He did not claim to have been perfect, or to have won every battle. He claimed to have finished, and to have kept faith.

Studd could have said the same. He had begun the course at Tedworth in 1878 and lost his way for a while. He had found it again at George’s bedside and run it, from then on, with all his strength: through China, America and India, into the heart of Africa, and to the end. He had stumbled often. He had hurt people. He had been, at times, more like a general than a shepherd. But he had not turned back, and he had not stopped trusting the Christ who had died for him. The crown Paul spoke of was not, he said, for him alone, “but also to all them that have loved his appearing” (2 Timothy 4:8, ASV). Studd had loved it. Whatever else is said about him, that must be said too.

fields.title: Only One Life
fields.body_html:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a grain of wheat fall into the earth and die, it abideth by itself alone; but if it die, it beareth much fruit.”

— John 12:24, ASV

After the Funeral

When Studd died in July 1931, the mission he had founded seemed close to collapse. It had been split. Its home organisation had largely walked away. It had perhaps thirty-five missionaries and almost no money. Its founder’s reputation had been damaged by quarrels, by his language and by the controversy over his morphine. Many observers in the evangelical world expected it to fade away.

It did not. Norman Grubb took over the leadership and, in a style very different from his father-in-law’s, rebuilt it. He was a gifted writer and teacher, and he gave the mission a theology of faith and fellowship that drew a new generation of recruits. By the time he retired in 1965, according to the Dictionary of African Christian Biography, WEC had grown from that faltering band of about thirty to some eight hundred missionaries in twenty countries. It has continued to grow. Today WEC International works in many countries around the world, with workers drawn from many nations, including, increasingly, from the churches of Africa, Asia and Latin America that missions like it helped to found.

The Forest Church

In the Congo, the work went on. In 1934 a missionary named Jack Harrison, known to the Congolese as Bwana Harri, began a Bible school at Ibambi to train Congolese pastors and evangelists. In the 1930s a revival broke out among the Budu at the village of Imbai, which the mission’s own accounts connect with the prayers of two missionary sisters, Lily and Ivy Roberts. In the early 1950s a fresh movement of the Spirit came to Ibambi and the surrounding stations. Norman Grubb, writing at the time, said that it came there, as at Wamba and Opienge, through the visit of an evangelist and his wife from Lubutu. In the mission writing of the time an “evangelist” almost always meant an African Christian worker, and there is every reason to think that this couple were Congolese. The revival that renewed the church Studd had founded was carried to it by Africans, as so much of the church’s growth had been from the beginning.

In the early 1950s the missionary doctor Helen Roseveare built a hospital and training centre in the area, and trained Congolese nurses and medical workers who carried health care into the villages. In 1964 the Simba rebellion swept through the region, and missionaries and Congolese Christians suffered imprisonment, violence and death. The church survived it. Today, as the Communauté Évangélique du Christ au Cœur d’Afrique, it is a large, self-governing Congolese church, with its centre at Isiro, its own pastors and leaders, and members counted in the hundreds of thousands. Studd lies buried at Ibambi among them.

His Words Today

Studd’s writings are still in print, nearly a century after his death. The Chocolate Soldier is reprinted by Christian publishers and read aloud in sermons. The rhyme about a rescue shop within a yard of hell, always credited to him, appears on posters, mugs and the walls of youth centres. The couplet beginning “Only one life,” which he loved but did not write, is one of the most quoted lines in evangelical Christianity, and the saying traditionally attributed to him, “If Jesus Christ be God and died for me, then no sacrifice can be too great for me to make for Him,” is quoted more often still.

That popularity is a sign of how much his life still speaks. It is also a reason for care. Some of those words cannot be traced to anything he published, and one of them he almost certainly did not write. Studd himself would not have minded. He cared nothing for his own reputation as a writer, and he would gladly have had his name taken off anything, so long as the message got through. But a life that has been reduced to a handful of quotations is easy to admire and hard to understand. The quotations show the fire. They do not show the cost, either to him or to those around him, and they do not show the people, in China, India and the Congo, whose own faith and courage were the real fruit of his life.

How to Remember Him

There are two easy ways to remember C. T. Studd, and both are wrong.

The first is to remember only the hero: the cricketer who gave up the Ashes for China, the young man who gave away a fortune, the old man who went to Africa to die. That Studd is real, and he deserves to be remembered. But on his own he becomes a kind of reproach, impossible to imitate and therefore easy to admire and forget. And he hides the people who paid for his heroism, among them his wife, his daughters, his colleagues, and many Congolese Christians who bore his severity.

The second is to remember only the problem: the domineering founder, the morphine, the quarrels, the dismissed son-in-law, the split mission. That Studd is real too, and his failures should be studied. But on his own he becomes a cautionary tale, and the caution is too easily turned into an excuse. It is very comfortable to decide that, because Studd went too far, it is wise not to go anywhere at all.

The truth is harder and more useful. Studd was a man who took the words of Jesus with complete seriousness, and gave everything he had in obedience to them. That is the heart of his life, and it is why he is still remembered. He was also a man whose zeal was not always governed by love, and who could not bear to be told he was wrong. That is the warning of his life. Both are true at once. The second does not cancel the first, and the first does not excuse the second.

The Grain of Wheat

Jesus spoke of a grain of wheat that falls into the earth and dies. If it does not die, it abides alone. If it dies, it bears much fruit. He was speaking first of his own death, and of the life that would come from it. He went on to apply it to his followers: “He that loveth his life loseth it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal” (John 12:25, ASV).

Studd’s life was a grain of wheat in that sense. He let go of his fortune, his fame, his health, his comfort, and in the end his life, in the conviction that only what was done for Christ would last. The fruit is real. It can be counted in the students who went overseas after hearing the Cambridge Seven, in the thousands of missionaries who have served with WEC, and above all in the Congolese church that grew in the forest where he is buried.

But the image of the grain of wheat also says something else. The fruit does not come from the grain. It comes from the life of God working in the soil after the grain has gone into it. Studd planted. Others watered: Priscilla, Buxton, Grubb, Harrison, Roseveare, and, above all, countless Congolese pastors, evangelists and believers whose names are known to God if not to us. God gave the increase. Studd would have been the first to say so. “I planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase. So then neither is he that planteth anything, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6-7, ASV).

Above all, his life asks a question that every reader must answer for himself or herself. It is not whether one should give everything to Christ; the New Testament settles that. It is how to give everything to Christ in a way that also honours the people around us: the spouse, the children, the colleagues, the people among whom we live and work. Studd answered the first question magnificently. He answered the second less well. Those who take his life seriously will want to learn from both.

And it asks one more thing of the Church that tells his story. It asks that the story be told whole, with the Congolese and Chinese believers, the wife, the daughters and the colleagues kept in view alongside the hero. A life is never lived alone, and the fruit of a life is never the work of one person. If Studd’s story is told in that way, it becomes not a monument to one man’s sacrifice but a picture of the body of Christ at work, with all its gifts and all its wounds. That is a picture worth keeping.

Only One Life

The lines he is recorded as sending his grandchildren in his last year, borrowed rather than his own, are the best summary of what he believed: “Only one life, ’twill soon be past, Only what’s done for Christ will last.” They are a challenge to every reader, as they were to him. Each of us has one life. It will soon be past. The question is what we will do with it.

Studd’s answer was everything. He gave it gladly, and he did not count the cost. His life suggests that the answer is right, and also that it must be given in love, with patience, and with humility enough to hear the counsel of others. A life given to Christ with all its strength but without love is, as Paul says, nothing. A life given to Christ with all its strength and love besides is the best thing a human being can do with the one life he has. Studd reached for that, and often grasped it, and sometimes missed it. He would want his readers to reach further, and to do it with more love than he did.

fields.title: Appendix A: Lessons from the Life of C. T. Studd
fields.body_html:
“Remember them that had the rule over you, men that spake unto you the word of God; and considering the issue of their life, imitate their faith.”

— Hebrews 13:7, ASV

The lessons below gather the themes of this book so that readers can return to them. C. T. Studd would not have wanted his life to be a pattern; he would have wanted it to point to Christ. Each lesson therefore rests on Scripture, not on his example alone. The letter to the Hebrews tells us to consider how those who went before us lived and died, and to imitate their faith, not every detail of their lives. In Studd’s case, some of the lessons are warnings.

1. Conversion Must Become Consecration

Studd was converted at eighteen and then, by his own account, lived for six years as if it made little difference. A faith that costs nothing is in danger of becoming nothing. “I have this against thee, that thou didst leave thy first love. Remember therefore whence thou art fallen, and repent and do the first works” (Revelation 2:4-5, ASV).

2. God Uses Crises to Wake Us

His brother’s illness showed him what his fame was worth. Hard providences are often God’s mercy in disguise. “This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God” (John 11:4, ASV).

3. Gifts Are for Giving

He loved cricket and played it superbly, and he did not despise it when he gave it up. Every gift is from God and may be offered back to him. “Every man that striveth in the games exerciseth self-control in all things. Now they do it to receive a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible” (1 Corinthians 9:25, ASV).

4. Obedience May Grieve Those We Love

His family opposed his going to China, and later his wife opposed his going to Africa. Following Christ can divide even loving homes, but it must never be an excuse for unkindness. “He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37, ASV).

5. The Messenger Must Become a Learner

In China he put on Chinese clothes and sat down to learn a hard language. The gospel crosses cultures through servants, not masters. “For though I was free from all men, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more” (1 Corinthians 9:19, ASV).

6. Treasure Is Found With Joy

He gave away a fortune and never regretted it. Generosity is not loss when the treasure is Christ. “In his joy he goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field” (Matthew 13:44, ASV).

7. Remember Where Wealth Comes From

His family’s money came from indigo grown by Indian labour, and much of it went back to India and to the poor. Christians who have inherited advantage should ask what they owe. “Charge them that are rich in this present world, that they be not highminded … that they be rich in good works, that they be ready to distribute” (1 Timothy 6:17-18, ASV).

8. Marriage Is a Partnership in the Work

Priscilla was a missionary in her own right, and without her there would have been no Heart of Africa Mission. Honour the partners whose work is done out of sight. “Salute Prisca and Aquila my fellow-workers in Christ Jesus” (Romans 16:3, ASV).

9. Small Graves Are Part of the Story

The Studds buried two infant sons, and their grandson lies at Nala. Missionary heroism has always had a hidden price, paid by families. “Jehovah gave, and Jehovah hath taken away; blessed be the name of Jehovah” (Job 1:21, ASV).

10. The Church Belongs to the People of the Land

In Shanxi and in the Congo, the church was built above all by Chinese and Congolese believers. Missionaries plant; local Christians carry the word. “From you hath sounded forth the word of the Lord … in every place” (1 Thessalonians 1:8, ASV).

11. Go Where Christ Is Not Named

He spent his last years among peoples who had very little Christian witness. That priority still matters. “Making it my aim so to preach the gospel, not where Christ was already named” (Romans 15:20, ASV).

12. Age and Weakness Are Not Final

He went to Africa at fifty-two, with asthma and broken health, and served for eighteen years. God is not limited by our limits. “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9, ASV).

13. Courage Without Love Profits Nothing

Studd gave his goods and his body, but some who worked with him did not feel loved. Sacrifice is not the same as love. “If I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but have not love, it profiteth me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3, ASV).

14. Speak the Truth, but Season It

His tracts woke many and wounded many. Strong words have their place, but grace must govern them. “Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt” (Colossians 4:6, ASV).

15. Do Not Recruit by Shame

The language of the recruiting sergeant can bring people to the field and break them there. Christ calls disciples by love, not by contempt. “Not of constraint, but willingly … neither as lording it over the charge allotted to you, but making yourselves ensamples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2-3, ASV).

16. Disagreement Is Not Disloyalty

He dismissed Alfred Buxton for trying to make peace. Leaders must learn to hear those who differ from them. “Faithful are the wounds of a friend” (Proverbs 27:6, ASV).

17. Every Leader Needs Counsel

He found it very hard to work inside any structure he did not control, and his mission nearly broke apart. Vision needs accountability. “Where no wise guidance is, the people falleth; But in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Proverbs 11:14, ASV).

18. Rest Is Also a Gift

He rose early and worked late for years, and expected others to do the same. God does not need our exhaustion. “It is vain for you to rise up early, To take rest late, To eat the bread of toil; For so he giveth unto his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2, ASV).

19. Judge the Suffering Gently

His use of morphine in his last years was criticised harshly. Christians should neither excuse wrongdoing nor condemn the sick without mercy. “Restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to thyself, lest thou also be tempted” (Galatians 6:1, ASV).

20. God Works Through Quarrels

The split of 1931 left two missions where there had been one, and both went on preaching Christ. God is not defeated by the failures of his servants. “Whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and therein I rejoice” (Philippians 1:18, ASV).

21. Finish the Course

For all his faults, he did not turn back. Faithfulness to the end is itself a gift of grace. “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith” (2 Timothy 4:7, ASV).

22. Only One Life

He loved the couplet he is recorded as sending to his grandchildren, lines not of his own making: “Only one life, ’twill soon be past, Only what’s done for Christ will last.” The question it asks belongs to every reader. “And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever” (1 John 2:17, ASV).

fields.title: Appendix B: Chapter-by-Chapter Study and Reflection Guide
fields.body_html:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deluding your own selves.”

— James 1:22, ASV

This guide is for personal reflection, small groups, or a reading course of about twenty-four weeks. Its purpose is not to make C. T. Studd an object of admiration or of blame, but to let his life hold up a mirror in which readers can examine their own discipleship under Scripture. Groups may find it helpful to begin each session with the chapter’s opening verse and to end with prayer. Several chapters raise hard questions about money, family, leadership, empire and illness. They are meant to be discussed honestly, not settled quickly.

Introduction - The Cricketer, the Crusader, and the Record

Central idea

The real Studd, heroic and difficult, is more useful to the Church than either the legend of total surrender or the cautionary tale.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 18:17; John 8:32.

Reflection

1. Why do we prefer our heroes simple? 2. How should we treat famous sayings whose source is unknown?

Chapter 1 - A Goodly Heritage

Central idea

Studd grew up with every advantage, on a fortune made from Indian labour, in a world that prized manliness and despised weakness.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 16:5-8; Mark 10:21-22; 1 Timothy 4:8.

Reflection

1. What advantages have you inherited, and from whose labour? 2. Which values of your upbringing have you never examined?

Chapter 2 - The Squire Who Sold His Horses

Central idea

A father’s late conversion and short, wholehearted Christian life opened the door for his sons.

Scriptures to revisit

Acts 16:31-34; John 3:16; John 5:24; Mark 4:18-19.

Reflection

1. Whose prayers lie behind your faith? 2. What “thorns” are choking the word in your life?

Chapter 3 - Fenner’s and the Oval

Central idea

Studd gave cricket the discipline he did not yet give to God, in a game divided by class.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Corinthians 9:24-27; James 2:1-5.

Reflection

1. What receives your best effort? 2. Where do you expect deference because of who you are?

Chapter 4 - “This Sickness Is Not unto Death”

Central idea

At his brother’s bedside he saw what fame was worth, and he returned to his first love.

Scriptures to revisit

John 11:1-4; Revelation 2:4-5; Matthew 10:37.

Reflection

1. Has a crisis ever shown you what really matters? 2. How do you weigh the objections of a loving family against a sense of call?

Chapter 5 - The Seven

Central idea

Seven privileged young men answered the call to China, and their example stirred students on both sides of the Atlantic.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 6:1-8; 1 Corinthians 1:26-29.

Reflection

1. Why did the Seven attract so much attention? 2. Who are the unnamed workers whose service no one publicises?

Chapter 6 - In Chinese Dress

Central idea

The China Inland Mission taught Studd to become a learner and a servant in a church that Chinese Christians were already leading.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Corinthians 9:19-23; Philippians 2:5-7.

Reflection

1. Where are you a beginner, and how does it feel? 2. What would it mean to serve as a guest rather than a master?

Chapter 7 - Treasure in a Field

Central idea

He gave away his inheritance with joy, to people who themselves lived by faith among the poor.

Scriptures to revisit

Matthew 13:44; 1 Timothy 6:17-19; Acts 20:35.

Reflection

1. Was his gift wise, and does that question matter? 2. What would it mean for you to be “ready to distribute”?

Chapter 8 - Scilla

Central idea

Priscilla Stewart was a missionary in her own right, and the marriage began with a shared choice to depend on God alone.

Scriptures to revisit

Romans 16:3-4; Acts 18:24-26; Ecclesiastes 4:9-12.

Reflection

1. How can a marriage be a partnership in God’s work? 2. Whose labour behind the scenes makes your own possible?

Chapter 9 - Lungan

Central idea

Years of hostility, small results, broken health and two infant graves were part of the cost of sowing in China.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 126:5-6; Job 1:21; Psalm 34:18.

Reflection

1. How do you measure faithfulness when results are few? 2. What do you make of the Chinese Christians who stayed in 1900?

Chapter 10 - Students and Soldiers

Central idea

In the quieter years in America and India he kept preaching, while growing restless for the unreached.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Timothy 4:1-5; Romans 15:20.

Reflection

1. How do you serve in seasons with no great venture? 2. Is restlessness always a sign of God’s call?

Chapter 11 - A Notice in Liverpool

Central idea

A provocative notice and an explorer’s report sent an ill man of nearly fifty to the Sudan, and began a pattern of struggle with committees.

Scriptures to revisit

Romans 10:13-15; Acts 13:1-3; Acts 14:26-27.

Reflection

1. How should Christians speak about peoples they do not know? 2. What does it mean to be sent by a church, and not only by God?

Chapter 12 - The Heart of Africa

Central idea

He went to the Congo against medical advice and his wife’s wishes, into a land only just released from the terror of the Free State.

Scriptures to revisit

Hebrews 11:8-10; Matthew 6:33; Philippians 4:19.

Reflection

1. How should a married Christian decide when a spouse disagrees about a call? 2. What does faith look like when it depends on the faith of others?

Chapter 13 - Niangara

Central idea

An honest witness shows the first year of the mission, including the habits of a master that the gospel calls us to lay down.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 4:5; Matthew 20:25-28; Proverbs 27:6.

Reflection

1. What did you make of the name Bwana and of required attendance at prayers? 2. What critics might help you see yourself more clearly?

Chapter 14 - The Chocolate Soldier

Central idea

His call to heroism was powerful, and it borrowed the language of wartime recruitment in ways that could wound.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Timothy 2:3-4; Matthew 20:28.

Reflection

1. Where is your faith a “chocolate soldier”? 2. When does a call to courage become a call by shame?

Chapter 15 - Nala and Ibambi

Central idea

The mission grew in the forest country among peoples who had already lived through a generation of upheaval and colonial demands.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 127:1-2; Isaiah 9:2.

Reflection

1. Why does it matter what the mission found when it came? 2. How do you hold together hard work and trust in God?

Chapter 16 - The Church in the Forest

Central idea

The word sounded forth from Congolese Christians, in their own languages, through their own evangelists, at their own cost.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Thessalonians 1:6-8; Revelation 7:9-10; 1 Corinthians 3:6-7.

Reflection

1. Whose names are missing from the stories you tell about your church? 2. What does self-support mean for a poor church?

Chapter 17 - The Crusade

Central idea

His vision for the whole world was a great gift; his language grew so extreme that it became hard to correct him.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Corinthians 4:10; Colossians 4:6; Ephesians 4:15, 29.

Reflection

1. What did the Crusade get right? 2. Is there a register of speech you use too often?

Chapter 18 - A Sharp Contention

Central idea

The dismissal of Alfred Buxton shows how virtues can harden into vices, and how God works even through quarrels.

Scriptures to revisit

Acts 15:36-41; 2 Timothy 4:11; 1 Corinthians 13:4-7; 3 John 9-10.

Reflection

1. When has disagreement been treated as disloyalty in your experience? 2. Is there a Mark you need to welcome back?

Chapter 19 - A Short Visit

Central idea

Twelve years of separation and one brief reunion were part of the cost of the work, borne above all by Priscilla.

Scriptures to revisit

Song of Solomon 8:6-7; 1 Corinthians 7:5; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-14; Ephesians 6:4.

Reflection

1. Where is the line between shared sacrifice and neglect? 2. How can the Church honour those whose service is unseen?

Chapter 20 - The Thorn and the Needle

Central idea

His use of morphine in pain and old age should be judged with honesty and with mercy.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 4:16-18; 2 Corinthians 12:7-10; 1 Timothy 5:23; Galatians 6:1-2.

Reflection

1. How should Christians speak about leaders who are ill? 2. What does it mean that grace is sufficient?

Chapter 21 - The Committee

Central idea

The crisis of 1931 split the mission, and showed the danger of vision without accountability.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 11:14; Hebrews 13:17; Philippians 1:15-18.

Reflection

1. Who was right in 1931, and why is that hard to say? 2. To whom are you accountable?

Chapter 22 - Hallelujah

Central idea

He died at his post, translating Scripture and praising God, and the Congolese church came in great numbers to bury him.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Timothy 4:6-8; Revelation 19:6; Psalm 116:15.

Reflection

1. What does it mean to finish the course? 2. Why does the grief of the Congolese Christians matter to the story?

Chapter 23 - Only One Life

Central idea

His life was a grain of wheat that bore real fruit, and it warns that zeal must be governed by love.

Scriptures to revisit

John 12:24-26; 1 Corinthians 3:6-7; 1 John 2:17.

Reflection

1. What in his life would you imitate, and what would you avoid? 2. What will you do with your one life?

fields.title: Appendix C: Chronology of the Life and Times of C. T. Studd
fields.body_html:
“So teach us to number our days, That we may get us a heart of wisdom.”

— Psalm 90:12, ASV

The dates below are meant as orientation. Dates confirmed by published records, such as cricket scores, are given plainly. Where the sources disagree, the disagreement is noted. Where a date rests only on the family’s accounts, it is marked as approximate or traditional.

1819 - Edward Studd

Studd’s father is born in Bombay on 25 December. He later makes a fortune as an indigo planter in Tirhut, Bihar.

1856 - A Second Marriage

Edward Studd marries Dorothy Sophia (Dora) Thomas at Bedford. Their sons include Kynaston (born 1858) and George (born 1859).

1860 - Birth

Charles Thomas Studd is born on 2 December at Spratton, Northamptonshire, the third son of Edward and Dora Studd.

1865 - The China Inland Mission

J. Hudson Taylor founds the China Inland Mission.

1866 - Salamander

Edward Studd’s horse Salamander wins the Grand National.

1871 - Tedworth

Edward Studd takes the lease of Tedworth House, Wiltshire, where he lays out a racecourse and a cricket ground.

c. 1875 - Edward Studd Converted

Edward Studd is converted at one of D. L. Moody’s meetings in London, most probably during the London campaign of 1875 (sources give dates from 1874 to 1877). He gives up racing and opens Tedworth to evangelistic meetings.

1877 - Edward Studd Dies

He dies in July, most sources say on 27 July (one gives 1876).

1878 - Conversion

In the summer holidays a visitor at Tedworth speaks to the three eldest brothers; Charlie is converted, by family tradition on the same day as Kynaston and George.

1879 - Cambridge

He leaves Eton, where by his biographers’ account he captained the eleven, and goes up to Trinity College, Cambridge. He plays for Middlesex from 1879 and for Cambridge from 1880.

1882 - The Ashes

Cambridge University beat the Australians at Fenner’s at the end of May; Studd scores 118 and 17 not out. He scores a further century against the Australians for MCC. On 14 August he completes 1,000 runs and 100 wickets for the season, the second player to do so after W. G. Grace. On 28–29 August he plays for England at the Oval (0 and 0 not out); Australia win by seven runs. On 2 September The Sporting Times prints its mock obituary of English cricket.

1882-1883 - Australia

He tours Australia with Ivo Bligh’s team and plays in four Tests; England win the series against Murdoch’s side. His last Test ends in February 1883. Career Test record: five matches, 160 runs, three wickets.

1883 - Captain and Graduate

He captains Cambridge and takes his degree. In November his brother George falls dangerously ill and recovers.

1883-1884 - Restored

He hears Moody again in London and returns to wholehearted faith. During 1884 he offers himself to the China Inland Mission.

1885 - The Cambridge Seven

The Seven tour universities in England and Scotland. Farewell meeting at Exeter Hall, 4 February; they leave London on 5 February and reach Shanghai on 18 March. Studd travels west towards the Han River, and later works in Shanxi. On 2 December he turns twenty-five.

1885-1886 - Across the Atlantic

Kynaston Studd tours American colleges; John R. Mott hears him at Cornell in January 1886. The Student Volunteer Movement begins at Mount Hermon in 1886.

1886 - A Missionary Band

Benjamin Broomhall publishes the record of the Seven, enlarged in 1887 as The Evangelisation of the World.

1887 - The Gift

Traditionally on 13 January, he gives away the bulk of his inheritance, reported at between £25,000 and £29,000, including about £5,000 each to Moody, Müller, George Holland and Booth-Tucker. Priscilla Stewart arrives in China with “the Hundred.”

1888 - Marriage

He marries Priscilla Livingstone Stewart, most accounts say at Tianjin on 7 April, before a Chinese pastor. She gives the £3,400 he had kept for her to the Salvation Army. They settle at Lungan (Lu’an, now Changzhi), Shanxi.

1889-1894 - Daughters and Sons

Grace (1889), Dorothy (9 July 1891), Edith (1892) and Pauline (10 February 1894) are born. Two sons die in infancy.

1894 - Home

With their health broken, the family returns to England, handing over their Lungan property to the Mission.

1896-1897 - America

He tours American universities for the Student Volunteer Movement for about eighteen months.

1900 - The Boxer Year

Missionaries and Chinese Christians are killed in Shanxi; the China Inland Mission loses 58 missionaries and 21 children. The Studds go to India.

1900-1906 - Ootacamund

He is pastor of the Union Church, Ootacamund (one account says seven years).

1906 - England

He returns to England in poor health and speaks at meetings.

1908 - Liverpool

He sees a notice about Africa and hears Karl Kumm speak.

1908 - The Belgian Congo

The Belgian state takes over the Congo Free State after an international campaign against its atrocities.

1910-1911 - The Sudan

He travels to the southern Sudan, concludes that the north-eastern Congo has no Protestant witness, and returns in 1911.

1912 - The Heart of Africa Mission

He applies to the Africa Inland Mission in November; the membership is ended by agreement within weeks of his departure. At the end of the year the Heart of Africa Mission is formed, with headquarters at 17 Highland Road, Upper Norwood. The Chocolate Soldier is usually dated to this year, though its published text refers to the Great War.

1913 - To the Congo

He sails with Alfred Buxton, most accounts say on 30 January, and travels through East Africa and Uganda to Lake Albert. They reach Niangara on 16 October. Four stations are opened in the next year and a half.

1914 - War

Quaint Rhymes for the Battlefield is published in London. News of the European war reaches Niangara on 19 August. Late in the year he leaves for England because of Priscilla’s illness.

1915 - Christ’s Etceteras

He holds meetings in England and publishes Christ’s Etceteras.

1916 - Return to Africa

He sails for the Congo with Edith and new recruits. So far as the record shows, he never returns to England.

1917 - A Wedding

Edith Studd marries Alfred Buxton in the Congo. The first baptisms are recorded around this time.

1919 - Worldwide Evangelisation Crusade

The mission becomes the Worldwide Evangelisation Crusade; Gilbert Barclay becomes Home Overseer. Pauline marries Norman Grubb.

1920 - The Grubbs

Norman and Pauline Grubb go to the Congo.

c. 1921-1922 - Ibambi

Studd moves his centre from Nala to Ibambi, in Budu country (sources give both years).

1920s - Expansion

New work begins in Amazonia (the Heart of Amazonia Mission), and workers are sent to Arabia and India. Conflicts grow within the Congo field.

c. 1927-1928 - Buxton Dismissed

Alfred Buxton visits America in 1927 to repair relationships; Studd later dismisses him as disloyal.

1928 - D.C.D. and a Visit

He publishes the D.C.D. booklet. Priscilla makes her only visit to the Congo, a short one; it is their last meeting.

1929 - Priscilla Dies

She dies at Málaga, Spain, on 15 January.

1930 - Kingwana

Luke and Acts in Kingwana, begun by Studd with Stapleton and Lowder, are published. The crisis with the London committee deepens.

1931 - Crisis and Death

Stanley Smith dies in China in January. The home committee seeks to remove Studd; Norman Grubb and David Munro take the mission’s records. Thirty-six missionaries from the Congo and Brazil fields form the Unevangelized Fields Mission. Studd dies at Ibambi on 16 July (one record gives 15 July), aged seventy, and is buried there.

1931-1965 - Grubb

Norman Grubb leads WEC, which grows from about thirty missionaries to some eight hundred in twenty countries.

1934 - Ibambi Bible School

Jack Harrison begins a Bible school at Ibambi for Congolese pastors and evangelists.

1960 - Independence

The Congo becomes independent. A complete Bible in the Swahili of eastern Congo is published.

1964 - The Simba Rebellion

Missionaries and Congolese Christians in the north-east suffer violence and captivity; the church survives.

2013 - Centenary

The Congolese church that grew from the mission, CECCA 16, celebrates a hundred years since Studd’s arrival at Niangara.

Conflicts grow within the Congo field. c. 1927-1928 - Buxton Dismissed Alfred Buxton visits America in 1927 to repair relationships; Studd later dismisses him as disloyal. 1928 - D.C.D. and a Visit He publishes the D.C.D. booklet. Priscilla makes her only visit to the Congo, a short one; it is their last meeting. 1929 - Priscilla Dies She dies at Málaga, Spain, on 15 January. 1930 - Kingwana Luke and Acts in Kingwana, begun by Studd with Stapleton and Lowder, are published. The crisis with the London committee deepens. 1931 - Crisis and Death Stanley Smith dies in China in January. The home committee seeks to remove Studd; Norman Grubb and David Munro take the mission’s records. Thirty-six missionaries from the Congo and Brazil fields form the Unevangelized Fields Mission. Studd dies at Ibambi on 16 July (one record gives 15 July), aged seventy, and is buried there. 1931-1965 - Grubb Norman Grubb leads WEC, which grows from about thirty missionaries to some eight hundred in twenty countries. 1934 - Ibambi Bible School Jack Harrison begins a Bible school at Ibambi for Congolese pastors and evangelists. 1960 - Independence The Congo becomes independent. A complete Bible in the Swahili of eastern Congo is published. 1964 - The Simba Rebellion Missionaries and Congolese Christians in the north-east suffer violence and captivity; the church survives. 2013 - Centenary The Congolese church that grew from the mission, CECCA 16, celebrates a hundred years since Studd’s arrival at Niangara.

fields.title: Appendix D: Notes on Sources and Method
fields.body_html:
“it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write unto thee in order … that thou mightest know the certainty concerning the things wherein thou wast instructed.”

— Luke 1:3-4, ASV

This appendix explains where the story told in this book comes from, how the sources were weighed, and which popular claims have been corrected or left open. It is written for readers who want to check the story for themselves, and for anyone who will retell it.

Grubb’s Biography

The standard life of Studd is Norman P. Grubb, C. T. Studd: Cricketer and Pioneer (London, 1933), reissued many times. Grubb was Studd’s son-in-law, his colleague in the Congo, and his successor as leader of WEC. His book is the main source for Studd’s inner life, his letters, and many of the best-known stories about him. It remains in copyright. This biography has therefore not quoted Grubb, has not followed his wording, and has used his book only as a source of facts, chiefly as those facts are reported in modern reference works and studies. Where an important fact appears to rest on Grubb alone, the text says so, or speaks of “the accounts” or “the family tradition.” Grubb’s later book about the Congo field, Christ in Congo Forests (1945), and his recorded reminiscences, as described by later reviewers, have been used in the same way.

Grubb was candid about many of Studd’s faults, including his quarrels and his use of morphine, and much of the hard material in this book ultimately comes from him. He was also a partisan in the crisis of 1931, and his account of it is the account of one side.

Public-Domain Sources

Broomhall. Benjamin Broomhall’s record of the Cambridge Seven, A Missionary Band (London: Morgan and Scott, 1886), enlarged as The Evangelisation of the World (1887), is in the public domain. It is the contemporary record of the Seven’s meetings and testimonies. The scanned editions could not be consulted directly while this book was being prepared, so Studd’s testimony from those years has been given in paraphrase, not quotation. Readers who wish to see his own words should consult the 1886 or 1887 text.

Studd’s own writings. Studd’s tract The Chocolate Soldier, or Heroism—The Lost Chord of Christianity is in the public domain and widely available. It is usually dated 1912, but its published text speaks of the Great War, so the familiar version cannot be earlier than 1914. Quaint Rhymes for the Battlefield (London: James Clarke, 1914), published under the pen-name of a Quondam Cricketer, and Christ’s Etceteras (1915) are also his. The D.C.D. booklet appeared in 1928. Studd’s letters, including his farewell letter to his grandchildren, have not been published in full in any source available to this book; the only words quoted from them are the two lines of verse he is recorded as including in that letter.

Cricket records. Studd’s scores and figures are taken from the standard cricket records, as gathered by CricketArchive and ESPNcricinfo, and from the published accounts of the 1882 Oval Test, including Wisden’s report. The mock obituary of English cricket appeared in The Sporting Times on 2 September 1882.

Other Witnesses and Studies

The diary of Hayes Perkins, who worked at Niangara in 1914, has been published online in instalments. It is the only independent eyewitness account of the mission’s first year used here. It has been used with care, as the view of one observer who did not share all of Studd’s convictions.

The entries on C. T. Studd, Alfred Buxton and Norman Grubb in the Dictionary of African Christian Biography provided the most important modern assessments of Studd’s leadership and of Buxton’s dismissal. A modern article in the Evangelical Times, based on research in the archives of the Africa Inland Mission, is the source for Studd’s brief membership of that mission in 1912–13. H. van ’t Veld’s study of Swahili Bible translation (1966) is the source for the Kingwana translation begun by Studd, Stapleton and Lowder. The histories published by WEC International and by Crossworld, the successor of the Unevangelized Fields Mission, were used for the mission’s later history and for the split of 1931. A modern chronology of Studd’s life compiled by Dorothy Ross was used for orientation. Genealogical records and local histories were used for the Studd family, Tedworth House and the births of the Studd daughters. Eileen Vincent’s life of Priscilla Studd, No Sacrifice Too Great, was not available to this book; it may contain details that would add to or correct what is said here about her.

These modern works remain in copyright, and this book has not reproduced them beyond a very few short quotations, which are attributed in the text.

The Congolese Side

The sources available for this book say very little about the Congolese men and women who were converted through the mission, worked with it, preached for it, and sometimes resisted it. That is a limitation of the sources, not of the people. This book has not invented names, speeches or scenes to fill the gap. It has tried instead to describe, from what is known, the choices and the costs of Congolese Christians, the colonial burdens under which they lived, and the church they built. A fuller history of the Congolese evangelists and pastors of the Heart of Africa Mission, drawing on the memory and records of CECCA 16, remains to be written, and would be a great gift to the wider Church.

Corrections to the Popular Story

His father’s conversion. It is often dated to 1877, the year of Edward Studd’s death. The accounts give dates from 1874 to 1877, but Moody’s great London campaign was in 1875, and the family tradition that Edward lived about two years after his conversion fits that date best.

George’s illness. It is often placed in 1884. The more detailed chronologies place it in November 1883, with Studd’s restoration following in the winter of 1883–84.

The Oval, 1882. Studd made no runs in the match. He was bowled by Spofforth for 0 in the first innings and was left not out, without facing a ball, in the second, when Ted Peate was bowled with England seven runs short.

The fortune. The amount is variously given as £25,000 or £29,000. The four gifts of about £5,000 each are well attested; the rest is less precisely recorded.

The Moody Bible Institute. Studd’s gift to Moody is often said to have founded the Moody Bible Institute. The Institute grew out of Moody’s training work in Chicago, which was being organised at about the time of the gift; it is fairer to say that the gift went to that work, if the usual account is right.

The wedding. Some accounts say that Xi Shengmo (Pastor Hsi) conducted it. This could not be confirmed and is left open.

Lungan. The city where the Studds worked in China is spelled in many ways in the older books, including Lungan-fu and Lungang-fu. It is the city then called Lu’an (Lu-ngan in the China Inland Mission’s spelling), now Changzhi, in south-eastern Shanxi.

The doctors. It is often said that the doctors forbade him to go to Africa. The sources say that he went against medical advice, which is not quite the same thing.

The Chocolate Soldier. It is sometimes called a late tract. It belongs to the beginning of the Africa years, not the end.

His death. Some accounts say that he refused the medical care his body needed. The cause of death was gallstones, for which no surgical treatment was available within reach of Ibambi; the fairer statement is that he had chosen long before not to leave the Congo.

Legends not used. Several dramatic stories told in popular books, including invented dialogue at his conversion, at his proposal and at the handing over of the £3,400, and a story of his cycling past every mission station in Africa in search of the unreached, have no source that could be checked and have not been used.

Quotations

“If Jesus Christ be God and died for me, then no sacrifice can be too great for me to make for Him.” Universally attributed to Studd and wholly in keeping with his life, but no printing in his lifetime has been traced, and the wording varies. It is quoted in this book as the saying traditionally associated with him.

“Some wish to live within the sound of church or chapel bell; I want to run a rescue shop within a yard of hell.” Always attributed to Studd, usually as a rhyme. The original printing has not been traced, and it is not quoted as his in the text.

“Only one life, ’twill soon be past, Only what’s done for Christ will last.” Studd is recorded as quoting this couplet to his grandchildren in a farewell letter in 1931. A longer poem built around it is often printed under his name, but the poem itself says that its author first heard the couplet from someone else, and no evidence has been found that Studd wrote either the couplet or the poem. It should be quoted as lines he loved, not as his composition.

“Hallelujah.” The tradition that this was his last word comes from his family and colleagues. There is no reason to doubt it, but it cannot be checked.

The Dictionary’s verdict. The judgement that he proved an obstinate and unreasonable leader and colleague comes from the Dictionary of African Christian Biography, not from any contemporary, and is given in this book in paraphrase.

Unconfirmed wording. Where the exact words of a source could not be checked against the original text, including the passages of The Chocolate Soldier, the Christ’s Etceteras pamphlet, Studd’s testimony of 1885, Ted Peate’s remark at the Oval and the mock obituary of English cricket, this book gives them in clearly attributed paraphrase rather than in quotation marks. The sayings traditionally attributed to Studd are quoted only where the text labels them as such.

Dates Still Uncertain

Several dates remain uncertain or disputed: the year of Edward Studd’s conversion and the exact date of his death; the date of the wedding at Tianjin; the details and dates of the deaths of the Studds’ two infant sons; whether Studd travelled alone to the Sudan in 1910; the date of sailing in 1913 (30 January in most accounts); the year of the move to Ibambi (1921 or 1922); the date and terms of Alfred Buxton’s dismissal; the length of Priscilla’s visit in 1928; and the day of Studd’s death (16 July in most sources, 15 July in one). The numbers given for the crowd at his funeral, from more than a thousand to two thousand, cannot be checked.

Scripture

All Scripture quotations are from the American Standard Version of 1901, in the public domain, checked against its published text. Words printed in italics in that version, as supplied by the translators, are given here in ordinary type.
